findings.situation: On a 2025 joint return, both spouses filed separate 2024 returns with Schedule D line 21 losses, but only one spouse actually has a carryover because the other's line 21 loss was not smaller than line 16 and line 15 would not have been negative.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 10: Use this worksheet to figure your capital loss carryovers from 2024 to 2025 if your 2024 Schedule D, line 21, is a loss and (a) that loss is a smaller loss than the loss on your 2024 Schedule D, line 16; or (b) if the amount on your 2024 Form 1040... line 15 would be less than zero... Otherwise, you don’t have any carryovers.
findings.why: The question says Yes merely because each 2024 Schedule D line 21 showed a loss, but the IRS text requires an actual carryover; with only one carryover the tool could use that return's figures rather than refuse.

findings.situation: The child spent an equal number of nights with each parent, and the higher-AGI parent signed Form 8332 releasing the claim to the other parent.
findings.irs_text: If the child was with each parent for an equal number of nights, the custodial parent is the parent with the higher adjusted gross income. (i1040gi 2025 p. 20)
findings.why: No parent lived with the child for "more of 2025," so a filer could truthfully answer No even though the release makes the rule apply. The tool would then compute as if no release existed.

findings.situation: The custodial parent signed a release that covers only other years, such as alternate years that skip 2025.
findings.irs_text: The release can be for 1 year, for a number of specified years (for example, alternate years), or for all future years, as specified in the declaration. (p501 2025 p. 22)
findings.why: The question asks whether the parent has "given the right to claim the child" and does not limit this to 2025, so the filer answers Yes. The rule does not apply for 2025, and the tool would compute that case correctly.

findings.situation: Only a post-2008 divorce decree, or a conditional release, gives the other parent the right to claim the child, with no unconditional Form 8332 or equivalent statement.
findings.irs_text: If the divorce decree or separation agreement went into effect after 2008, the noncustodial parent can't include pages from the decree or agreement instead of Form 8332... The form or statement must release the custodial parent's claim to the child without any conditions. (i1040gi 2025 p. 20)
findings.why: The question says Yes for a right given "under a divorce decree or separation agreement" of any date or with conditions. Such a release is not effective, so the normal rules apply, and the tool handles those.

findings.situation: A release was signed, but the child did not get over half of their support from the parents, or was not in either parent's custody for more than half of 2025.
findings.irs_text: 2. The child received over half of the child's support for 2025 from the parents... 3. The child is in custody of one or both of the parents for more than half of 2025. (i1040gi 2025 p. 20)
findings.why: The question asks only about the release, so the filer answers Yes. Without conditions 2 and 3 the special rule does not apply, and the ordinary computation is correct.

findings.situation: It is unclear which parent the child "lived with for more of 2025" when a parent works nights, or when the parents separated during the year.
findings.irs_text: If, due to a parent's nighttime work schedule, a child lives for a greater number of days, but not nights, with the parent who works at night, that parent is treated as the custodial parent... If the parents divorced or separated during the year... the custodial parent is the one with whom the child lived for the greater number of nights during the rest of the year. (p501 2025 p. 22)
findings.why: "Lived with for more of 2025" could mean days, nights, or the whole calendar year. The IRS test counts nights after separation, with a day-based exception for night work, so filers may identify the wrong parent as the one who must have signed.

findings.situation: A child disappeared in mid-2025, but law enforcement did not presume a non-family kidnapping until early 2026, before the return was filed, so the months-lived count could fall to 6 or fewer.
findings.irs_text: "The child is presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family." (p501, 2025, p. 13); "In the year the kidnapping occurred, the child lived with you for more than half of the part of the year before the date of the kidnapping." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The IRS text ties the year to when the kidnapping occurred and sets no deadline for the presumption, but the question asks whether the child was presumed kidnapped "at any time during 2025." This filer could truthfully answer NO, and the tool would then compute the residency lines as false even though the kidnapped-child treatment may apply.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped for a few days in 2025, was returned, and lived with the filer for well over six months anyway.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped ... (even if the child has since been returned)"; IRS: "To meet this test, your child must have lived with you for more than half the year." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The filer must answer YES, but the child meets the residency test on actual time lived, so the months count gives the correct result. The tool refuses a case it computes correctly.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped during 2025 but did not live with the filer for more than half of the part of the year before the kidnapping, or for more than half of the part of the year after the child's return.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child who, at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped, but the following statements must be true." followed by statements 2 and 3 on time lived before the kidnapping and after the return (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question tests only statement 1, so the filer answers YES even though the special treatment is unavailable. The ordinary months count, which the tool computes, would correctly apply if the child also fell short of more than half the year.

findings.situation: A child still presumed kidnapped during 2025 is past the end of the special treatment because the child would have reached age 18, or there was a determination of death, in an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "This treatment applies for all years until the earlier of: 1. The year there is a determination that the child is dead, or 2. The year the child would have reached age 18." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question has no age or death cutoff, so a filer with a continuing presumption answers YES after the treatment has ended. The ordinary months count would correctly decide these lines, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: The person presumed kidnapped was 18 or older, or was a relative such as a sibling, niece, or nephew rather than the filer's own child.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped" (p501, 2025, p. 13); "To meet this test, a child must be: Your son, daughter, stepchild, or foster child, or a descendant ... Your brother, sister, half brother, half sister, stepbrother, or stepsister, or a descendant" (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: "A child" could mean a minor, the filer's own offspring, or anyone who fits the qualifying-child relationship test. Filers in the same situation could therefore answer differently, and the question does not say which meaning applies.

findings.situation: A married dependent who does not file a joint return for 2025, or files a joint return only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid, and is otherwise claimable.
findings.irs_text: If the person is married but doesn’t file a joint return or files a joint return only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid, you may be able to claim that person as a dependent. (i1040gi p. 21, Married person)
findings.why: The question asks whether the person was married at the end of 2025, so it forces YES for this filer even though the IRS permits the dependent claim; the tool then refuses instead of computing the allowed dependency.

findings.situation: A filer provides in-kind support, such as housing, that counts as support, and together with another person provides more than half with no one over half, but no one literally pays more than half of living costs.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: 'provided more than half of your relative’s support'; p. 19: 'provided over half of the person’s support'
findings.why: The question asks about paying 'living costs,' not providing or contributing 'support,' so a filer with in-kind support can truthfully answer NO while the multiple-support rule applies; the tool would then treat the support test as failed.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer’s spouse is one of the multiple supporters but the filer personally is not, so the filer can answer NO to being 'among them' even though the spouse’s support must be covered.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: 'you and another person(s) provided more than half of your relative’s support'
findings.why: The question says 'you' rather than 'you or your spouse'; on a joint return that omission can produce a NO even when the spouse’s contribution creates the multiple-support situation.

findings.situation: The support facts exist (two or more people including the filer together provide more than half, no one over half) but the person is not actually claimed under a multiple support agreement.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: 'special rules may apply that would treat you as having provided over half of the support'
findings.why: The question asks only about support contributions, so a filer without an agreement or claim must still answer YES and is refused although the tool could compute no qualifying relative correctly.

findings.situation: The support facts exist for a person who is not a relative and did not live with the filer all year.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: 'your relative (or a person who lived with you all year as a member of your household)'
findings.why: The question uses only 'this person' and omits the relationship/household condition, so a truthful YES can be given even though the tool would correctly compute that the person is not a qualifying relative.

findings.situation: A custodial parent has released the claim to the child on Form 8332, and the noncustodial parent, with whom the child did not live for more than half of 2025, claims the child.
findings.irs_text: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent... only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents" (i1040gi 2025, p. 20); see also "unless the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents... applies" (p. 21).
findings.why: The noncustodial parent fails the lived-with test and is only treated as having a qualifying child, so the custodial filer can truthfully answer NO to "meet the conditions." The tool then computes dependent.qualifying_child as true for a filer who has released the claim, and the question also does not catch a noncustodial filer whose line computes false on the lived-with helper.

findings.situation: A child who was married at the end of 2025 and is not filing a joint return lives with the filer, but the filer cannot claim the child as a dependent and the divorced-or-separated-parents exception does not apply.
findings.irs_text: "If the child was married, see Married child, later" (i1040gi 2025, p. 41); "A child who was married at the end of 2025 is a qualifying child only if (a) you can claim the child as your dependent, or (b) you could have claimed the child as your dependent except for the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents" (p. 44).
findings.why: The question asks only about other people's claims, so a filer can truthfully answer NO when no one else qualifies. The computed dependent.eic_child has no married-child condition and returns true for a child the text excludes.

findings.situation: The child lives with the filer and another person and provided over half of their own support, so the child fails the support test for dependent.qualifying_child but meets the EIC conditions for the other person.
findings.irs_text: Question: "under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)"; IRS: "Who didn't provide over half of their own support for 2025" (i1040gi 2025, p. 17).
findings.why: The EIC branch forces YES, which also refuses dependent.qualifying_child. That line would correctly compute false from the support helper without any tie-breaker, because the child is not a dependent-rule qualifying child of anyone.

findings.situation: The filer is the child's only parent among the eligible claimants, such as a parent living with the child and the filer's own parent, so the tie-breaker necessarily resolves in the filer's favor.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025"; IRS: "If only one of the persons is the child's parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent" and "you can claim Lee as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, pp. 21, 44).
findings.why: The filer must truthfully answer YES and is refused, although the tool's computed true result is the correct outcome. This over-refusal is conservative, but it does block a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: Another person meets the qualifying-child tests on paper but will not or need not claim the child, for example because that person is not filing or is filing only for a refund.
findings.irs_text: "Even if a child meets the conditions to be the qualifying child of more than one person" and "If you and any other person can claim the child as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, p. 21); compare "Check 'No' if the other person isn't required to file, and isn't filing" (p. 41, Step 3, question 6).
findings.why: A filer could read "meet the conditions" as covering only the listed relationship, age, joint-return, residency and support tests, and answer YES. A filer could also read it as requiring someone who can actually claim the child, by analogy to the non-filer carve-out on p. 41, and answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer has foreign-source qualified dividends but no foreign-source capital gain or loss, so the filer can answer NO even though the Form 1116 instructions require possible adjustments to those qualified dividends before line 1a or line 5 and thus line 35.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 9, Foreign Qualified Dividends and Capital Gains (Losses): "If you have foreign source qualified dividends or foreign source capital gains (including any foreign source capital gain distributions) or losses, you may be required to make certain adjustments..."
findings.why: The screening question and box label ask only about a capital gain or loss; they never mention foreign-source qualified dividends, so the NO path treats any required qualified-dividend adjustment as zero or ignores it.

findings.situation: A filer has a foreign-source capital gain or loss but no adjustment is required, or the filer qualifies for the adjustment exception and elects not to adjust, so line 35 can be computed correctly without Worksheets A or B, yet the question forces YES.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 9: "You can elect not to make the adjustments to your qualified dividends and capital gains if you qualify for the adjustment exception"; and "No adjustments required ... include the amount ... without adjustment on line 1a."
findings.why: The question asks about any capital gain or loss from sources outside the United States, but the IRS adjustment obligation is conditional; when no adjustment is required or elected, the unadjusted amount flows correctly into line 35.

findings.situation: This year, the filer (or spouse) has a loss on line 15 of one category's Form 1116 and income on line 15 of another, so the loss has to be allocated on line 16. No earlier-year loss is involved, so the filer truthfully answers NO and the tool leaves line 16 at zero.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 21, Line 16 adj. 2: "If you have a loss on line 15 of one Form 1116 and you have income on line 15 of one or more other Forms 1116, you must reduce the foreign income by a pro rata share of the loss before you use any remaining loss to reduce U.S. source income."
findings.why: The question asks only about a loss from 'an earlier year' that is 'not yet recaptured'. A foreign loss from this year still has to go on line 16, so it changes line 35, and nothing in the wording reaches it.

findings.situation: This year, the filer (or spouse) has a net U.S.-source loss, such as a U.S. rental loss, that has to be spread across the foreign categories on line 16. The filer answers NO because nothing comes from an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 21, Line 16 adj. 3: "If you have a net loss from U.S. sources, proportionately allocate that loss among the separate categories of your foreign income. ... A U.S. loss includes a rental loss on property located in the United States."
findings.why: The question names a U.S. loss only when it reduced foreign income 'in an earlier year'. A U.S. loss from this year reduces line 17 and the credit, but this filer gets through the screen and the tool computes no adjustment.

findings.situation: This year, a business loss attributable to a foreign category is disallowed under section 461(l), which requires a line 16 increase. The filer answers NO because the question is only about earlier-year losses still to be recaptured.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 20, Line 16 adj. 1: "Increase the amount on line 15 by the amount of any business loss that is disallowed under section 461(l) to the extent it is attributable to the separate category of income of the applicable Form 1116."
findings.why: This is a required line 16 adjustment that the computed line 35 leaves out. The question's wording, which asks about earlier-year losses not yet recaptured, does not cover it.

findings.situation: In an earlier year, a loss from one foreign country reduced income from another country in the same category, for example two passive investments. The filer answers YES even though no loss account was created.
findings.irs_text: Question: "did a loss from abroad reduce your ... U.S. income or other foreign income"; i1116 p. 21, adj. 2: "If the loss reduces foreign source income [in another Form 1116 category], you must create ... a separate limitation loss account"
findings.why: A separate limitation loss account arises only when a loss in one category offsets income in a different category. Netting between countries within one category happens in Part I and creates nothing to recapture, but 'other foreign income' reads as covering it, so the tool refuses a return it could compute.

findings.situation: A filer whose earlier foreign or U.S. loss has been partly absorbed in later years, or whose earlier return didn't track loss accounts, may not know whether the loss is 'not yet recaptured'.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 21, adj. 4: "a part of your foreign income (in the same category as the loss) is recharacterized as U.S. source income in each following tax year"
findings.why: Recapture happens over several years, limited by later foreign income and a 50% cap, so 'not yet recaptured' depends on account balances many filers never worked out. A filer could read it as 'the loss was used up' and answer NO when a balance remains.

findings.situation: A filer accrued foreign tax in an earlier year and in 2025 the foreign tax liability was redetermined by audit without any refund or change to an amount actually paid.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 19: 'additional taxes paid or accrued as the result of an audit by a foreign taxing authority'; i1116 p. 2: 'foreign tax redeterminations that occurred in the current tax year and that relate to prior tax years.'
findings.why: The question asks only about tax you 'paid' that was refunded or changed, so an accrual-basis filer whose prior-year accrued tax is redetermined could truthfully answer NO; Schedule C is still required.

findings.situation: A partnership or S corporation reports to the filer a change in foreign income tax liability for a prior year.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 9: 'The partnership or S corporation has already apportioned the change in foreign income tax liability and has reported it to you... Include these amounts on each of the applicable Schedules C (Form 1116).'
findings.why: The question asks about foreign tax 'you' paid, but the entity paid the tax and the filer could truthfully answer NO even though Schedule C is required.

findings.situation: A filer had U.S. Virgin Islands tax paid for an earlier year refunded or changed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'In 2025, was foreign tax you ... paid for an earlier year refunded or changed?' i1116 p. 2: 'Don’t use Form 1116 to figure a credit for taxes paid to the U.S. Virgin Islands. Instead, use Form 8689.'
findings.why: The unqualified 'foreign tax' wording can make the filer answer YES, but Form 1116 line 35 correctly ignores Virgin Islands tax, so Schedule C (Form 1116) is not needed.

findings.situation: A filer paid additional foreign tax in 2025 that relates to an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'In 2025, was foreign tax you ... paid for an earlier year refunded or changed?'
findings.why: A filer could read 'paid for an earlier year' as tax paid during the earlier year or as tax paid in 2025 for an earlier year, and could read 'changed' as including or excluding an additional assessment.

findings.situation: A filer paid foreign tax on mineral income but did not claim percentage depletion, so no line 12 reduction is required.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 20: Taxes on foreign mineral income. Reduce taxes paid or accrued on mineral income from a foreign country or U.S. territory if you took a deduction for percentage depletion under section 613 for any part of the mineral income.
findings.why: The screen asks whether any foreign tax relates to foreign minerals, so this filer must answer YES; but with no section 613 percentage depletion the line 12 reduction is zero and the tool would compute line 35 correctly if allowed.

findings.situation: A filer has foreign oil and gas taxes that do not exceed the section 907 formula, so the line 12 reduction is zero.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 20: The amount of the reduction is the amount by which your foreign oil and gas taxes exceed the amount of your combined foreign oil and gas income for the year multiplied by a fraction...
findings.why: The screen asks whether any foreign tax relates to foreign oil or gas, requiring YES even though no excess and no reduction exist.

findings.situation: A filer with a line 13 high-tax kickout adjustment reads 'another reduction' as covering that adjustment.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 20: Line 13. You must adjust the foreign taxes paid or accrued if they relate to passive income that is treated as other category income because it is high taxed.
findings.why: The phrase 'another reduction' is undefined; it could mean only line 12 reductions or any adjustment/reduction to foreign taxes, so a filer could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: The filer files jointly in 2025 with the same spouse, but carries an unused foreign tax from an earlier joint return through a year in which they filed separately.
findings.irs_text: p514 p. 39: '3. You and your spouse file a joint return for the current tax year, to which you carry an unused foreign tax from a tax year for which you and your spouse filed a joint return, but through a tax year for which you and your spouse filed separate returns.'
findings.why: The question asks about an earlier joint return with someone the filer is not filing jointly with now, so this filer truthfully answers NO; Pub. 514 still requires an allocation between spouses.

findings.situation: The filer has an excess limit from an earlier joint return that must be allocated, but no foreign tax itself is carried into 2025 from that joint return.
findings.irs_text: p514 p. 39: 'You may have to allocate an unused foreign tax or excess limit for a tax year in which you and your spouse filed a joint return.'
findings.why: The question asks only whether foreign tax is carried from the joint return, so a filer with only an excess limit from that return can answer NO; the tool then ignores the required excess-limit allocation.

findings.situation: The filer carries an unused foreign tax from a separate-return year through an intervening joint-return year into 2025.
findings.irs_text: p514 p. 39: '2. You and your spouse file separate returns for the current tax year, to which you carry an unused foreign tax from a tax year for which you and your spouse filed separate returns, but through a tax year for which you and your spouse filed a joint return.'
findings.why: The phrase 'from an earlier joint return' could mean the tax originated in the joint year, or merely passed through a joint year; a reasonable filer could answer either way even though allocation is required.

findings.situation: An unmarried filer (single or head of household) who was a full-time student or unable to care for themselves must answer YES and is refused, even though deemed income appears to be available only on a joint return, so the tool's actual earned income would be correct.
findings.irs_text: p503 (2025) p. 11: 'These rules also apply if you are a student or not able to care for yourself and are filing a joint return.' Compare i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'These rules for a spouse who was a student or disabled also apply to you if you were a student or disabled.'
findings.why: The question asks 'were you ... a full-time student ... or physically or mentally not able to care for yourself' without regard to filing status. Pub. 503 limits the filer's own deemed income to joint returns, although i2441 p. 4 states no such limit, so this finding depends on following Pub. 503.

findings.situation: A filer who was a student or unable to care for themselves, and whose actual earned income met or exceeded the $250 or $500 floor in every such month, must answer YES although deemed income would not change lines 4 or 18.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'If you also worked during that month, enter the higher of $250 (or $500) or your actual earned income for that month.'
findings.why: The question asks only about status ('were you ... a full-time student ... or ... not able to care for yourself'), not whether the floor raises income in any month. Where actual earnings are the higher figure every month, the tool's sum of actual earned income is the correct result.

findings.situation: A filer enrolled full-time for 5 or more months only in a correspondence school, an internet-only school, or an on-the-job training course can truthfully answer YES and is refused, although that enrollment does not qualify for deemed income.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'A school doesn't include an on-the-job training course, a correspondence school, or a school offering courses only through the Internet.'
findings.why: The question says 'a full-time student at a school' and does not give this exclusion, so an ordinary reading of 'school' includes these programs. Without deemed income, the tool's actual earned income is correct for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer with a temporary illness or injury, or a disability that did not prevent self-care, could reasonably answer either way to 'physically or mentally not able to care for yourself at any time'.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 1: 'Persons who can't dress, clean, or feed themselves because of physical or mental disabilities are considered not able to care for themselves. Also, persons who must have constant attention to prevent them from injuring themselves or others are considered not able to care for themselves.'
findings.why: The question omits the IRS test, and 'not able to care for yourself at any time' could be read to include short periods of needing help. A filer who reads it loosely may be refused unnecessarily, while one who reads it strictly may answer NO despite meeting the IRS test.

findings.situation: A filer has allowed investment expenses directly connected with investment income, such as depreciation or K-1 investment expenses, and does not make the alternative line 4g allocation, so answers NO.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, line 5: 'Investment expenses are your allowed deductions, other than interest expense, directly connected with the production of investment income. For example, depreciation or depletion allowed on assets that produce investment income is an investment expense. Include investment expenses ... reported to you on Schedule K-1...'
findings.why: The question asks only about the alternative line 4g allocation and never mentions investment expenses. A NO answer makes the tool treat line 5 as zero, ignoring those allowed expenses.

findings.situation: A filer has investment interest expense and other deductible investment expenses, and the interest/ordinary-dividend income test is met, so the no-file exception should fail; the filer answers NO to the alternative-allocation question.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 3, Who Must File: 'You don’t have to file Form 4952 if all of the following apply. • Your investment income from interest and ordinary dividends minus any qualified dividends is more than your investment interest expense. • You don’t have any other deductible investment expenses. • You don’t have any carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024.'
findings.why: Because the question does not ask about other deductible investment expenses, a NO answer lets the tool zero line 5 and wrongly treat the filing exception as satisfied, so the required-test line can be false when the IRS text requires filing.

findings.situation: On a joint return, only the spouse made the alternative line 4g allocation, and the filer answers NO because the question does not mention the spouse.
findings.irs_text: f4952 pp. 3–4, line 4g: 'you can elect to include part or all of these amounts in investment income' and 'you can treat less of the amount on line 4e as attributable to line 4g and more to line 4b.'
findings.why: The question is singular and does not say 'you or your spouse.' On a joint return a filer can answer NO about their own election, causing the tool to ignore the spouse’s alternative allocation.

findings.situation: A filer has no carryover but does have other deductible investment expenses, such as depreciation or depletion on investment assets or K-1 investment expenses, so they answer NO and line 5 is computed as zero.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, Line 5: "Investment expenses are your allowed deductions, other than interest expense, directly connected with the production of investment income. For example, depreciation or depletion allowed on assets that produce investment income is an investment expense. Include investment expenses incurred directly by you or reported to you on Schedule K-1..."
findings.why: Line 5 and the filing-exception test in the `required` helper depend on these expenses, but the question asks only about a prior-year carryover. findings.situation: A filer had disallowed investment interest in an earlier year that was fully used by 2024, so their 2024 Form 4952 line 7 is zero, but they may still answer YES because they once had a carryover.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 1, line 2: "Disallowed investment interest expense from 2024 Form 4952, line 7"; p. 3: "You don't have any carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024."
findings.why: "Any prior-year disallowed investment interest carryover" does not tie the answer to the amount on 2024 Form 4952 line 7. A filer could read it as any past carryover, even one already used up, and the tool would refuse a case it computes correctly.

findings.why: The question treats 'dividends' as within the supported slice and never asks about Alaska Permanent Fund dividends; a filer can truthfully answer NO, but the tool would count them as investment income.

findings.situation: A filer has a nondeductible miscellaneous itemized investment expense, such as investment advisory fees, that is not an allowed Form 4952 line 5 investment expense.

findings.situation: Line 3 of the 2025 form needs any prior-year CRD that is still unallowed. findings.situation: The HSA's assets are used for the filer's benefit without the filer personally borrowing, trading with, or using them, for example the HSA invests in a business the filer owns or pays a third party in a way that benefits the filer.

question:
Does any of these apply?

- someone enrolled in a Marketplace policy was not lawfully present in the United States
- for any month, anyone in your tax family was eligible for minimum essential coverage other than coverage in the individual market, including:
  - Medicare Part A or Part C
  - Medicaid
  - the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP)
  - TRICARE
  - certain benefits for veterans and their families
  - health coverage for Peace Corps volunteers
  - employer-sponsored coverage that was offered and was affordable and provided minimum value (other than during a waiting period before the benefits begin; the offer is affordable for the employee if the employee's share of the annual cost of self-only coverage is not more than 9.02% of household income (Form 8962, line 3), whatever family coverage costs, and for another member of the tax family allowed to enroll if the employee's share of the annual cost of coverage for the employee and the family members allowed to enroll is not more than 9.02% of household income)
  - employer-sponsored coverage the person actually enrolled in (including COBRA or retiree coverage) even if it was not affordable or did not provide minimum value
  - other health coverage the Department of Health and Human Services designates as minimum essential coverage
- you or a family member were offered or covered by a qualified small employer HRA (QSEHRA, W-2 box 12 code FF) or an individual coverage HRA for 2025
- any part of a month's premium was not paid by the due date of your return, not including extensions (or, for coverage you enrolled in retroactively after a successful eligibility appeal, by the 120th day after the appeals decision), or a Form 1095-A shows zero in column A for a month whose premium you paid
- advance payments were made for someone who is in no one's tax family
- a Marketplace determination that you or a family member was ineligible for Medicaid or CHIP was later found to be based on incorrect information given with intentional or reckless disregard for the facts

findings.situation: A tax family member who is not enrolled in any Marketplace policy (for example, a dependent child on Medicaid or on a parent's employer plan) has other MEC, while only the filer is enrolled through the Marketplace.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 4: "If an individual in your tax family is not enrolled in a qualified health plan, or is enrolled in a qualified health plan but is eligible for MEC ... that individual is not part of your coverage family."
findings.why: The question asks about 'anyone in your tax family', so this filer answers YES. That person's MEC does not change the PTC for the Marketplace enrollees, so the tool's computation from Form 1095-A would be correct.

findings.situation: An employer offer was in fact affordable under 9.02% of actual household income, but the filer gave the Marketplace accurate information and the Marketplace found the filer eligible for APTC.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 5: "employer-sponsored coverage is not considered affordable if, when you or a family member enrolled in a qualified health plan, you gave accurate information about the availability of employer coverage to the Marketplace, and the Marketplace determined that you were eligible for APTC"
findings.why: The question's affordability test only looks at the 9.02% threshold, so the filer answers YES. Under the IRS text the person is not eligible for that coverage, so the tool computes the lines correctly.

findings.situation: Actual 2025 income made a family member income-eligible for Medicaid or CHIP, but the Marketplace, given accurate information, had determined the person ineligible for Medicaid or CHIP and eligible for APTC.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 6: "the individual is treated as not eligible for Medicaid or CHIP for purposes of the PTC for the duration of the period of coverage under the qualified health plan ... even if your actual 2025 income suggests that the individual may have been eligible"
findings.why: The bullet 'eligible for ... Medicaid' leads this filer to answer YES. The person is treated as not eligible, so the tool's computation is correct. The question's separate bullet only covers determinations based on intentionally or recklessly incorrect information.

findings.situation: After leaving a job, a former employee was offered affordable, minimum-value COBRA or retiree coverage but did not enroll in it.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 6: "if you leave your employment and are offered post-employment coverage such as COBRA or retiree coverage, you are not considered eligible for that post-employment coverage unless you actually enroll in the coverage"
findings.why: The bullet 'employer-sponsored coverage that was offered and was affordable and provided minimum value' excludes only waiting periods, not post-employment offers. This filer answers YES even though the person is not eligible and the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A family member was eligible for other MEC for only part of a month, for example Medicaid or employer coverage that began mid-month.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 3: "An individual is generally considered eligible for MEC for the month only if they were eligible for every day of the month"
findings.why: 'For any month, anyone ... was eligible' can be read as covering partial-month eligibility, which would mean answering YES. Under the IRS rule that month is not a month of eligibility.

findings.situation: A filer whose Marketplace coverage began mid-month, or who had a 2025 premium refunded in 2025, answers YES, and the tool refuses line 25 even though line 25 is only the APTC reported in Form 1095-A column C, which neither adjustment changes.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 17, Column (f): "Enter on lines 12 through 23, column (f), the amount of the monthly APTC reported on Form 1095-A, lines 21 through 32, column C"; i8962 p. 18, Line 25: "Enter the amount from line 11(f) or add lines 12(f) through 23(f)"
findings.why: Both adjustments in the question act only on the monthly credit amount, through enrollment premiums and first-of-month enrollment. They feed column (e) and line 24, not column (f) and line 25. The tool computes line 25 correctly in every YES situation.

findings.situation: A filer whose 2025 premium refund the Marketplace has already netted out of Form 1095-A column A must answer YES to "any premiums for a 2025 month of that Marketplace coverage were refunded in 2025", even though the tool's use of column A as reported is already correct.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 4: "The enrollment premiums are the total amount of the premiums for the month, reduced by any premium amounts for that month that were refunded in 2025 ... Form 1095-A, Part III, column A, reports the enrollment premiums."
findings.why: The IRS text says column A reports enrollment premiums, which are defined net of 2025 refunds. A refund already reflected there needs no adjustment by the filer. The question asks only whether a refund happened, not whether column A omits it.

findings.situation: A filer whose coverage began mid-month cannot tell whether to answer YES when Form 1095-A column A already shows no premium for that partial month, a case the tool already treats correctly.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 4: "Generally, if coverage in a qualified health plan began after the first day of the month, you are not allowed a monthly credit amount for the coverage for that month."
findings.why: The question asks only about the start date. It does not ask whether the 1095-A reports a premium or APTC for that month. A filer could reasonably answer either way when the 1095-A already shows nothing for the partial month.

findings.situation: A filer claims the 60% allowance in 2025 for used long-production-period property or certain aircraft acquired before January 20, 2025, and placed in service in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 6: "Property with a long production period and certain aircraft acquired after September 27, 2017, and before January 20, 2025, is eligible for a special depreciation allowance of 60% ... and can be either new property or certain used property." The 40% election for post-January 19 property also allows "60% for property with a long production period and certain aircraft."
findings.why: The computed helper reads "the full allowance or the 40% allowance." A filer claiming the 60% allowance could truthfully answer no, so the used-property line is never asked even though the allowance applies to used property.

findings.situation: A filer elects the qualified production property allowance in 2025 for used nonresidential real property placed in service after July 4, 2025.
findings.irs_text: i4562 pp. 7-8: "You can elect to take a special depreciation allowance for qualified production property (QPP) by designating up to 100% of the depreciable basis... Eligible property can be either new property or certain used property."
findings.why: The QPP allowance is a designation of basis, not a class-wide allowance. It is also not "the full allowance or the 40% allowance" named in the helper, so a filer could answer no. Used QPP would then be treated as not used.

findings.situation: A filer who elected the special allowance for a specified fruit or nut plant grafted in 2025 but not yet placed in service.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 6: "the special depreciation allowance only applies for the first tax year in which the plant is planted or grafted. The plant will not be treated as qualified property ... in the subsequent tax year in which it is placed in service."
findings.why: The gate requires the property to be placed in service in 2025, but this allowance is claimed in the planting or grafting year, before the plant is placed in service. Grafting onto existing stock could raise an original-use question that the gate never reaches.

findings.situation: Property placed in service in 2025 with the 50% allowance for qualified reuse and recycling property.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 7: "The original use of the property must begin with you after August 31, 2008."
findings.why: Used property cannot qualify for this allowance, so asking whether it was used before adds questions without affecting any amount.

findings.situation: A business that does not produce energy for sale, such as a farm, store or office, places in service energy property like solar panels, a wind turbine or geothermal equipment for its own use.

findings.situation: The filer had full-year coverage and column A is the same every month, but the printed column B varies from month to month and is wrong for a reason other than a blank/zero month or an unreported change. Examples: no APTC was paid and the Marketplace filled column B with incorrect varying amounts, or the filer otherwise has reason to believe the Marketplace reported the wrong SLCSP premium. The correct SLCSP premium turns out to be the same for all 12 months.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 14: "If either of these two situations applies to you, or if you have reason to believe the Marketplace reported the wrong applicable SLCSP premium, you must determine the correct applicable SLCSP premium for every month. If the correct applicable SLCSP premium is not the same for every month of 2025, check 'No'"; "1. No APTC was paid for your coverage. ... column B, of Form 1095-A may be wrong, left blank, or reported as -0-."
findings.why: When the form is not printed the same every month, the computed condition counts only 'blank or zero in a covered month, or an unreported change'. It drops the 'no APTC paid' and 'reason to believe the Marketplace reported the wrong' grounds, so the gate is false and the line is forced to false. Under the text, a correction that yields the same premium every month lets the filer check 'Yes' on line 10 and use line 11.

findings.situation: A filer who is married filing separately meets all three tests to be treated as unmarried but leaves line A unchecked, for example because they claim only the exclusion and no credit, so the tool asks for the spouse's earnings even though line 19 should hold the filer's own earnings.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 19: "Are you considered unmarried under that rule? Yes. Enter your earned income (from line 18) on line 19." p. 2, Line A: "If your filing status is married filing separately and you meet the requirements to claim the credit ... you must check the box on line A."
findings.why: Line A is tied to claiming the credit, while the line 19 rule depends only on being treated as unmarried. The computed condition can therefore hold when the IRS text gives the spouse's earnings and the spouse's student or disabled status no role. This is the cheap direction: it asks extra questions and drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer whose only 2025 installation was a small wind turbine may answer no, because the question lists 'solar panels, a battery, insulation, windows, doors, or heating, cooling or hot-water equipment' after a colon, which reads as a complete list that leaves out wind.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'Qualified small wind energy property costs are costs for property that uses a wind turbine to generate electricity for use in connection with your home located in the United States.'
findings.why: The phrase 'saves or makes energy' covers a wind turbine, but the list after the colon omits it, so a filer who reads the list as exhaustive answers no and line f5695.wind_if_any is silently zero. Adding 'a wind turbine' to the list, or 'for example' before it, would close this.

findings.situation: A filer who installed solar panels, a solar water heater, a wind turbine, a geothermal heat pump or a battery at a second or vacation home in 2025 may read 'at home' as meaning only their main residence and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'The home doesn't have to be your main home.' (solar electric, solar water heating, small wind, geothermal); p. 2: 'If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025, enter the total of those costs'
findings.why: Part I credits allow any home the filer used as a residence, but 'at home' can be read as the filer's main home only. Saying 'at any home you lived in during 2025' would remove the ambiguity.

findings.situation: The gate holds for installations that earn no credit, for example Part II items at a home that is not the filer's main home, items without the required energy-efficiency certification, or Part II work on a newly constructed home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Qualified energy efficiency improvements are the following building envelope components installed on or in your main home that you owned during 2025'; p. 1: 'The energy efficient home improvement credit (Part II) is only available for existing homes.'
findings.why: A yes to the gate in these cases only leads to follow-up questions and drops no amount, which is acceptable because gates lean to yes.

findings.situation: A married couple files jointly and the spouse installed a qualifying biomass stove in a separate main home, while the filer installed none.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: "If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. 1. Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home."
findings.why: The gate says only "A biomass stove or biomass boiler was installed" and does not say "by you or your spouse"; the filer could truthfully answer no for themselves, but the IRS text still requires a separate Form 5695 for the spouse's main home and a line 29e/f amount.

findings.situation: A biomass stove or boiler is installed at a home outside the United States.

findings.why: The gate condition refers only to installation at a home and does not require the home to be located in the United States, so it can hold where the IRS gives no line 29e/f amount.

findings.situation: A filer installs a qualifying central air conditioner in 2025 for cooling or comfort, not 'to save or make energy,' and pays for no home energy audit; the outer helper is false, so the computed gate is false even though line 22a or 22b has an amount.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'Line 22a. Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive central air conditioner that achieves the highest efficiency tier ...'; i5695 p. 1: 'A 30% credit ... may be allowed for: ... Central air conditioners.'
findings.why: The IRS line allows the cost based on qualifying central air conditioner property, not on the filer's subjective energy-saving purpose or on having a home energy audit. The gate adds that prerequisite and can drop the line for a qualifying installation.

findings.situation: The gate treats any installed central air conditioner as potentially within scope, while the IRS line requires the unit to achieve the highest CEE efficiency tier in effect at the start of the calendar year and to have a QMID for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'achieves the highest efficiency tier that has been established by the Consortium for Energy Efficiency (CEE)'; i5695 p. 1: 'if you are claiming the energy efficient home improvement credit for specified property placed into service in 2025, you must include ... QMID.'
findings.why: The cited text states efficiency-tier and QMID conditions for line 22a and line 22b, but the gate condition is only that a central air conditioner was installed.

findings.situation: A filer could read 'anything was installed ... to save or make energy' either to include a high-efficiency central air conditioner or to exclude an air conditioner because it cools rather than saves or makes energy.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'A 30% credit ... may be allowed for: ... Central air conditioners.'
findings.why: The phrase is purpose-based and not defined; either reading changes whether the gate asks the gated central-air-conditioner cost questions.

findings.situation: A central air conditioner is installed in 2025 but does not meet the highest CEE efficiency tier or lacks a QMID; the gate is true but IRS line 22a or 22b has no allowable amount.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'achieves the highest efficiency tier ...'; i5695 p. 1: 'must include the four-character alphanumeric unique qualified manufacturer identification number (QMID)'
findings.why: The gate only checks installation, so it asks and can hold when every gated line is zero under the efficiency-tier and QMID rules.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse installed qualifying exterior doors at the spouse's separate main home, but the taxpayer did not install any at his or her own home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'If both you and your spouse owned and lived apart in separate main homes ... If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. 1. Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.why: The IRS text requires accounting for the spouse's separate main home on the joint return, but the gate only asks 'Exterior doors were installed' without saying 'you or your spouse'; the taxpayer could answer no as to himself or herself and drop lines 19a, 19d, and 19e.

findings.situation: Only one Energy Star exterior door was installed.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'Line 19a. Enter the amount you paid for the most expensive exterior door that meets the Energy Star program requirements.'
findings.why: The IRS line applies to one door, but the gate says plural 'Exterior doors were installed'; a filer with a single door could reasonably read the plural as not met.

findings.situation: A non-Energy Star exterior door, or an exterior door at a home that is not the taxpayer's main home, was installed.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'most expensive exterior door that meets the Energy Star program requirements'; i5695 p. 3: qualified energy efficiency improvements are 'installed on or in your main home that you owned during 2025'.
findings.why: The gate is only 'Exterior doors were installed,' so it can be true even though the IRS would give lines 19a, 19d, and 19e no amount.

findings.situation: A qualifying furnace is installed as part of a home reconstruction and the taxpayer's original use of the reconstructed home begins in 2025, but the physical installation was completed before 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: '...in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins.'
findings.why: The IRS treats reconstruction costs as paid when original use begins, so line 24a/24b can have an amount for 2025 even though the gate's first helper ('installed in 2025') is false.

findings.situation: A nonqualifying natural gas furnace is installed; the gate only asks whether a furnace was installed.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Lines 24a Through 24d: '...furnaces ... that achieve the highest efficiency tier established by the CEE...'; oil units also must meet 2021 Energy Star and fuel-blend criteria.
findings.why: The cited line conditions the amount on the highest CEE tier (and additional oil criteria), while the gate condition is merely installation of any natural gas, propane, or oil furnace or hot water boiler.

findings.situation: A joint filer's spouse installed a qualifying furnace in the spouse's separate main home, and the gate does not say whether it covers the spouse.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows.'
findings.why: Because the gate says only 'A ... was installed' and not 'you or your spouse,' a joint filer could reasonably answer no for a spouse's separate-home furnace that the IRS instructions include.

findings.situation: A natural gas furnace that does not meet the highest CEE tier is installed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Lines 24a Through 24d: '...furnaces ... that achieve the highest efficiency tier established by the CEE...'
findings.why: The gate condition holds on any furnace installation, but the IRS line gives no amount unless the efficiency tier (and oil criteria where applicable) is met.

findings.situation: Geothermal heat pump property was installed during construction of a new home and finished in late 2024, and the filer (or spouse) first moved in during 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins."
findings.why: These costs are treated as paid in 2025, so they belong on line 4. But the filer can truthfully answer no to "Anything was installed in 2025 at a home," because the installation was completed in 2024.

findings.situation: Geothermal heat pump property was installed in 2024 as part of reconstructing the filer's home, and the filer's original use of the reconstructed home began in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins."
findings.why: The cost is treated as paid in 2025 and goes on line 4. The gate asks only whether something was installed in 2025, so a truthful no drops it.

findings.situation: A condominium association or housing cooperative installed geothermal heat pump property for the building in 2025, and the filer is treated as having paid a proportionate share.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation."
findings.why: A unit owner may not count the association's building-wide project as something "installed ... at a home" of theirs. That owner would answer no, even though their share belongs on line 4.

findings.why: The IRS text requires separate Forms 5695 for each spouse's main home and combining line 30, so the spouse's insulation can produce a line 18a amount. The gate's insulation helper is not worded as 'you or your spouse,' so a truthful no can silently drop the spouse's amount.

findings.situation: Insulation is installed as part of new-home construction, or the installed material provides structural support or a finished surface, so the gate is true but line 18a is zero.

findings.situation: The gate tests only for a current loss or deduction item or a box 16 code D distribution, but the cited Who Must File section has four triggers and the gate drops two of them.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, Who Must File: "Form 7203 is filed by S corporation shareholders who: • Are claiming a deduction for their share of an aggregate loss ... • Received a non-dividend distribution ... • Disposed of stock in an S corporation (whether or not gain is recognized), or • Received a loan repayment from an S corporation." Gate: "a loss or deduction item, or a distribution (box 16, code D)"
findings.why: The cited text states the filing condition, and the gate's condition is narrower. It omits stock dispositions and loan repayments, so it is not the stated condition.

findings.situation: A shareholder had no current-year loss or distribution but received a repayment of a loan they had made to the S corporation.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Received a loan repayment from an S corporation"; p. 4, Line 34, "The character of the gain on repayment is dependent on whether the debt is evidenced by a formal note or is an open account"
findings.why: Form 7203 is required and Part II applies, since the repayment produces gain measured against debt basis. The computed gate is false, so the loans question is never asked and is treated as false.

findings.situation: A shareholder sold or otherwise disposed of S corporation stock during the year with no loss item and no distribution.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Disposed of stock in an S corporation (whether or not gain is recognized)"; p. 3, "If a portion of your stock is redeemed, sold, or otherwise disposed of during the year, attach two separate forms. Use the first to figure your stock basis at the date of sale"
findings.why: Form 7203 is required, and lines 1 and 2 (beginning basis and additions) determine basis at the sale. The gate is false, so those lines are set to zero.

findings.situation: A shareholder whose current K-1 shows no loss item and no distribution is claiming a loss that was suspended in a prior year for lack of basis.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Are claiming a deduction for their share of an aggregate loss from an S corporation (including an aggregate loss not allowed last year because of basis limitations)"; p. 4, Column (b), "Enter any loss or deduction items disallowed due to basis limitations in prior years that were carried forward"
findings.why: The gate is computed from the current K-1's loss/deduction and code D items, so it does not see a carried-forward loss. Lines 1, 2, the election and the loans question are then never asked.

findings.situation: The K-1 shows a deduction item, but income items exceed it, so there is no aggregate loss and no distribution.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Are claiming a deduction for their share of an aggregate loss from an S corporation"
findings.why: The gate fires on any loss or deduction item, not only on an aggregate loss. It may therefore ask questions when Form 7203 is not required.

findings.situation: A filer whose only carryover is a prior-year unallowed CRD from a rental real estate activity they do not list as a 2025 rental (for example, no 2025 income or loss for that property), so the count of listed rentals with a held-back loss is 0 even though line 3 must take the CRD.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Line 3: "If you have prior-year unallowed commercial revitalization deductions (CRD) from rental real estate activities, treat that dollar amount as negative and combine with lines 1d and 2d. Enter the combined amount on line 3 and enter “CRD” ..."
findings.why: Line 3 takes the CRD directly, not through a listed activity's column (c). A gate that counts listed rentals can therefore be false while line 3 still needs the CRD amount.

findings.situation: A filer with a CRD carryover but no ordinary prior-year unallowed loss may not count the rental as having "a loss held back," because the instructions treat a CRD as a deduction distinct from passive losses.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 1, Reminders: "If you have prior-year unallowed CRDs limited by the passive loss rules, you may continue to include them in the calculations"
findings.why: The parenthetical in the helper label tries to fold the CRD in. But a filer answering a per-rental count can reasonably read "loss held back" as the Part VII column (c) loss only and leave out a CRD that line 3 takes directly.

findings.situation: On a joint return where only the spouse's rental carries a prior-year unallowed CRD, the gate's count wording does not say it covers the spouse's rentals.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Line 3: "If you have prior-year unallowed commercial revitalization deductions (CRD) from rental real estate activities..."
findings.why: The gated question names the spouse, but the gate's count ('rentals listed') does not. If the spouse's rentals are not listed or counted, the gate can be false.

findings.situation: A filer whose listed rental carries only an ordinary prior-year unallowed loss and no CRD passes the gate even though line 3 has no CRD amount.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Part IV Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: Ordinary carryovers go to lines 1c/2c, not to the line 3 CRD entry, so the gate is broader than the gated line needs. This costs only an extra question.

findings.situation: A person divorced in 2025 whose then-spouse had a family HDHP but was not an eligible individual during the marriage (for example, enrolled in Medicare) is still asked and answers yes, so the interview ends even though the family-coverage rule does not apply.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan"
findings.why: The family-coverage rule requires both spouses to be eligible individuals, but the question asks only whether the other person had a plan covering more than one person. A yes in this case is wrong but only costs questions, so it is reported without changing the verdict.

findings.situation: A filer made a qualified HSA funding distribution early in 2024 and stopped being an eligible individual during its testing period. They became eligible again by December 1, 2024, used the last-month rule for 2024, and then stopped being eligible again in 2025. Because the 2024 QHFD testing period was already failed, the computed condition is false, so the last-month-rule question is never asked and line 18 is zero.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 9, Part III: 'Use Part III to figure any additional income ... for failure to be an eligible individual during the testing period for: • Last-month rule ... or • A qualified HSA funding distribution'; Line 18: 'Enter on line 18 the excess of the amount contributed over the redetermined amount.' Line 19: 'Enter the total of any qualified HSA funding distribution.'
findings.why: The instructions treat the two testing periods as separate and give each its own line, with nothing saying that failing the QHFD testing period cancels the last-month-rule inclusion. The 'Year parameter hsa.no' branch therefore drops a line 18 amount that the IRS text requires.

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 QHFD testing period and 2024 last-month-rule testing period are both failed in 2025, for example by losing HDHP coverage in mid-2025. The tool treats the QHFD failure as already failed and never asks about the last-month rule.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2, Testing period: 'If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period ... you will have to include in income the total contributions made that would not have been made except for the last-month rule.' i8889 p. 8, Testing period: '... you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual.'
findings.why: Both inclusions arise in the same year from the same failure, and the IRS text requires each one. A gate that turns off the last-month-rule question whenever the QHFD testing period has failed misses the line 18 amount.

findings.situation: A married person whose own HDHP coverage started, ended or changed type during 2025 (bucket 'changed'), for example self-only from July to December, while the spouse had a family HDHP in those months.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 3, rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage. Disregard any plan with self-only coverage."
findings.why: The 'changed' branch sets the condition to false, so the spouse's family coverage is never asked and is treated as false. Rule 1 applies to every Line 3 computation, including the monthly Limitation Chart and the last-month rule (rules 2, 4 and 5), so the family amount is silently dropped for those months.

findings.situation: A married person with a self-only HDHP on the first day of all twelve months who was not an eligible individual in every month (for example enrolled in Medicare from October), while the spouse had a family HDHP.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan. Disregard any plans with self-only coverage."
findings.why: The condition requires eligibility in every month, so it is false here. In the months when both spouses were eligible, the IRS text treats the filer as having family coverage, which sets the monthly limit under rule 5's worksheet.

findings.situation: A person with a self-only HDHP all year who was married for part of 2025 but not at year-end (divorced or widowed), whose spouse had a family HDHP during the months of the marriage.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 3, rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage."
findings.why: The condition tests marital status only at the end of 2025, while the gated question asks about "any month of 2025". Rule 1 is not limited to year-end marital status, so the spouse's family coverage in the married months is never asked.

findings.situation: A married person with self-only coverage and full-year eligibility whose spouse had a family HDHP but was not an eligible individual in any month (for example the spouse was on Medicare all year).
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan."
findings.why: The question is asked although the deemed-family treatment in this passage requires both spouses to be eligible. This leans to yes and is harmless by design.

findings.situation: A filer who was not an eligible individual in a month of 2025 that falls after the testing period for the 2024 transfer had already ended (for example a March 2024 transfer and a loss of eligibility in October 2025) is still asked.

findings.why: The condition tests any month of 2025 rather than only the months inside the testing period, so it holds where the text gives no amount.

findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 8, Testing period: "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income"

findings.situation: A filer whose HDHP coverage started, ended or changed type during 2025 (for example self-only January to June, family July to December) was also covered all year by a general-purpose health FSA or HRA, their own or their spouse's.
findings.irs_text: p969 (2025) p. 5, Other employee health plans: "An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA." i8889 (2025) p. 2: "you must be covered under a high deductible health plan (HDHP) and have no other health coverage except certain disregarded coverage."
findings.why: The FSA/HRA bar applies whatever the HDHP coverage pattern, but in the 'changed' branch the condition is forced false, so the FSA question is never asked and the line is treated as false. Unless the month-by-month path (not shown here) separately asks about the FSA/HRA, the refusal is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer with the same HDHP type all year truthfully answers no to the three-conditions question for a reason that affects only some months (for example Medicare enrolment from October, or other coverage that ended in March) and also had a general-purpose health FSA or HRA in the other months.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: "You must be, or be considered, an eligible individual on the first day of a month to take an HSA deduction for that month"; p969 (2025) p. 5: "An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA."
findings.why: The FSA/HRA still decides eligibility for the remaining months, but the condition is false, so the line is set to false without asking. The gate is only safe if the monthly path captures FSA/HRA coverage on its own, which the cited text and gate do not show.

findings.situation: A filer with a general-purpose health FSA reads the three-conditions question "with no other health coverage that is not disregarded" and may or may not count the FSA as other health coverage.
findings.irs_text: p969 (2025) p. 5: "An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA."
findings.why: The gate wording does not say whether an FSA/HRA counts as other health coverage. One reading answers yes and reaches the FSA question; the other answers no and the FSA line is zeroed without being asked, leaving the outcome to the unshown monthly path.

findings.situation: A filer who met the three conditions in every month with one coverage type had no HSA contributions from any source for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4: "Use Part I to figure: Your HSA deduction, Any excess contributions you made (or those made on your behalf)"
findings.why: With no contributions, FSA/HRA coverage changes nothing, yet the question is still asked; this is harmless by design.

Disregard any plans with self-only coverage."; Line 3 rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage."
findings.why: The helper as shown says only "HDHP coverage on the first day of every month", not coverage the person "had or was treated as having". The spouse-attribution help appears only on the gated December 1 question, which is never asked on a self-only answer, so December 1 is set to self-only ($4,300) where the IRS text gives family ($8,550).

findings.situation: A person covered by a self-only HDHP all year who was also covered by a family HDHP at the same time for some or all months could answer self-only in all twelve to the upstream helper.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 1: "If you were covered by both a self-only HDHP and a family HDHP at the same time, you are treated as having family coverage during that period."
findings.why: The helper's three choices do not say that simultaneous coverage counts as family. A truthful self-only answer skips the December 1 question, whose help is the only place this rule is explained.

findings.situation: A filer whose coverage changed and who had HDHP coverage on December 1, 2025 but was not an eligible individual that day (for example, enrolled in Medicare or with other disqualifying coverage) may answer self-only or family and be offered the last-month rule.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: "You may consider yourself an "eligible individual" for the entire year if you are an eligible individual on the 1st day of the last month of the tax year (December 1, for most individuals)."
findings.why: The December 1 helper is worded as HDHP coverage rather than eligible-individual status, so the condition can hold where the IRS text makes the last-month rule unavailable; this is over-inclusion, not a dropped amount.

findings.situation: The account beneficiary died in 2025 with no designated beneficiary or with the estate named. The HSA's value goes on the decedent's own final return, which may be a joint return with the surviving spouse. Asked about the decedent, the gate question gets a truthful no: the decedent was the owner and did not get the HSA because someone else died.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: "If the account beneficiary's estate is the beneficiary, the value of the HSA as of the date of death is included on the account beneficiary's final income tax return. Complete Form 8889 as described above, except you should complete Part I, if applicable."
findings.why: On the decedent's final return the HSA's date-of-death value is an amount, and the inherited-case line must not fall back to the spouse-treated-as-own default. The gate question only asks whether the filer received an HSA from someone else who died, so it never reaches the owner's own final return when the estate is the beneficiary.

findings.situation: A non-spouse beneficiary whose benefactor died before 2025 and who received nothing from the account in 2025 answers yes, because the help says to answer yes whatever year the owner died.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: "the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death"
findings.why: That account stopped being an HSA in an earlier year, so the inherited-case line gives it no 2025 amount. The yes only costs an extra question.

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 qualified HSA funding distribution had a testing month in 2024 in which they were not eligible (for example, December 2024), but they were eligible in every 2025 month of the testing period; the gate holds and the question's window includes 2024 months, so the filer answers yes.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: "you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual"; p. 9: "Include the amount in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual."
findings.why: A failure in 2024 belongs on the 2024 return, so the 2025 line has no amount. The gate holding here only costs extra questions and does not drop an amount. The question's window ("From the month of that transfer") could also be limited to 2025 months.

findings.situation: A filer contributed a qualified HSA funding distribution in 2024 and stayed eligible through the whole testing period, but was not eligible in some 2025 month after the testing period ended.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: "lasts through the last day of the 12th month following that month"
findings.why: The gate holds, but the filer truthfully answers no to the gated question, so the line correctly stays zero. This only costs one extra question.

findings.situation: A filer whose non-rolled-over distributions paid medical bills, but some bills were incurred before the HSA was set up, reimbursed by insurance, or were premiums that don't qualify, could answer the computed helper yes.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Line 15: "Only include on line 15 distributions from your HSA that were used to pay you for qualified medical expenses not reimbursed by insurance or other coverage and that you incurred after the HSA was established." p. 2: "Expenses incurred before you establish your HSA are not qualified medical expenses."
findings.why: The helper question says only "used to pay qualified medical expenses" and does not state the after-establishment, unreimbursed and premium limits. A yes skips the detailed question, so line 15 is taken as all distributions and is overstated.

findings.situation: A filer with a deemed distribution (prohibited transaction) or an excess contribution withdrawn after the return due date, whose actual withdrawals all went to medical bills, could answer yes that all non-rolled-over distributions paid qualified medical expenses.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: "Any deemed distribution will not be treated as used to pay qualified medical expenses." p. 8, Line 15: "Do not include the distribution of an excess contribution taken out after the due date, including extensions, of your return even if used for qualified medical expenses."
findings.why: Filers may not think of a deemed distribution or a late excess withdrawal as a distribution that 'paid' expenses, or may believe the late excess withdrawal counts because it was spent on medical care. A yes leaves these amounts in line 15 when the text excludes them.

findings.situation: When there were no HSA distributions, the computed condition is false (hsa.no), so the tool asks the medical-expense amount even though lines 14a–14c are zero.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Line 14a: "Enter the total distributions your HSAs made in 2025."
findings.why: With no distributions, line 15 has no effect, so asking the question costs only an extra question.
