findings.situation: Married spouses with separate HSAs and family HDHP coverage who file a joint return must also split the family limit on line 6, but the computed gate is false unless filing status is married filing separately.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025, use the following rules to figure the amount on line 6"; gate: "Filing status married filing separately" = true and "Married at the end of 2025 and treated as having family coverage at any time during 2025" = true
findings.why: The cited condition is spouses with separate HSAs and family coverage, with no filing-status test. The gate adds a married-filing-separately requirement the text does not state. This is harmless only if the tool handles joint returns' separate-HSA allocation somewhere else.

findings.situation: A spouse who had an HSA during 2025 but closed or rolled it out before the filer answers could read 'Does your husband or wife have' in the present tense and truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"
findings.why: The question asks about now, not 2025. The help says to count an HSA with nothing put into it for 2025, but it does not say to count an account that no longer exists, so a filer could answer no while the line 6 split still applies.

findings.situation: On a married-filing-separately return, the question opens with "For this person (you, or your spouse on a joint return)", which refers to a joint return that cannot exist in this case.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "divide the amount on line 5 equally between you and your spouse, unless you both agree on a different allocation"
findings.why: A separate filer could be unsure whose HSA is being asked about. The joint-return framing conflicts with the gate's limit to separate returns and with the line's label, "A separate return's spouse had an HSA".

findings.situation: A filer contributed a qualified HSA funding distribution in early 2025 (for example, February 2025) and stopped being an eligible individual later in 2025 (for example, October 2025). Because the testing period began in 2025, not 2024, the computed condition is false.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: "The testing period begins with the month in which the traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution is contributed to the HSA ... you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual."
findings.why: A 2025 contribution can fail its testing period within 2025, which puts an amount on Part III line 19 for 2025, so the disability exception matters. The gate only recognizes testing periods that began in 2024, so it treats the disability answer as false and the exception is lost.

findings.situation: A filer's testing period for a 2024 qualified HSA funding distribution (or for the 2024 last-month rule) was failed in 2025, and the filer reads the helper question as asking whether the failure happened in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 9: "Include the amount in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual." Gate helper: "the testing period of a qualified HSA funding distribution contributed in 2024 was failed, or the last-month rule was used for 2024"
findings.why: "Was failed" does not say when, so a filer could answer as of the 2024 return and say no even though the failure occurred in 2025. That wrong no drops the 2025 inclusion.

findings.situation: A filer still holds an HSA but stopped being an eligible individual (lost HDHP coverage) because of disability, and reads "stop being able to have an HSA" as closing or losing the account.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2: "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled"; p. 2: "You can receive distributions from an HSA even if you are not currently eligible to have contributions made to the HSA."
findings.why: The test is eligibility to contribute, not having an account. A filer who still has the account could answer no to "stop being able to have an HSA" and lose the disability exception.

findings.situation: A filer contributed a qualified HSA funding distribution in March 2024, so the testing period ended March 31, 2025, and lost eligibility in August 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: "lasts through the last day of the 12th month following that month"
findings.why: The gate holds because the filer was ineligible in some month of 2025, but that month falls after the testing period ended, so there is no failure and no Part III amount.

findings.situation: A filer used the last-month rule for 2024 or made a 2024 qualified HSA funding distribution, and lost eligibility in 2025 because of death.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2: "other than because of death or becoming disabled"
findings.why: Death also excuses the failure, so no Part III amount arises even though the gate holds.

findings.situation: A tax-family member turned down an employer offer, but the Marketplace, given accurate information about the offer, found them eligible for APTC; the computed condition still holds and the gated question is asked.

findings.why: Here the offer is treated as unaffordable, so the gated line should be false, but the condition is true and a filer may answer Yes. That is extra questions or an unneeded stop, not a dropped amount.

findings.situation: Someone was offered employer coverage they did not take, but only in months with no Marketplace coverage, or only during a waiting period, or only as post-employment COBRA or retiree coverage.

findings.situation: A filer who owns a small business buys a group health plan through that business and could have enrolled in it while on Marketplace insurance.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 5: 'MEC includes: ... Most types of employer-sponsored coverage; and • Other health coverage the Department of Health and Human Services designates as MEC.'
findings.why: The gate's help says 'Insurance you bought on your own outside the Marketplace does not count,' so a business owner could read a plan their own company bought as insurance they bought themselves and answer no. The gated question f8962.mec_other names exactly this case ('a plan from a business they own'), and the gate's examples ('a job's plan') do not clearly reach it.

findings.situation: Someone on the return was offered COBRA or retiree coverage and did not enroll, or could only get an employer plan after a waiting period. That person may answer yes because they 'could have had' that coverage.

findings.why: The gate holds in these cases, but none of the gated lines carries an amount for them. The help on the job-offer question excludes them, so the only cost is a few extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) owns no shares, gets no Form 1099-DIV and has no taxable interest, but a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust paid foreign income tax and passed it through to the filer on a Schedule K-3 or Schedule K-1.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 1: "Qualified payee statements include Form 1099-DIV, Form 1099-INT, Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S), or similar substitute statements."
findings.why: The entity paid the foreign tax, so the filer can truthfully answer no to "Have you ... ever paid income tax to a foreign country". The filer also owns no shares and has no interest, so the computed condition is false and a creditable foreign tax is dropped.

findings.situation: Even when the gate opens, the gated question tells the filer to add only box 7 of Form 1099-DIV, box 6 of Form 1099-INT and tax they paid themselves, so foreign tax reported on a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) or Schedule K-3 is left out of ftc.taxes.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 1: "All the income and any foreign taxes paid on it were reported to you on a qualified payee statement ... Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S)"
findings.why: The list in the question omits a source of foreign tax that the IRS text names, so a filer following the question literally enters too little.

findings.situation: Foreign tax was withheld at source on foreign royalties, rents or gains, and the filer never wrote a payment to the foreign government.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "You can take a credit for income, war profits, and excess profits taxes paid or accrued during your tax year to any foreign country or U.S. territory"; p. 3: "the day you paid the foreign taxes (or on the day the tax was withheld)"
findings.why: A filer could read "paid income tax to a foreign country" as excluding tax withheld by a payer, and answer no.

findings.situation: The filer has U.S.-only taxable interest or shares of U.S. companies, or paid foreign income tax in some earlier year but not in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "taxes paid or accrued during your tax year to any foreign country or U.S. territory"
findings.why: No creditable foreign tax exists for 2025, so the gate opens with nothing to enter; this is acceptable leaning to yes.

locators: pp. 1–2, election to claim the foreign tax credit without filing Form 1116; p. 25, Line 20, regular tax

pp. 1–2, election to claim the foreign tax credit without filing Form 1116; p. 25, Line 20, regular tax; p. 3, Foreign Taxes Not Eligible for a Credit, item 5, "Foreign taxes withheld on a dividend from a corporation, if you haven’t held the stock for at least 16 days within the 31-day period that begins 15 days before the ex-dividend date", and item 6, "Foreign taxes withheld on a dividend to the extent that you have to make related payments on positions in substantially similar or related property"

findings.situation: A filer's only foreign tax came through a mutual fund (1099-DIV) or a partnership/S corporation K-1. That filer generated an excess on Form 1116 in an earlier year, such as 2019, still within the 10-year carryforward, and filed only Form 1040 and its schedules for 2024. The filer could read 'paid income tax to a foreign country' as not covering tax withheld by a fund or entity, answer no, and then also answer no to the 2024-forms question.
findings.irs_text: i1116 (2025) p. 19, Line 10: "You can carry back 1 year and then forward 10 years any foreign tax you paid or accrued to any foreign country or U.S. territory ... on income in a separate category that is more than the limitation."
findings.why: The carryforward covers any foreign tax paid or accrued, including tax passed through on a 1099-DIV or K-1. The gate's wording 'paid income tax to a foreign country' can reasonably be read as excluding such indirect payments, and the fallback question about the 2024 return misses carryovers from earlier years when 2024 had no extra forms.

findings.situation: A filer who once paid foreign tax but never exceeded the limitation, or always used the election to claim the credit without Form 1116, satisfies the gate even though line 10 can have no amount.
findings.irs_text: i1116 (2025) p. 19, Line 10: "You can't carry over unused foreign taxes paid or accrued in a year to which the election doesn't apply to or from any year for which you made the election."
findings.why: The condition asks only whether foreign tax was ever paid, not whether any excess carryover arose, so it triggers the question in situations where the carryover is necessarily zero.

findings.situation: A filer whose 2024 return included any unrelated form (for example Form 8889 or Form 2441) satisfies the second branch without any foreign tax history.
findings.irs_text: i1116 (2025) p. 19, Line 10: "Enter the unused foreign taxes in the separate category from another tax year that are eligible to be carried forward to or back to 2025."
findings.why: Any non-1040 form on the 2024 return makes the computed condition true even though no foreign tax exists to carry over.

locators: p. 19, Line 10, "Enter the unused foreign taxes in the separate category from another tax year that are eligible to be carried forward to or back to 2025"

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 Schedule B line 8 showed a carryover, but a foreign tax refund, an audit or a larger actual carryback to 2023 has since cut it to zero, and the filer has excess foreign taxes in 2025 that create a new carryover.
findings.irs_text: i1116sb p. 1, Who Must File: 'if you're filing Form 1116 that has a foreign tax carryover in the prior tax year, the current tax year, or both, you must file Schedule B'; Line 2: 'Report on lines 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, etc., any adjustments resulting from events that occurred between the filing of your prior year tax return and the filing of your current year tax return.'
findings.why: After the adjustment nothing is left to carry into 2025, so the filer can truthfully answer no to 'Are any of your ... unused foreign taxes carried to 2025 from another tax year?'. The computed condition is then false and f1116sb.changed is never asked, but Schedule B is still required and its line 2 still needs a negative adjustment.

findings.situation: A filer files a joint 2025 return with the same spouse and carries foreign tax from an earlier joint year through a year when they filed separately, or files separately in 2025 and carries foreign tax from a separate-return year through a joint year.
findings.irs_text: p514 p. 39, Allocations Between Spouses: '2. You and your spouse file separate returns for the current tax year, to which you carry an unused foreign tax from a tax year for which you and your spouse filed separate returns, but through a tax year for which you and your spouse filed a joint return. 3. You and your spouse file a joint return for the current tax year, to which you carry an unused foreign tax from a tax year for which you and your spouse filed a joint return, but through a tax year for which you and your spouse filed separate returns.'
findings.why: The gate is reached in both cases, but the gated question only asks about tax 'carried into 2025 from an earlier joint return with someone you are not filing jointly with now'. Situation 3 uses the same spouse now, and in situation 2 the tax comes from a separate return, so the filer answers no and the required allocation (a refusal) is missed.

findings.situation: A filer who carries foreign tax only from their own earlier separate returns, with every year in between also separate, gets the carryover question and both gated questions.
findings.irs_text: p514 p. 39: 'For a tax year in which you and your spouse file separate returns, you figure the unused foreign tax or excess limit by using only your own separate income, deductions, taxes, and credits.'
findings.why: No allocation between spouses is needed here, so f1116sb.split has no amount. Asking costs only a question.

locators: p. 19, Line 10, "Enter the unused foreign taxes in the separate category from another tax year that are eligible to be carried forward to or back to 2025"

findings.situation: A filer's only foreign taxes fail the holding-period or related-payment rules, so creditable foreign taxes after reductions are $0 and the computed condition is false, yet those taxes can still be deducted on Schedule A.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "even if you take the credit for eligible foreign taxes for the year, you can take a deduction for the following. ... Taxes on income or gain that aren't creditable because you don't meet the holding period requirement"; i1040sca p. 7, Line 6: "Include on this line income taxes you paid to a foreign country"
findings.why: Schedule A line 6 covers foreign income taxes paid, not just creditable ones. Gating sa.foreign_tax_deduct on creditable taxes after reductions being above zero never asks this filer the question, and the deductible amount is dropped.

findings.situation: A partner gets foreign taxes passed through on a Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), or an estate or trust beneficiary gets them on a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), but owns no shares, received no 1099-DIV, had no taxable interest and paid no foreign tax directly.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 1: "Qualified payee statements include Form 1099-DIV, Form 1099-INT, Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S)"; p. 2: "You paid or accrued certain foreign taxes to a foreign country or U.S. territory"
findings.why: The helper counts foreign taxes only for share owners, 1099-DIV or interest recipients, or people who 'paid income tax to another country'. A partner or beneficiary whose tax was paid by the entity can truthfully answer no, so the creditable taxes come out zero and the election and Form 1116 questions are never asked.

findings.situation: A filer paid income tax to a U.S. territory such as Puerto Rico or Guam and had no other qualifying trigger.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "You paid or accrued certain foreign taxes to a foreign country or U.S. territory"; "For purposes of the credit, U.S. territories include Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa."
findings.why: The helper's trigger is 'ever paid income tax to another country'. A filer who paid tax to a U.S. territory can truthfully say no, so taxes creditable under the IRS text never reach the gated lines.

findings.situation: A filer who once paid foreign income tax in an earlier year, or who owns shares with no foreign tax, is asked the trigger question.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "income, war profits, and excess profits taxes paid or accrued during your tax year"
findings.why: 'Ever paid' reaches past years, but the computed amount must still be positive, so this only costs extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer, or spouse on a joint return, has applied for an ITIN but is not issued one by the return's due date (including extensions).
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "5. Filers and students must have been issued a TIN by the due date of their 2025 return (including extensions)."
findings.why: The computed condition counts someone who has only applied for an ITIN, so it holds even when the TIN requirement fails and the American opportunity credit is not allowed. This only means extra questions are asked; no amount is dropped.

findings.situation: The filer and spouse have SSNs or ITINs, but the American opportunity credit is barred for the student for another reason, such as the student having no TIN, 4 prior years of the credit, a felony drug conviction, or no Form 1098-T.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "Generally, you can claim the American opportunity credit for a student on a 2025 tax return only if all of the following seven requirements are met."
findings.why: The gate tests only the filers' identification numbers, so it holds where other requirements leave the gated lines with no effect. This direction is acceptable by design.

findings.situation: A never-married filer in a registered domestic partnership in California, Nevada or Washington files as single or head of household. The computed condition is false, so the tool never asks about community income or a pension earned during the partnership.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: "This publication is also for RDPs who are domiciled in Nevada, Washington, or California. RDPs ... must generally follow state community property laws and report half the combined community income ... RDPs aren't married for federal tax purposes. They can use the single filing status or, if they qualify, the head of household filing status."
findings.why: The helper looks only for a marriage (a stated filing status, or a single or head-of-household filer who was once married). A never-married RDP fails it, yet the text gives that RDP community income.

findings.situation: A never-married RDP receives a civil service annuity, pension or military retirement pay earned during the partnership while domiciled in a community property state. The gate is false, and the gated question would not cover this case even if it were asked.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 6: "it may be community income if it is based on services you performed while married (or during the registered domestic partnership) and domiciled in a community property state"; p. 5: "participation in the pension while married (or during the registered domestic partnership)"
findings.why: The text treats retirement pay earned during a registered domestic partnership like pay earned during a marriage. The gate requires a marriage, and the question asks only about a 'husband or wife'.

findings.situation: An RDP and their partner have different domiciles, and the partner is domiciled in California, Nevada or Washington. The gate is false, so the spouse-domicile question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2, Domicile: "If you and your spouse (or your RDP) have different domiciles, check the laws of each to see if you have community property, community income, or both."
findings.why: The cited text applies the domicile rule to an RDP as well as a spouse. The gate covers only a marriage, and the question asks only about a 'husband or wife'.

findings.situation: A single filer who divorced years ago, and who neither lives in a community property state nor receives retirement pay earned there, is still asked both questions.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: "This publication is for married taxpayers who are domiciled in one of the following community property states."
findings.why: Being married at some time in the past makes the gate true, even when the text gives these lines no effect. This is an acceptable lean toward yes.

findings.situation: A filer claims only the credit for other dependents (no CTC, ACTC, or EIC) and had an ODC denied after 2015 for a non-math/clerical reason, so Schedule 8812 line 8 is not greater than line 11 and the computed gate is false.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 2: 'If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error, you must attach Form 8862 to your tax return to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC unless an exception applies.'
findings.why: The gate's line-8-over-line-11 test does not hold for an ODC-only return, so the tool never asks about the prior ODC disallowance and treats it as false, even though the IRS text makes that prior disallowance matter when claiming ODC.

findings.situation: A filer currently claims EIC and had an EIC disallowance before 1996, or claims CTC/ODC and had a CTC/ODC disallowance before 2016, which the question's 'ever' wording captures.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: 'if your EIC for a year after 1996 was reduced or disallowed'; i1040gi p. 39: 'for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced'
findings.why: The gate is true because a current credit is claimed, and the broad 'ever' question would produce a yes even though the cited Form 8862 rules start only after 1996 or 2015; this is a yes-leaning wide gate, not a dropped amount.

findings.situation: A filer who is single or head of household and has never been married is a registered domestic partner in Nevada, Washington, or California and lived there in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 23: 'Nevada, Washington, and California domestic partners. A registered domestic partner in Nevada, Washington, or California must generally report half the combined community income of the individual and their domestic partner.'
findings.why: The gate is false because the filer has never been married, so the community-property question is not asked and the line is zero, even though the IRS text requires the domestic partner to split community income.

findings.situation: A single or head-of-household filer in a common-law marriage recognized by the state is asked only 'Have you ever been married?'
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6: 'You are living together in a common law marriage recognized in the state where you now live or in the state where the common law marriage began.'
findings.why: The gate does not say that a recognized common-law marriage counts as married; a filer who had no formal ceremony could reasonably answer no, making the gate false and dropping the marriage-related lines.

findings.situation: A filer uses qualifying surviving spouse status for 2025 after a spouse died in 2023 or 2024 and did not remarry.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6: 'For the next 2 years, you may be entitled to the special benefits described later under Qualifying Surviving Spouse.'
findings.why: The gate is true for qualifying surviving spouse status, but the spouse did not die in 2025 and the filer was not married during 2025, so every gated line is zero.

findings.situation: A filer separated under an interlocutory (not final) divorce decree at the end of 2025 may answer 'no' to 'Were you married at the end of 2025?', even though the IRS treats them as married and they could still be considered unmarried under the live-apart rules.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 14: "But if, at the end of 2025, your divorce wasn't final (an interlocutory decree), you are considered married."; p501 p. 6, Considered married: "4. You are separated under an interlocutory (not final) decree of divorce."
findings.why: Neither the question nor its helper says that a pending, non-final divorce still counts as married. A filer who reasonably answers no gets the considered-unmarried line silently set to false and may lose head of household status.

findings.situation: A filer in a common law marriage recognized by their state may say they have never been married, or answer no to 'Were you married at the end of 2025?', because there was no ceremony or license.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6, Considered married: "2. You are living together in a common law marriage recognized in the state where you now live or in the state where the common law marriage began."
findings.why: The 'has been married at some time' helper and the 'Were you married' question do not mention common law marriage. A filer can read 'married' as formal marriage only, which would skip the considered-unmarried question even though the filer is married for tax purposes.

findings.situation: A married couple filing a joint return, or a filer legally separated under a final decree of separate maintenance who still describes themselves as married, passes the gate even though the considered-unmarried line can't affect them.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 15, Married persons who live apart: "You file a separate return from your spouse."; p501 p. 6: "You are considered unmarried for the whole year if, on the last day of your tax year, you are either: • Unmarried, or • Legally separated from your spouse under a divorce or separate maintenance decree."
findings.why: The considered-unmarried rule applies only to a married person filing a separate return. Joint filers and legally separated filers are asked a question that can't change their result, which is acceptable because the gate leans to yes.

findings.situation: A K-1 shows a section 1231 loss in box 10, or another partnership loss outside boxes 1, 2, 3, 8, 9a, and 14 code A, but no loss in the listed boxes.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3, Basis Limitations: 'a partner may only claim their share of a partnership loss (including a capital loss) to the extent it doesn’t exceed their adjusted basis in the partnership'
findings.why: The basis question can matter for any partnership loss, but the computed gate is false when the only loss is in an unlisted box such as box 10, so the basis_short question is silently skipped.

findings.situation: A K-1 shows a section 179 expense deduction in box 12, or another deduction from an activity, and the partner has amounts not at risk, but no loss in the listed boxes.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8, At-Risk Limitations: 'These losses and deductions include a loss on the disposition of assets and the section 179 expense deduction'; and 'if you have (a) a loss or other deduction from any activity ... and (b) amounts in the activity for which you aren’t at risk, you’ll have to complete Form 6198'
findings.why: The gate tests only net losses in boxes 1, 2, 3, 8, 9a, and 14A, so it is false for a section 179 or other deduction even though the at-risk question matters.

findings.situation: A K-1 shows a box 1 loss that is fully covered by basis and has no not-at-risk amounts.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3, Basis Limitations: loss allowed only 'to the extent it doesn’t exceed their adjusted basis'; p. 8, At-Risk Limitations: Form 6198 only if there are 'amounts in the activity for which you aren’t at risk'
findings.why: The gate is true on any loss, so it asks the basis and at-risk questions even though the IRS text would allow the loss and require no limitation.

findings.situation: A non-manager LLC member or other partner who is not a limited partner has box 2 rental real estate income or loss and helped make management decisions, but the gate is false because item G is not general partner or LLC member-manager.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: 'Limited partners can’t actively participate unless future regulations provide an exception' and 'You may be treated as actively participating if you participated ... in making management decisions'
findings.why: The IRS text excludes limited partners, not every non-general/LLC-manager partner. An other LLC member's management decisions can therefore matter even though the gate skips the question and treats the line as false.

findings.situation: A general partner or LLC member-manager has a box 2 amount but owns less than 10% of the activity, including the spouse's interest, so the gate asks about management decisions even though active participation is unavailable.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: 'You aren’t considered to actively participate ... if ... your interest (including your spouse’s interest) in the activity was less than 10% (by value)'
findings.why: The IRS text adds a 10% ownership threshold that the gate does not check, so the gate can hold in a case where the answer cannot establish active participation.

p. 11, Special allowance for a rental real estate activity, "Management decisions that can count as active participation include approving new tenants, deciding rental terms, approving capital or repair expenditures"

findings.situation: A partnership reports only deductions or credits from a rental dwelling that a partner used personally above the 14-day/10% threshold, but boxes 2 and 3 show no amount.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: If you have net income (loss), deductions, or credits from any of the following activities, treat such amounts as nonpassive; item 2: The rental of a dwelling unit any partner used for personal purposes during the year for more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of the number of days that the residence was rented at fair rental value.
findings.why: The gate checks only boxes 2 and 3, which are net rental income/loss boxes. The cited special rule also covers deductions and credits from the dwelling activity, so the gate can be false even though the dwelling line matters.

findings.situation: The cited special-rule condition is personal use over the greater of 14 days or 10% of fair-rental days, but the gate condition is only that box 2 or box 3 shows an amount.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: The rental of a dwelling unit any partner used for personal purposes during the year for more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of the number of days that the residence was rented at fair rental value.
findings.why: The gate tests a different event, presence of a net rental amount, rather than the personal-use threshold. It can be true without personal use or false when only deductions or credits from the dwelling are reported.

findings.situation: Box 2 or box 3 shows a net rental amount, but no partner used a dwelling unit personally above the 14-day/10% threshold.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: The rental of a dwelling unit any partner used for personal purposes during the year for more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of the number of days that the residence was rented at fair rental value.
findings.why: The gate is true merely because a net rental amount is present, so it asks the dwelling question even though the special rule does not apply.

locators: p. 11, Special rules for certain other activities, "The rental of a dwelling unit any partner used for personal purposes during the year for more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of the number of days that the residence was rented at fair rental value"

findings.situation: A partner has no Box 1 ordinary business income or loss but has deductions or credits from the partnership activity, so material participation under test 5 still affects whether those items are passive.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'Effect of determination. Income (loss), deductions, and credits from an activity are nonpassive if you determine that: • You materially participated...' and passive amounts include 'deductions, and credits'.
findings.why: The gate requires Box 1 to show an amount, so it would skip test 5 even though the IRS makes material participation matter for deductions and credits from the activity.

findings.situation: A limited partner meets the factual criteria of test 2 or test 3 but not test 1, so test 5 is still needed because limited partners may qualify only under item 1, 5, or 6.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'Limited partners. If you’re a limited partner, you must meet item 1, 5, or 6 above to qualify as having materially participated.'
findings.why: The gate treats any meeting of tests 1-3 as making test 5 unnecessary; for a limited partner, tests 2 and 3 do not qualify, so skipping test 5 can drop the only applicable prior-year test.

findings.situation: The gate is keyed to failure of tests 1-3, not to the 5-of-10 prior-year participation condition stated for test 5.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'You materially participated in the activity for any 5 tax years (whether or not consecutive) during the 10 tax years that immediately precede the tax year.'
findings.why: The cited text states test 5's own condition—5 tax years in the preceding 10—but the gate condition is 'Box 1 shows an amount and tests 1, 2 and 3 are not met,' a different event and time frame.

findings.situation: A partner meets test 4 (significant participation) but not tests 1-3, so material participation is already established, yet the gate still asks test 5.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'The activity was a significant participation activity for the tax year, and you participated in all significant participation activities ... during the year for more than 500 hours.'
findings.why: Test 4 already makes the activity nonpassive, so the test 5 question is unnecessary; the gate does not exclude test 4.

locators: p. 9, Individuals (other than limited partners), "You materially participated in the activity for any 5 tax years (whether or not consecutive) during the 10 tax years that immediately precede the tax year"

findings.situation: A general partner participated 80 hours and no other individual participated, so test 3 fails only because it is not more than 100 hours, while test 2 can still be met.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: Your participation in the activity for the tax year constituted substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals; and test 3 requires more than 100 hours.
findings.why: The gate requires that the partner worked less than someone else, but test 3 can fail solely because the partner did not work more than 100 hours; the tool then treats the substantially-all question as false and drops a possible nonpassive amount.

findings.situation: A limited partner owned a general partnership interest at all times during the tax year and otherwise qualifies under test 2, but the gate is limited to a general partner.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: If you're an individual (either a general partner or a limited partner who owned a general partnership interest at all times during the tax year), you materially participated ... if one or more of the following apply.
findings.why: The cited person includes a limited partner with a general partnership interest at all times, while the computed gate is limited to a general partner, so it can be false for a filer the IRS text includes.

findings.situation: A filer did substantially all of the participation but would not describe it as nearly all of the work, because nearly all sounds like a higher threshold.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: constituted substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals.
findings.why: The gated question says nearly all of the work, not substantially all the participation; a truthful no to nearly all could be read as no even though the statutory test is met.

findings.situation: A general partner worked 50 hours and less than someone else but did not do substantially all, so the gate asks even though test 2 is not met.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: Your participation in the activity for the tax year constituted substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals.
findings.why: The condition holds because the partner worked 500 hours or less and less than someone else, but the IRS text gives no material participation under test 2 if the partner did not do substantially all.

locators: p. 9, Individuals (other than limited partners), "constituted substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals"

findings.situation: A partner's trade or business activity shows no amount in box 1 but has other items from that activity, such as a section 179 deduction, other deductions, or credits, and the partner materially participated in a personal service activity in 3 earlier years.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the partnership"; "Income (loss), deductions, and credits from an activity are nonpassive if you determine that: • You materially participated in a trade or business activity of the partnership"
findings.why: Material participation, including test 6, decides whether all of the activity's income, deductions and credits are passive, not only box 1. Because the gate requires a box 1 amount, it is false here and test 6 is treated as not met, so these items are wrongly treated as passive.

findings.situation: A partner materially participated for 3 earlier years in a service business outside the listed fields in which capital isn't a material income-producing factor, so the partner truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "A personal service activity involves the performance of personal services in the field of health, law, engineering, architecture, accounting, actuarial science, performing arts, or consulting, or any other trade or business in which capital isn't a material income-producing factor."
findings.why: The gated question lists only the named fields and leaves out the catch-all for any business where capital isn't a material income-producing factor. Such a filer meets test 6 but answers no, so the line is wrongly recorded as false.

locators: p. 9, Individuals (other than limited partners), "The activity was a personal service activity and you materially participated in the activity for any 3 tax years"

findings.situation: A married filing jointly filer is not a general partner, but the filer's spouse is the general partner and worked in the partnership in 2025; the computed gate is false because item G is not checked for the filer.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 9: 'Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership ... is counted toward material participation.'
findings.why: The IRS counts the spouse's work toward the filer's material participation, so tests 4 or 7 can apply; the gate only checks the filer's item G general-partner status and omits the spouse.

findings.situation: A limited partner owned a general partnership interest at all times during 2025 and met none of tests 1, 2, 3, and 5; the computed gate can be false if item G is not checked as general partner.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 9: 'If you’re an individual (either a general partner or a limited partner who owned a general partnership interest at all times during the tax year), you materially participated in an activity only if one or more of the following apply.'
findings.why: The IRS expressly lets that limited partner use the listed tests, including tests 4 and 7, but the gate requires general partner/LLC member-manager item G true, so it can suppress the gated test 4/7 lines.

findings.situation: The gate condition is for a general partner who met none of tests 1, 2, 3, and 5, while its cited authority is the limited-partner rule requiring tests 1, 5, or 6.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 9: 'If you’re a limited partner, you must meet item 1, 5, or 6 above to qualify as having materially participated.'
findings.why: The cited text states a different person (limited partner) and different tests (1, 5, or 6) than the gate's general-partner condition (none of 1, 2, 3, 5).

findings.situation: A filer worked over 100 hours in another business in which the filer materially participated under another test, and is unsure whether the question's 'other businesses where you worked over 100 hours' includes that business.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 9: 'A significant participation activity is any trade or business activity in which you participated for more than 100 hours during the year and in which you didn’t materially participate under any of the material participation tests (other than this test).'
findings.why: The gated question says only 'over 100 hours,' not 'significant participation activity'; it can be read to include businesses excluded by the IRS definition.

findings.situation: A general partner has a box 1 amount and checked item G but did no work in the partnership in 2025; the computed gate can still be true because it does not test the 'worked in the business' helper.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 9: 'You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours during the tax year' or 'you participated in the activity on a regular, continuous, and substantial basis during the tax year.'
findings.why: With no participation, the IRS gives tests 4 and 7 no amount, but the gate can still ask them because the computed helpers only check box 1 and item G.

findings.situation: A filer whose spouse meets the 750-hour and more-than-half tests but who did not materially participate in the partnership's rental real estate activity answers yes and is refused, though box 2 stays passive.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 14, Box 2: "the income (loss) in box 2 isn’t from a passive activity if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier) and you materially participated in the activity"
findings.why: Nonpassive treatment needs both real estate professional status and material participation in the activity. The question tests only the hours, so some yes answers lead to a refusal the text does not call for.

findings.situation: The computed condition is true for every filer with a box 2 amount and no rental or royalty of their own, including filers who plainly are not real estate professionals.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 14, Box 2: "Generally, the income (loss) reported in box 2 is a passive activity amount for all partners."
findings.why: For most filers with a box 2 amount it is passive and the gated line has no effect. Asking them costs only one question, which matches the gate's lean to yes.

findings.situation: A general partner with a box 2 amount actively participates by arranging repairs or other services in a significant and bona fide sense but does not help make management decisions.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "You may be treated as actively participating if you participated, for example, in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense."
findings.why: The gate is false because it requires helping make management decisions, so it skips the 10%-ownership line and treats it as false; the IRS text treats arranging services as an alternative way to actively participate.

findings.situation: The gate asks the 10%-ownership line only after management decisions, while the cited active-participation rule also treats arranging for others to provide services as sufficient.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "You may be treated as actively participating if you participated, for example, in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense."
findings.why: The cited text states an alternative condition, 'or arranging for others to provide services,' that the gate omits; the gate condition differs by event/activity.

findings.situation: A corporation is a general partner with a box 2 amount and helps make management decisions.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "Estates (other than qualifying estates), trusts (other than qualifying revocable trusts that made a section 645 election), and corporations can’t actively participate."
findings.why: The gate would be true and ask the 10%-ownership line, but the IRS says corporations cannot actively participate, so the gated line has no amount for them.

findings.situation: A general partner had more than 500 total hours, but some hours were investor-type or avoid-passive-loss work that the IRS excludes from material participation, so counted participation was 500 or less and test 3 could matter.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'work in connection with the activity isn’t counted toward material participation if either of the following applies' and lists work to avoid the passive loss or credit limitations or work 'in your capacity as an investor.'
findings.why: The gate turns off test 3 based on 'worked ... 500 hours or less' without regard to the IRS rule excluding certain work; a filer with more than 500 gross hours but 500 or fewer counted hours can fail the gate while still needing the test 3 question.

findings.situation: A limited partner who owned a general partnership interest at all times worked more than 100 hours and at least as many hours as anyone else, so test 3 applies under the IRS text.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'either a general partner or a limited partner who owned a general partnership interest at all times during the tax year' and test 3: 'You participated ... for more than 100 hours ... and ... wasn’t less than ... any other individual.'
findings.why: The gate requires the 'General partner or LLC member-manager (item G)' helper, so it does not ask test 3 for a limited partner with a general partnership interest at all times, even though the IRS text includes that person in the individual material participation tests.

findings.situation: The gate's cited text is the limited-partner rule, but the gate condition is a general partner who worked 500 hours or less.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9, Limited partners: 'If you’re a limited partner, you must meet item 1, 5, or 6 above to qualify as having materially participated.'
findings.why: The cited condition applies to limited partners and excludes item 3, while the gate condition applies to general partners and uses a 500-hour-or-less threshold to decide when to ask item 3.

findings.situation: The gated question asks whether 'you (or your spouse)' worked more than 100 hours, which could be read as each spouse separately or as their combined hours.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership ... is counted toward material participation.'
findings.why: The IRS counts both spouses' work toward material participation, but the question does not state that the hours are combined; a filer with 60 hours each could answer no even though combined hours exceed 100.

findings.situation: A general partner worked 500 hours or less in an activity that is not a trade or business or rental real estate activity, where the IRS material participation tests do not make the gated line matter.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the partnership, and (b) if you were a real estate professional ... in each rental real estate activity held through the partnership.'
findings.why: The gate can be true for a general partner under 500 hours even when the activity is outside the material participation determination, so it may ask an unnecessary question; this is a wide gate only.

findings.situation: The partnership distributes property with a zero adjusted basis (for example, fully depreciated equipment), so box 19 shows code C with $0 or no dollar figure, and the filer may answer that box 19 shows no amount.
findings.irs_text: Code C is used to report the partnership's adjusted basis in property other than money immediately before the property was distributed to you (i1065sk1 2025 p. 25)
findings.why: Box 19 reports the partnership's basis in the property, not the distribution's value, so a real distribution can appear as a code with a zero amount. "Show an amount" can be read as requiring a nonzero dollar figure. A filer reading it that way answers no, and the tool sets b19_other_if_any to false even though box 19 shows a code other than A.

findings.situation: Box 19 shows only a code A cash amount that does not exceed the filer's basis in the partnership interest.
findings.irs_text: To the extent the cash and the FMV of the securities (reduced by the reduction amount) received exceed the adjusted basis of your partnership interest immediately before the distribution, the excess is treated as gain (i1065sk1 2025 p. 25)
findings.why: The gate holds, but neither gated line ends up with an amount: there is no non-A code and no excess over basis. This only costs two extra questions.

findings.situation: The partnership sold depreciable real property used in its business, so the gain is net section 1231 gain reported in box 10 and its unrecaptured section 1250 portion is reported in box 9c, while box 9a is blank.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9c: "Report unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of the partnership's business assets on line 5. ... If the partnership reports only unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of its business assets, it'll enter a dollar amount in box 9c." Box 10: "If the amount is ... a gain, report it in column (g) of Form 4797, line 2."
findings.why: Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale of business assets comes from section 1231 gain, which the partnership reports in box 10, not box 9a. So box 9c can show an amount when box 9a is empty. A filer who truthfully answers no to the box 9a question never reaches the 9b/9c question, and the box 9c amount the Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain Worksheet needs is dropped.

findings.situation: The partnership's collectibles gain is exactly offset by other long-term capital losses, so box 9a nets to zero or is blank while box 9b shows the collectibles gain.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9b: "Report collectibles gain or loss on line 4 of the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet—Line 18 in the Instructions for Schedule D (Form 1040)."
findings.why: Box 9a is a net figure across all long-term items, so it can be zero while the collectibles component in box 9b is not. The 28% Rate Gain Worksheet still uses the box 9b amount when the filer has other capital gains, so gating on box 9a drops it.

findings.situation: A filer reads the help text "Both are parts of the gain in box 9a" while box 9c reflects section 1231 gain shown in box 10.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 pp. 15-16: "The information reported in boxes 9b and 9c relates to collectibles (28%) gain (loss) and unrecaptured section 1250 gain flowing through the partnership."
findings.why: The IRS text does not say 9b and 9c are parts of box 9a. The help text tells the filer otherwise, which can lead them to assume 9b and 9c don't matter when 9a is blank, and would wrongly support the gate.

locators: p. 15, Box 9a. Net Long-Term Capital Gain (Loss), "Report the net long-term capital gain (loss) on Schedule D (Form 1040), line 12"
p. 16, Box 9b. Collectibles (28%) Gain (Loss), "Report collectibles gain or loss on line 4 of the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet"

findings.situation: A partnership sells depreciable real property used in its business, reports the gain as net section 1231 gain in box 10, and enters the unrecaptured portion in box 9c, leaving box 9a blank because it has no net long-term capital gain.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9c: "Report unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of the partnership's business assets on line 5" and "If the partnership reports only unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of its business assets, it'll enter a dollar amount in box 9c."
findings.why: Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from business assets normally comes through section 1231 gain (box 10), not box 9a. So box 9c can carry an amount while box 9a is blank, and the computed condition is false and drops the box 9c amount.

findings.situation: A partnership's collectibles gain in box 9b is exactly offset by other long-term capital losses, so box 9a nets to zero or blank while box 9b shows an amount.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9b: "Report collectibles gain or loss on line 4 of the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet—Line 18 in the Instructions for Schedule D (Form 1040)."
findings.why: Nothing in the cited text makes box 9b depend on box 9a. Box 9a is a net figure that can be zero while box 9b is not, and in that case the gate drops an amount that belongs on line 4 of the worksheet.

findings.situation: The gated lines are labeled "asked only when box 9b or 9c shows an amount", but the computed condition also requires box 9a to show an amount.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9b/9c (no text conditions boxes 9b or 9c on box 9a)
findings.why: The description of the gate and its computation differ, and the extra box 9a requirement has no basis in the cited text. The box 9b/9c helper alone would be the right gate.

locators: p. 16, Box 9b. Collectibles (28%) Gain (Loss), "Report collectibles gain or loss on line 4 of the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet"
p. 16, Box 9c. Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain, "If the partnership reports only unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of its business assets, it’ll enter a dollar amount in box 9c"

findings.situation: A partnership activity has a prior-year unallowed loss carried forward on the 2024 Form 8582, but the 2025 K-1 shows no amount in box 1, 2 or 3. For example, the activity broke even this year, or the K-1 reports only other items.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV/Part V Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: Column (c) needs the carried-forward loss for every activity that has one, whether or not columns (a) or (b) show a current-year amount. The computed condition is false whenever boxes 1–3 are blank, so the carryforward is silently dropped from lines 1c/2c.

findings.situation: In a year with blank boxes 1–3, a filer disposes of the partnership interest or keeps it with no current operating items, and still holds unallowed losses from earlier years.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Columns (d) and (e): "Combine income and losses in columns (a) through (c) for each activity, and either enter the overall gain for the activity in column (d) or enter the overall loss for the activity in column (e)."
findings.why: Columns (d)/(e) contemplate an activity whose only entry is column (c). Gating on current-year box 1–3 amounts excludes exactly this case.

findings.situation: A filer is asked whether a loss was "held back on an earlier return" and must classify it as "from the business (box 1)", "rental real estate (box 2)" or "other rentals (box 3)".
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV: "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The IRS text identifies the amount by the prior Form 8582 Part VII column (c), not by "held back" or by K-1 box. A filer may not recognize a suspended passive loss (or a prior-year CRD) as "held back", or may not know which current-year box an earlier suspended loss belongs to.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A partnership's K-1 shows no amount in box 1, 2 or 3 this year, but the filer's 2024 Form 8582, Part VII, column (c), shows an unallowed loss carried forward from that partnership's business activity. The computed condition is false, so the prior-year loss is zeroed.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part V, Column (c): "Enter the unallowed losses for the prior years for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The IRS text asks for the prior-year unallowed loss for each activity whether or not the activity has current-year income or loss. Tying the gate to a box 1–3 amount drops carryforwards from activities that are inactive this year. Those carryforwards can still be allowed against other passive income or on disposition.

findings.situation: A filer is asked whether a loss was 'held back' from the business in box 1.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: 'Held back' could be read as losses suspended under the basis or at-risk limits rather than prior-year passive losses unallowed on Form 8582. The question does not point to Form 8582, Part VII, column (c). A filer whose only carryforward is a passive loss could answer no.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A filer carries a prior-year unallowed rental real estate loss from this partnership, but this year's Schedule K-1 shows nothing in boxes 1, 2 and 3 (for example, the activity broke even or had no current-year items), so the outer helper is false and the carryover is set to zero without asking.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: Prior-year unallowed losses carry forward to column (c) whether or not the K-1 shows a current-year amount. Making the gate depend on a nonzero box 1, 2 or 3 drops a carryover the IRS text requires the filer to enter.

findings.situation: The inner helper "Held-back loss from rental real estate (box 2)" does not say whether it means a loss carried over from a prior year's Form 8582 or a loss limited this year, so a filer could answer no about a 2024 carryover.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: "Held back" names neither the year nor Form 8582 Part VII. A filer who reads it as this year's limitation, or who doesn't connect it to the 2024 form, could answer no and lose the carryover.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A filer has a prior-year unallowed loss from a partnership's other-rental activity (box 3), carried on the 2024 Form 8582, but the 2025 K-1 shows no amount in boxes 1, 2 or 3. For example, the activity broke even or was inactive this year.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Part V, Column (c): "Enter the unallowed losses for the prior years for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The instructions require the prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) whether or not the activity has current-year income or loss. The computed condition is false whenever boxes 1, 2 and 3 are blank, so the carryover is silently set to zero and never reaches line 2c.

findings.situation: A filer who actively participated in a rental real estate activity in both years has a prior-year unallowed loss from it, but the current K-1 shows nothing in boxes 1, 2 or 3.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582. Enter the total of column (c) from your 2025 Part IV on Part I, line 1c"
findings.why: Part IV column (c) also takes the carryover with no requirement that the activity show a current-year amount. Gating on current-year boxes 1 to 3 drops it.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A partner is a real estate professional with more than 500 hours in a rental real estate activity held through the partnership, but box 1 shows no ordinary business income or loss.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'You must determine if you materially participated ... in each trade or business activity held through the partnership, and ... in each rental real estate activity'; 'You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours during the tax year.'
findings.why: The gate requires box 1 to show an amount, but box 1 is ordinary business income or loss; material participation test 1 can be met and matter for a rental real estate activity without any box 1 amount, so the condition is false and the gated line is dropped.

findings.situation: The filer did not work in the business, but the filer's spouse did more than 500 hours in the partnership activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership ... is counted toward material participation.'
findings.why: The gate helper asks only whether the filer worked in the business; the cited text counts the spouse's work too, so a truthful no on the helper can wrongly suppress a spouse-only more-than-500-hours test.

findings.situation: A filer reads 'worked in the business' as limited to ordinary trade or business work and not work in connection with a rental real estate activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership.'
findings.why: The IRS phrase is activity-based and includes rental real estate activity, while 'in the business' can reasonably be read more narrowly.

findings.situation: Box 1 shows an amount and the filer worked in the business for 10 hours, not more than 500 hours.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours during the tax year.'
findings.why: The gate holds and asks the hours question even though test 1 is not met; this is an unnecessary yes-gate question, not a dropped amount.

locators: p. 9, Individuals (other than limited partners), "You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours during the tax year"
p. 9, Work counted toward material participation, "any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership"

findings.situation: A filer did not make management decisions but did arrange for others to provide services in a significant and bona fide sense, and otherwise met the 10% ownership test.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: You may be treated as actively participating if you participated, for example, in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense.
findings.why: The gate asks only about management decisions, so it can be false and force the 10%-all-year line to false even though the IRS text allows active participation through arranging services; the 10% test still matters.

findings.situation: A filer made management decisions but at some time during the year had less than 10% interest, including the spouse’s interest.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: You aren’t considered to actively participate in a rental real estate activity if, at any time during the tax year, your interest (including your spouse’s interest) in the activity was less than 10% (by value) of all interests in the activity.
findings.why: The cited active-participation condition includes the 10%-at-any-time limit, while the gate condition is management decisions alone; the gate can hold even though the source condition says there is no active participation.

locators: p. 5, Special allowance for a rental real estate activity, "You aren’t considered to actively participate in a rental real estate activity if, at any time during the tax year, your interest (including your spouse’s interest) in the activity was less than 10% (by value) of all interests in the activity"

findings.situation: The S corporation passes through deductions or credits from a dwelling-unit rental that a shareholder used personally, for example a section 179 deduction (box 11), other deductions (box 12) or rental credits (box 13), while box 2 and box 3 are blank because the rental's net income is zero or is reported only through those other items.
findings.irs_text: If you have net income (loss), deductions, or credits from either of the following activities, treat such amounts as nonpassive ... 1. The rental of a dwelling unit any shareholder used for personal purposes ... (i1120ssk 2025 p. 5)
findings.why: The rule reaches deductions and credits from the dwelling rental, not just net rental income. The computed gate looks only at boxes 2 and 3, so in this case it is false and the nonpassive treatment is silently dropped.

findings.situation: The S corporation has a fiscal tax year, and the shareholder's personal use falls in its tax year but not in calendar 2025, or the reverse.
findings.irs_text: used for personal purposes during the year for more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of the number of days that the residence was rented at fair rental value (i1120ssk 2025 p. 5)
findings.why: The question asks about use 'In 2025', while the text measures use 'during the year', which means the corporation's tax year. A filer of a fiscal-year S corporation could count the wrong period and truthfully answer no.

findings.situation: A filer with a box 2 amount who meets the 750-hour/half-of-work-time test but did not materially participate in the S corporation's rental real estate activity is asked the question, and a Yes refuses the return, although box 2 stays passive.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 6, Box 2: "the income (loss) in box 2 isn't from a passive activity if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier) and you materially participated in the activity"
findings.why: The gate and the question do not test material participation in the corporation's activity, so the question is reached, and a refusal can follow, where the IRS text keeps box 2 passive. This leans to yes by design.

findings.situation: Box 17 shows code V with an asterisk or "STMT" and no dollar figure, because the section 199A information (QBI, W-2 wages, UBIA, section 199A dividends) is on an attached statement; a filer could truthfully say box 17 shows no amount, which skips the code V question and drops the QBI deduction inputs.
findings.irs_text: f1120ssk p. 1: "17 Other information"; i1120ssk p. 17, Code V: "The S corporation will provide the information you need to figure your deduction."
findings.why: Box 17 holds information, not only amounts, and code V is usually reported by statement rather than as a single figure in the box. Asking whether the box "shows an amount" lets a truthful no skip a code that is present.

findings.situation: Box 17 shows only statement-type codes with no dollar figure, such as code D (basis of energy property), AJ (excess business loss statement) or AW (reportable transactions); a filer could truthfully say no amount is shown, so the other-codes question that should stop the interview is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 15, Code D: "If the corporation provides an attached statement for code D, use the information on the statement..."; p. 18, Code AW: "Any information you need to complete a disclosure statement for reportable transactions..."
findings.why: These codes appear in box 17 as information or statement references rather than amounts. A truthful no on "shows an amount" skips the refusal for out-of-scope codes.

findings.situation: A filer sees a code letter in box 17 with "STMT" or "*" where a number would go and must decide whether that counts as box 17 "show[ing] an amount".
findings.irs_text: f1120ssk p. 1: "17 Other information"; footnote "* See attached statement for additional information."
findings.why: "Amount" can reasonably be read as a dollar figure only, or as any entry in the box. The gate should ask whether box 17 shows any code or entry at all.

findings.situation: A filer has a section 179 expense deduction from the S corporation and amounts not at risk, but no loss in boxes 1, 2, 3, 7, or 8a.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: 'These losses and deductions include a loss on the disposition of assets and the section 179 expense deduction.'
findings.why: The IRS at-risk text applies to the section 179 expense deduction, but the gate counts only losses in boxes 1, 2, 3, 7, and 8a; with no such loss the gate is false and the not-at-risk question is skipped.

findings.situation: A filer has a loss on disposition of assets (for example, a section 1231 loss) and amounts not at risk, but no loss in boxes 1, 2, 3, 7, or 8a.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: 'These losses and deductions include a loss on the disposition of assets and the section 179 expense deduction.'
findings.why: The gate's listed loss boxes do not include a loss on disposition of assets, so the condition can be false even though the cited text says at-risk limitations apply.

findings.situation: The cited text states the Form 6198 condition as a loss or other deduction plus amounts not at risk, while the gate uses only losses in the listed boxes.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: 'Generally, if you have (a) a loss or other deduction from any activity carried on as a trade or business or for the production of income by the corporation, and (b) amounts in the activity for which you aren’t at risk, you will have to complete Form 6198...'
findings.why: The gate differs by omitting 'other deduction' and by not matching the cited loss-or-deduction plus not-at-risk condition.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the question asks 'Is any money or property you put into it' and does not say whether the spouse's money or property is included.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: 'Any cash or property contributed to a corporate activity, or your interest in the corporate activity...'
findings.why: A filer could reasonably read 'you' as only the filer, so a spouse's not-at-risk contribution might be answered no; the question should cover the spouse on a joint return.

locators: p. 3, At-Risk Limitations, "you will have to complete Form 6198, At-Risk Limitations, to figure your allowable loss for the activity"

findings.situation: An S corporation shareholder has no box 1 amount but has a rental real estate activity held through the corporation with a passive loss and materially participated under test 2, 4, or 7.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: 'You must determine if you materially participated ... in each rental real estate activity held through the corporation'; 'If you have a passive activity loss or credit, use Form 8582...'
findings.why: The gate's worked helper is false whenever box 1 does not show an amount, so the tool never asks the other-tests question and zeros the line even though material participation can matter for the rental activity and passive loss.

findings.situation: Only the filer's spouse worked in the S corporation activity, and the spouse's work alone satisfies test 2, 4, or 7.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: 'Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through an S corporation ... is counted toward material participation.'
findings.why: The gate's 'Worked in the business' helper does not mention the spouse, so a spouse-only participant could answer no and the gate would be false even though the gated question and IRS text count the spouse's work.

findings.situation: The filer's only work is investor-type work that the IRS says is not counted toward material participation.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: 'You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren't directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the activity' and such work isn't counted.
findings.why: The gate can be true because the filer 'worked,' even though the IRS text gives no material participation amount for investor work.

findings.situation: On a 2025 joint return, this S corporation's K-1 belongs to the spouse, whose 2024 passive loss was disallowed on a separate 2024 return (unmarried or married filing separately), so the filer can truthfully say no loss was held back on 'your 2024 return'.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part V, Column (c): "Enter the unallowed losses for the prior years for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The spouse's carryover from their own 2024 Form 8582 belongs in column (c) of the 2025 joint Form 8582. The question asks only about 'your 2024 return' and doesn't mention a spouse's separate 2024 return, so a truthful no drops the amount.

findings.situation: A loss from this corporation arose in 2022 or 2023 and was still unallowed when the 2024 return was filed, but no new loss arose in 2024, and the filer reads 'held back on your 2024 return' as covering only a 2024 loss.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: Column (c) holds all accumulated prior-year unallowed losses, not just 2024's. The gate wording can be read as asking only whether a 2024 loss was disallowed, although the help pointing to Part VII, column (c) lessens the risk.

locators: p. 10, Column (c), "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity"

findings.situation: The shareholder worked more than 100 hours in the S corporation with no one else working more, but Schedule K-1 box 1 shows no amount, so the tool's 'Worked in the business' helper is false and the under-500 gate is false.
findings.irs_text: You must determine if you materially participated ... in each trade or business activity held through the corporation; You participated ... for more than 100 hours during the tax year, and your participation ... wasn’t less than ... any other individual (i1120ssk p. 4).
findings.why: The IRS material participation test is not conditioned on box 1 showing an amount; the gate can therefore drop a true test-3 line when box 1 is zero.

findings.situation: The S corporation has a fiscal tax year that is not the 2025 calendar year, so the shareholder's hours in 2025 differ from the hours in the corporation's tax year.
findings.irs_text: All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the corporation’s tax year (i1120ssk p. 4); the gated question asks work more than 100 hours in it in 2025.
findings.why: The gated question uses calendar 2025, while the cited text requires measuring participation over the corporation's tax year.

findings.situation: The shareholder spent more than 100 hours in the S corporation only doing investor-type work that the IRS says is not counted, but the gated question asks broadly about 'work' and the help says to compare hours.
findings.irs_text: Work ... isn’t counted toward material participation if ... You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren’t directly involved in the day-to-day operations (i1120ssk p. 4).
findings.why: The gate can be true on hours that the IRS excludes from material participation, so it may ask the gated question when the IRS gives no amount.

findings.situation: A real estate professional gets a rental real estate loss in box 2 and nothing in box 1, so the gate is false and the more-than-500-hours test is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation; and (b) if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier), in each rental real estate activity held through the corporation."
findings.why: Material participation, including the 500-hour test, also matters for rental real estate activities reported outside box 1. Gating on box 1 alone sets the hours line to false for these filers.

findings.situation: A shareholder's trade or business activity shows up only in boxes other than box 1 (for example a box 10 or other trade-or-business item listed on the attached activity statement), so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "If the corporation has more than one activity, it will attach a statement to your Schedule K-1 that identifies each activity ... and specifies the income (loss), deductions, and credits from each activity."
findings.why: The passive-activity test applies to every trade or business activity's income, deductions and credits, not only to box 1 ordinary income. A box 1 condition can miss activities that matter.

findings.situation: The S corporation has a fiscal year, and the filer counts hours in calendar 2025 instead of hours in the corporation's tax year.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the corporation's tax year"; test 1: "more than 500 hours during the tax year"
findings.why: Both the gate helper ("worked in the corporation's business in 2025") and the gated question ("more than 500 hours in it in 2025") use calendar 2025, but the cited text measures participation over the corporation's tax year.

findings.situation: The corporation runs more than one activity, and the filer is asked about hours "in it" (the corporation) rather than in each activity.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation"
findings.why: Material participation is decided activity by activity. A corporation-wide hours question can be read as total hours or as hours per activity.

findings.situation: The filer counts hours worked before owning the stock, or investor-type work such as reviewing financial statements, and so answers yes.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "(where you own your stock at the time the work is done)"; "You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren't directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the activity."
findings.why: Neither the gate nor the gated question excludes non-counting work, so they can come out true where the IRS text gives no material participation. This leans to yes and does not change the verdict.
