findings.situation: A person born on any day of 1976 after January 1 is only 49 at the end of 2025, yet the computed gate holds and the question is asked.

findings.why: Only a person born January 1, 1976 can be treated as age 50 at the end of 2025, because age is reached the day before the birthday. Anyone born after 1975 has the gate open but the line is no. Anyone born before 1976 is clearly 50 or older, so this open-year line is not needed for them.

findings.situation: A filer born in 1971 on any day other than January 1 turns 54 during 2025, so the gate holds but the filer can only answer no and the age-55 amount never applies.

findings.why: Only someone born on January 1, 1971 is close to 55 on December 31, 2025. Everyone else born in 1971 is 54, so for them the question costs a few extra prompts. findings.situation: A person whose HSA got an excess contribution in an earlier year, still in the account, but who had no HSA contributions or distributions in 2025, so no Form 8889 was entered and the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: f5329 (2025) p. 2, Part VII: "Complete this part if you, someone on your behalf, or your employer contributed more to your HSAs for 2025 than is allowable or you had an amount on line 49 of your 2024 Form 5329."; line 42: "Enter the excess contributions from line 48 of your 2024 Form 5329."
findings.why: Part VII applies whenever a prior-year excess carries forward, even with no 2025 HSA activity. Such a person may have no Form 8889 to enter, so a count of Forms 8889 can be zero while the 6% tax on line 49 still applies to the carried-over excess.

findings.situation: The gate cites the Part II (education/ABLE distributions) and Part IX (missed required minimum distributions) conditions, but the gated line is the Part VII HSA carryover, whose stated condition is different.

findings.situation: A person made no nondeductible contribution for 2025 (line 1 is zero) but has basis from nondeductible contributions in earlier years and took a 2025 traditional IRA distribution.

findings.why: Part I must be completed here, so line 2 carries the prior basis from the Total Basis Chart and the line-4 distribution question is answered yes. findings.why: Part I applies, so line 2 holds the prior basis and the conversion question is answered yes. The gate is false because line 1 is zero, which drops the basis and the refusal.

findings.situation: The gate uses whether an RMD is possible (born 1952 or earlier or inherited account), but Form 5329 Part IX is completed only if the filer actually did not receive the required minimum distribution.
findings.irs_text: f5329 (2025) p. 3, Part IX: 'Complete this part if you did not receive the minimum required distribution from your qualified retirement plan.'
findings.why: The cited condition is the event of a missed RMD, while the gate is a broader possibility screen; the gate condition differs from the stated condition.

findings.situation: A filer born in 1952 or earlier who is still working for a non-5% employer and has not retired has no RMD yet from that qualified plan.

findings.why: The gate is true because of age, but the IRS text delays the RMD until retirement for a non-5% owner, so the gated line is zero.

findings.situation: A filer born in 1952 or earlier who owns only a Roth IRA has no lifetime RMD.
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 9: 'Roth IRA. There are no minimum required distributions during the lifetime of the owner of a Roth IRA.'
findings.why: The gate is true because of age, but the IRS text imposes no RMD during the owner's lifetime, so the gated line is zero.

findings.situation: A participant born in 1963, 1964 or 1965 turns 62, 61 or 60 during 2025, but the gate is false for them, so the line takes the age-50 parameter and drops the higher $5,250 SIMPLE catch-up limit.
findings.irs_text: p560 (2025) p. 16: "allow participants to make a higher amount of catch-up contributions in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63. For 2025 and 2026, the higher limit on catch-up contributions to SIMPLE plans for such participants is $5,250."
findings.why: Attaining age 60–63 in 2025 means being born in 1962 through 1965. The gate tests only 1962 and 1966, and the fallback assumes everyone else is 50–59 or 64 and over, so three birth years in the 60–63 band get no higher limit.

findings.situation: The gate assumes the exact birth date decides the band in the boundary years, but the cited text sets the band by the age attained during the tax year, which the birth year alone decides.
findings.irs_text: p560 (2025) p. 16: "in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63" and "age 50 or over at the end of the calendar year"; the gate is "Born in 1962 or 1966 (a year in which the birth date decides whether the SIMPLE catch-up age band is 60 to 63)"
findings.why: Under 'attain age in the tax year', everyone born in 1962 reaches 63 in 2025 and everyone born in 1966 reaches 59, whatever their birth date. The gate's 'open years' do not match the time frame the cited text states.

findings.situation: A filer born in 1966 is asked their age even though they reach only 59 in 2025, and a filer born in 1962 is asked even though they always reach 63.
findings.irs_text: p560 (2025) p. 16: "in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63"
findings.why: For both birth years the answer is already fixed by the birth year, so the question is redundant. It drops no amount.

findings.situation: A person born on January 1 or January 2, 1960 is treated as reaching 65 on December 31, 2024 or January 1, 2025, so they cannot die in 2025 before reaching 65, yet the condition still holds and the question is asked.
findings.irs_text: If a taxpayer was born before January 2, 1961, but died in 2025 before reaching age 65 ... A person is considered to reach age 65 on the day before the person's 65th birthday. (i1040gi p. 110)
findings.why: Only people whose 65th birthday or the day before it fell in 2025 can die in 2025 before reaching 65, so these two 1960 birth dates cost an extra question but never carry an amount.

findings.situation: Any living person born in 1960 or on January 1, 1961 meets the condition and is asked the question, though the answer is always No.
findings.irs_text: Death of a taxpayer in 2025. If a taxpayer was born before January 2, 1961, but died in 2025 before reaching age 65, then the taxpayer doesn't qualify for the enhanced deduction for seniors. (i1040gi p. 110)
findings.why: The rule applies only to people who died in 2025, so for living people the gate asks a question whose line is always false. The cost is small and the gate leans to yes by design.

findings.situation: A filer born in 2011 or later (for example, a 13-year-old filing their own first return to get back withholding) is under age 16 at the end of 2025, but the computed condition 'born in 2010' is false, so the question is never asked and the line is set to no.

findings.why: Anyone born from 2010 through 2025 can be under 16 at the end of 2025. A gate that checks only for birth year 2010 misses every younger filer that this restriction covers.

findings.why: The cited condition is age under 16 at the end of 2025 combined with first-time-filer status. 'Born in 2010' covers a different set of birth years and ignores first-time-filer status.

findings.situation: A filer has a post-2017 business loss that was fully suspended, for example a passive loss under section 469 or an at-risk loss under section 465. With no other QBI they filed no Form 8995 that year, and the loss is allowed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p. 3: "When losses or deductions previously suspended by other Code provisions are allowed in calculating taxable income, the qualified portion of the loss or deduction allowed under each provision is treated as a qualified net loss carryforward from a separate trade or business when calculating the current year's QBI deduction. See Line 3."; p. 4, Line 3: "Include here the qualified portion of trade or business (loss) carryforward allowed in calculating taxable income in the current year"
findings.why: Line 3 takes an amount from a suspended loss released this year even if no prior return included Form 8995 or 8995-A. This filer truthfully answers No, so line 3 is zeroed. The gated question also asks only for a prior line 16, which never contains such released suspended losses.

findings.situation: A filer has a PTP loss from 2018 or later that was suspended under the passive loss rules, and no Form 8995 was filed that year. In 2025 the loss is allowed, for example on disposing of the interest.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p. 4: "When losses or deductions previously suspended by other Code provisions are allowed in calculating taxable income, the qualified portion of the loss or deduction allowed for each PTP is treated as a qualified net loss carryforward from a separate PTP when calculating the current year's QBI deduction. See Line 7."; Line 7: "Include here the qualified portion of PTP (loss) carryforward allowed in calculating taxable income in the current year, even if the loss was from a PTP that you no longer hold an interest in"
findings.why: Line 7 gets an amount, and the tool should refuse because REIT/PTP carryforwards are out of scope. A filer with no prior Form 8995 or 8995-A answers No, so the refusal is never reached and line 7 is silently treated as zero.

findings.situation: A prior return included Form 8995 or 8995-A, but its lines 16 and 17 were zero, and no suspended loss is allowed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: f8995 line 16: "Total qualified business (loss) carryforward. Combine lines 2 and 3. If greater than zero, enter -0-"
findings.why: The condition holds even though both gated lines are zero. This only costs the filer extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer itemized for 2024 and got a 2025 reimbursement of 2024 medical bills, but none of the medical bills were deductible because they stayed below the 7.5%-of-AGI floor.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 26, Recovery limited to deduction: "You don't include in your income any amount of your recovery that is more than the amount you deducted in the earlier year."
findings.why: The gate holds and both questions are asked. But the 2024 deduction is zero, so none of the reimbursement is included and the gated lines change nothing. Gates lean to yes, so this costs a few questions but drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer whose recoveries are fully includible without any worksheet, as in Example 30, still goes through the gate because the computed condition only checks for a 2024 recovery while itemizing.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 25, Example 30: "Your total recoveries are less than the amount by which your itemized deductions exceeded the standard deduction ... so you must include your total recoveries in your income for 2025."
findings.why: The medical lines still matter here, because the deduction caps the amount recovered. So this only shows the gate is broader than the literal "Worksheet 2 is used" label, and it does not narrow coverage.

findings.situation: A filer's lender refunded or credited 2024 mortgage interest in 2025, but no Form 1098 shows the refund in box 4. This can happen when the lender didn't issue a 1098, reported the credit some other way, or the filer has no copy.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: "If you received a refund or credit in 2025 of mortgage interest paid in an earlier year, the amount should be shown in box 4 of Form 1098."
findings.why: The IRS says the refund 'should be' shown in box 4, not that it always is. A filer could read the gate's parenthetical '(Form 1098 box 4)' as requiring a box 4 amount and answer no, which drops a Worksheet 2, line 2 amount.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse alone holds the mortgage and received the 2025 refund of 2024 interest that the couple deducted on their joint 2024 Schedule A.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27, Worksheet 2, line 2: "Enter the total of all other Schedule A (Form 1040) refunds or reimbursements"
findings.why: Neither gate question mentions the spouse ('you itemized', 'Was any of it'). A filer could read the question as asking only about their own refunds and answer no for a spouse's Form 1098 refund.

findings.situation: In 2025 a filer receives a reimbursement of an itemized deduction from a year before 2024, such as a 2023 casualty loss reimbursement. The worksheet for that year needs a line 2 amount, but the gate only asks about money paid back for 2024.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27: "If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year, such as a state income tax refund from 2024 and a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted."
findings.why: Both the gate and the gated lines are tied to 2024. A recovery of an earlier year's Schedule A deduction has no path, so a truthful filer answers no and the line 2 amount for that year is dropped.

findings.situation: A filer who deducted state and local general sales taxes in 2024 and got a refund of those taxes may treat it as a state/local tax refund. That filer could answer no to whether the refund was for "something else you itemized."
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27, Worksheet 2, footnote 2: "If you deducted state and local general sales taxes and received a refund of those taxes, include the amount on line 2"
findings.why: Sales tax refunds belong on line 2, not lines 1a/1b. The question's "something else" does not say that only state/local income, real estate and personal property taxes are excluded, so a filer could reasonably read a state sales tax refund as already covered.

findings.situation: A filer receives an insurer's reimbursement of 2024 medical expenses or a casualty loss. The filer may not think of it as a "refund" and answers no.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27, Worksheet 2, line 2: "Enter the total of all other Schedule A (Form 1040) refunds or reimbursements"
findings.why: The gate question asks only whether any of it was a "refund," while line 2 also covers reimbursements from third parties. A filer could reasonably read "refund" narrowly.

findings.situation: A filer paid and deducted real estate tax in 2024 for an earlier assessment period (for example, a 2023 property tax bill paid in 2024), and part of that tax was refunded in 2025.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 26, Worksheet 2a, line 2: "Enter the refunds received for state and local real estate taxes and state and local personal property taxes"; line 4: "real estate taxes, and personal property taxes paid in 2024 (generally, this is the amount reported on your 2024 Schedule A (Form 1040), line 5d)"
findings.why: The worksheet counts refunds of taxes paid and deducted in 2024, whatever period the bill covers. A filer could read "a refund of 2024 real estate or personal property tax" as tax for the 2024 assessment year, answer no, and drop a refund the line requires.

findings.situation: Spouses filing jointly for 2025 who filed separate 2024 returns, and whose only money paid back is a 2024 state income tax refund that falls outside the 'generally' exception, would truthfully answer no to the scope helper, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27, Worksheet 2: "You generally don't need to use this worksheet if you file Form 1040 or 1040-SR and the recovery is for state or local income taxes paid for the immediately preceding tax year. If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year, such as a state income tax refund from 2024 ... complete a separate worksheet for each year"; line 1a: "State/local income tax refund or credit"
findings.why: The worksheet covers state and local income tax refunds on line 1a, and the exception only 'generally' applies. The scope helper excludes every state or local income tax refund, so these filers never see the two-returns question. The gated question's own help says the opposite: 'A state income tax refund counts as money back.'

findings.situation: A joint 2025 filer gets a state income tax refund plus another recovery, or only a state income tax refund, and must decide how to answer the scope helper.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27, Worksheet 2: "complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted"
findings.why: The scope helper says 'other than a state or local income tax refund,' but the gated question's help says 'A state income tax refund counts as money back.' A filer could reasonably read state refunds as either inside or outside the questions.

findings.situation: A joint 2025 filer whose only recovery is for an expense deducted in 2023 or earlier, or for a credit rather than a deduction, gets the gate as true even though the 2024 two-returns question gives no amount.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27, Worksheet 2: "such as a state income tax refund from 2024 and a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year"
findings.why: The scope helper covers recoveries from any earlier year and also credits, but the gated line only matters for deductions taken on 2024 returns.

locators: p. 27, Worksheet 2, "Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted"
p. 27, Worksheet 2, "complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted"

findings.situation: On a 2025 joint return, the spouse got a 2025 insurance reimbursement, mortgage interest refund or property tax refund for an expense the spouse itemized on their own separate or single 2024 return, while the filer took the standard deduction for 2024; the filer can truthfully answer no to the itemizing question, so every gated line is zeroed.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Deductions not itemized: "If you didn’t itemize deductions for the year for which you received the recovery of an expense that was deductible only if you itemized, don’t include any of the recovery amount in your income"; p. 25, Total recovery included in income: "If you recover any itemized deduction that you claimed in an earlier year, you must generally include the full amount of the recovery in your income"
findings.why: The scope question covers the spouse, but the follow-up "Did you itemize deductions on Schedule A for 2024?" asks only about the filer. A spouse who itemized for 2024 must include the recovery, yet the gate can be false.

findings.situation: The lender applied a refund of 2024 mortgage interest as a credit to the loan or escrow instead of paying cash, so the filer may not think they were "paid back".
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Mortgage interest refund: "If you received a refund or credit in 2025 of mortgage interest paid in an earlier year, the amount should be shown in box 4 of Form 1098"
findings.why: "Paid back" reads naturally as a cash payment. A filer who received only a credit, or a third-party insurance reimbursement, could reasonably answer no to the scope question even though the IRS treats the amount as a recovery.

findings.situation: The filer itemized for 2024, and the only 2025 recovery is of a nonitemized deduction, such as a payment on a previously deducted bad debt, or of a credit.

findings.situation: Spouses who filed a joint 2024 Form 1040 and file jointly again for 2025 are still asked whether their refunds came from two separate 2024 returns, even though their refund is tested against a single 2024 return.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 90, line 4: "Enter your total itemized deductions from your 2024 Schedule A, line 17"; line 5: "Enter the amount shown below for the filing status claimed on your 2024 Form 1040 or 1040-SR"
findings.why: The two-returns question only matters when a 2025 joint return combines refunds from two separate 2024 returns. Asking every joint filer costs one extra question, and a filer who answers no on a non-joint return loses nothing, because a non-joint 2025 return carries only the filer's own refund from the filer's own 2024 return.

findings.situation: A filer who advertised the property only through free listings, or who paid for advertising in a year other than 2025, could answer yes to the bare 'Advertising' prompt even though no 2025 advertising expense goes on line 5.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents' commissions, and depreciation."
findings.why: The gate prompt gives no year and does not say the advertising must be a paid expense, so it can be answered yes when line 5 would be zero. This only costs one extra question.

findings.situation: A filer sees the gate prompt 'For this rental property — Cleaning and maintenance,' which is only a line label, so it is not clear what a yes or no means.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses..."
findings.why: The gate does not ask whether any cleaning and maintenance expense was paid in 2025 for this property. A filer could answer about something else, such as whether the property needs cleaning or whether a tenant does it, and say no despite a deductible payment.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse paid for cleaning or maintenance of the property, but the gate does not mention the spouse.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column."
findings.why: The gated input asks for 'your share,' but the gate prompt names no payer. A filer might answer only for themselves and say no when only the spouse paid.

findings.situation: A filer paid for routine upkeep and has to decide whether it is 'maintenance' or a repair that belongs on another line.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees..."
findings.why: The gate does not say 'not repairs' the way the gated input does. A filer who thinks of their upkeep as repairs could answer no and leave out cleaning or maintenance that belongs on line 7.

findings.situation: A filer did the cleaning and maintenance personally, or paid for a capital improvement, and answers yes.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Do not deduct the value of your own labor or amounts paid for capital investments or capital improvements."
findings.why: The gate holds even though the IRS text gives no line 7 amount for one's own labor or for capital improvements.

findings.situation: The gate reads only 'Commissions' with no verb, payer or year, so a filer who paid an agent a leasing commission could read it as asking about commissions received, or about some other year, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents’ commissions, and depreciation.'
findings.why: The deductible amount is commissions paid or incurred as a rental expense. The bare label does not say 'paid', 'expense' or 'to an agent', so a truthful no is possible even when line 8 has an amount.

findings.situation: A filer whose property manager took a leasing commission out of the rent collected, rather than being paid it separately, might not think of it as a commission they paid and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct ... agents’ commissions'
findings.why: Agent commissions netted against rent are still deductible commissions. The terse gate gives the filer no cue to count them, so the line could be dropped.

findings.why: Tax advice and preparation are the only items the cited text names for line 10, but the gate never mentions them; only the gated question that follows it does. A truthful no would drop a deductible amount.

findings.situation: The gate is a bare label, not a question, and does not say what period counts or whose fees count on a joint return.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: "Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate or royalty properties."
findings.why: Without 'Did you or your spouse pay any ... in 2025?', a filer could take it as asking about the property's history or only their own payments. The gated question uses 'paid in 2025 (your share)', but the gate is the only prompt the filer answers before it.

findings.situation: A filer with a royalty property who pays for tax advice on it may answer no because the gate says 'this rental property'.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: "...related to your rental real estate or royalty properties."
findings.why: Line 10 also covers royalty properties. If this rental document also handles royalty columns, 'rental property' could lead a royalty filer to answer no.

findings.situation: A filer whose only professional fees were legal fees to defend title, recover, or develop the property answers yes, but those fees get no line 10 amount.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: "Do not deduct legal fees paid or incurred to defend or protect title to property, to recover property, or to develop or improve property. Instead, you must capitalize these fees..."
findings.why: The gate catches fees the IRS text sends to basis. This costs only an extra question, and the help shown with the gated question excludes them.

findings.situation: A rental with an operating profit on line 21 is sold at a loss reported on Form 4797, the activity's overall result is a loss, and some of the investment is not at risk; line 21 is not below zero, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: The at-risk rules in most cases limit the amount of loss (including loss on the disposition of assets) you can claim to the amount you could actually lose in the activity. ... you must complete Form 6198 to figure your loss if you have: • A loss from an activity carried on as a trade or business or for the production of income (i1040se 2025 p. 3)
findings.why: The at-risk test applies to the activity's loss, which includes disposition losses that are not on line 21. Testing only line 21 < $0 drops a Form 6198 limit the IRS text requires.

findings.situation: A filer's nonrecourse mortgage comes from a regular bank that also receives a fee because of the filer's investment in the property, so the filer truthfully answers No.
findings.irs_text: A qualified person cannot be: ... • A person who receives a fee due to your investment in real property (or a person related to that person). (i1040se 2025 p. 3)
findings.why: The question and help exclude any mortgage from a regular lender and list only the seller, a co-owner, relatives and controlled companies. A bank that earns a fee from the investment is not a qualified person, so that debt is not at risk and the question misses it.

findings.situation: A filer whose property was placed in service before 1987 has a line 21 loss and answers Yes, but the at-risk rules do not apply.
findings.irs_text: However, the at-risk rules do not apply to losses from an activity of holding real property placed in service before 1987. (i1040se 2025 p. 3)
findings.why: The gate and question hold although Form 6198 gives no limit for this property.

findings.situation: A filer with ordinary property or liability insurance reads it as a 'similar arrangement' and answers Yes.
findings.irs_text: protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement (excluding casualty insurance and insurance against tort liability) (i1040se 2025 p. 3)
findings.why: The question does not exclude casualty and tort insurance, so some filers will answer Yes when every amount is at risk.

findings.situation: A filer has a nonrecourse loan secured by their own property outside the activity, and the question's phrase 'owed by no one personally' leads them to answer Yes.
findings.irs_text: Nonrecourse loans ... that are not secured by your own property (other than property used in the activity). (i1040se 2025 p. 3)
findings.why: Nonrecourse debt secured by the filer's other property is at risk. The question does not carve this out, so it can return Yes when no limit applies.

findings.situation: The gate question is only "For this rental property — Other", so a filer can't tell what they are confirming or that it means every rental expense not covered by the earlier expense questions.

findings.why: The gate never says "expenses" or "not listed elsewhere". A filer with an unlisted cost, such as bank fees, pest control, or HOA dues, could read the bare word "Other" as asking about something else and answer no, which silently zeroes line 19.

findings.why: Under tracing, that interest belongs to this rental, so line 13 gets an amount. The gate asks only "For this rental property — Other interest" and does not say that the loan can be secured by, or held for, something else.

findings.situation: A filer who pays interest on this rental but has no Form 1098 in their name, or pays points or loan fees, cannot tell whether that is "other" interest or the mortgage interest asked about elsewhere.

findings.situation: A filer whose only rental costs this year were routine maintenance, such as painting a room or cleaning gutters, could truthfully answer no to a question that says only 'Repairs', so the maintenance deduction is dropped.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: "You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance. ... Repairs and maintenance costs are those costs that keep the property in an ordinarily efficient operating condition. Examples are fixing a broken lock or painting a room."
findings.why: Line 14 covers both repairs and maintenance, but the gate names only repairs. A filer who thinks of painting or upkeep as maintenance rather than repair would answer no and line 14 would be set to zero. The gated amount question ('Repairs (not improvements)') also leaves out maintenance.

findings.situation: A filer who paid only for improvements, such as replacing an entire HVAC system, might answer yes to the bare 'Repairs' gate even though line 14 gets no amount.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: "However, you cannot deduct the cost of improvements. ... Examples of improvements are adding substantial insulation or replacing an entire HVAC system."
findings.why: The gate does not exclude improvements, so it can be answered yes when line 14 is zero. The help text on the gated question limits the cost of this to extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer who bought items they think of as supplies but that are capital investments or improvements, or that were paid outside 2025, could tick the gate even though line 15 gets no amount for them.
findings.irs_text: Do not deduct the value of your own labor or amounts paid for capital investments or capital improvements. (i1040se 2025 p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21)
findings.why: The gate is a bare expense-category tick with no year and no capital exclusion, so it can hold when line 15 is zero. Gates are meant to lean yes, so this does not change the verdict.

findings.situation: A filer who rents out only part of a home and bought supplies used partly for personal purposes would tick the gate, but only the rented-part share is deductible.

findings.why: The gate also covers purely personal supply purchases. The gated helper takes the amount before the personal-use division, so no deductible amount is lost.

findings.situation: A filer with an oil or gas royalty property had state or local taxes withheld by the producer from royalty payments. The gate asks only about taxes 'For this rental property', so a royalty owner could truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 4: "Enter on line 4 the gross amount of royalty income, even if state or local taxes were withheld from oil or gas payments you received. Include taxes withheld by the producer on line 16."
findings.why: The IRS text puts producer-withheld taxes on royalty property on line 16. The gate is framed around a rental property, and the gated question asks about 'Property tax and other taxes on it, paid in 2025', which does not clearly reach taxes withheld from royalty payments.

findings.situation: A filer whose taxes on the property were withheld or paid by someone else, such as a producer or payer, sees only the bare label 'Taxes'. They could reasonably read it as taxes they paid themselves and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: "You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs..."; Line 4: "Include taxes withheld by the producer on line 16."
findings.why: The gate question gives no description of which taxes count, so a filer cannot tell whether withheld taxes or taxes on a property that is only partly rented make the answer yes.

findings.situation: A filer whose only line 17 expense is telephone calls to the renter, with no electricity, gas, water or similar bills for the property, could truthfully answer no to a bare "Utilities" question, so the deductible call costs are dropped.
findings.irs_text: Line 17 — "You can deduct the cost of ordinary and necessary telephone calls related to your rental activities or royalty income (for example, calls to the renter)." (i1040se 2025, p. 7)
findings.why: The only text the IRS gives under Line 17 assigns telephone call costs to this line. Many filers do not think of phone calls as "utilities," and the gate does not mention telephone costs.

findings.situation: A filer who pays for a phone line or calls partly used for the rental cannot tell whether the bare label "Utilities" covers those costs, or whether a personal residence line counts.
findings.irs_text: "However, the base rate (including taxes and other charges) for local telephone service for the first telephone line into your residence is a personal expense and is not deductible." (i1040se 2025, p. 7)
findings.why: The gate gives only the one-word label and no examples, while the cited text is entirely about telephone costs and their limits. Filers could read the label either way.

findings.situation: A filer rents land with improvements, such as Charlie's $300,000 land plus $100,000 of improvements (25% depreciable), so line 1b is not 'land', the computed condition rental.is_land is false, and the gated question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: p925 (2025) p. 16: "The unadjusted basis of the improvements ($100,000) equals 25% of the unadjusted basis of all property ($400,000) used in the rental activity. Charlie's net passive income from the activity ... is treated as nonpassive income."
findings.why: As specified, the gated line is asked only when is_land is true, and in that branch the Choose always yields false. When is_land is false (property has buildings), the line is forced to false unasked. So the less-than-30% test is never asked in the one case that needs it, the case the IRS example shows.

findings.situation: The cited text's condition is 'less than 30% of the unadjusted basis of the property is subject to depreciation', but the gate's condition is 'land only (line 1b = land)'.
findings.irs_text: p925 (2025) p. 16: "less than 30% of the unadjusted basis of the property is subject to depreciation"
findings.why: Land only (0% depreciable) is a subset of the cited condition, not the condition itself. The gate should be 'less than 30% depreciable' or simply always ask when the property is not land only, not 'land only'.

findings.situation: A filer who got the property by gift or inheritance, or exchanged into it, is asked about 'what it cost (before depreciation)', while the rule turns on unadjusted basis, which for such property is not the price paid.
findings.irs_text: p925 (2025) p. 16: "less than 30% of the unadjusted basis of the property is subject to depreciation"
findings.why: 'What it cost' can reasonably be read as the purchase price only. A filer with carryover, stepped-up or substituted basis might compute the split differently or think the question doesn't apply.

findings.situation: An activity rents more than one class of property, so the simple days-per-stay average across all rentals is over 30, but the income-weighted average the IRS prescribes is 7 days or less (for example, one 365-day rental of a low-income class plus ten 2-day rentals of a class earning 99% of gross rental income: simple average 35 days, weighted average about 5.6 days).
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3: "If the activity involves renting more than one class of property, multiply the average period of customer use of each class by the ratio of the gross rental income from that class to the activity's total gross rental income. The activity's average period of customer use equals the sum of these class-by-class average periods weighted by gross income."
findings.why: The gate tells the filer to divide total rented days by the number of stays, with no income weighting by class. A filer following that instruction answers no, so the 7-days-or-less exception (Exception 1a) is never asked and the line is forced to false.

findings.situation: A rental period crosses the tax year boundary (for example, a lease that started in a prior year), and the filer cannot tell whether to count all days of the stay or only days in the tax year, or whether to count the stay at all.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3: "dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals during the tax year"
findings.why: The gate question and its help ("Divide the days it was rented by the number of separate stays") do not say which rentals count or how to count days for a period that spans two years. A filer could reasonably read it either way and land on the other side of 30 days.

findings.situation: A beneficiary of an employee who died before August 21, 1996, who made no after-tax contributions, has cost on Simplified Method Worksheet line 2 made up only of the death benefit exclusion; a truthful answer to the after-tax contributions question is No, so the Simplified Method question is never reached.

findings.situation: The royalty's Schedule E line 21 shows net income, but a loss on disposing of the royalty property (reported outside line 21) gives the activity an overall loss, and some amounts in it are not at risk.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'The at-risk rules in most cases limit the amount of loss (including loss on the disposition of assets) you can claim' and 'you must complete Form 6198 to figure your loss if you have: • A loss from an activity'
findings.why: The at-risk test applies to the activity's loss, including disposition losses that never reach line 21. The computed condition 'line 21 < $0' is false here, so the not-at-risk question is never asked.

findings.situation: The filer contributed property (not cash) to the royalty activity, and a guarantee or stop-loss agreement protects it against loss.

findings.why: The question asks only about 'money you put in'. A filer whose protected contribution was property could truthfully answer no.

findings.situation: The filer borrowed on full personal liability from someone who has an interest in the royalty activity, or from a relative of such a person.

findings.situation: A professional gambler’s only gambling winnings are trade-or-business winnings reportable on Schedule C, so the line 8b gambling-winnings helper is zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8b: “Enter gambling winnings not attributable to a trade or business”; p525 p. 33: “If you’re in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C.”
findings.why: The gate is computed from gambling winnings that, under the cited line 8b, exclude trade-or-business winnings; a professional with only Schedule C winnings can therefore have a false condition even though the gated professional-gambling line matters.

findings.situation: A professional gambler has a loss year with no positive gross gambling winnings.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: “a professional gambler cannot claim a loss on Schedule C (Form 1040) in a loss year, even if gambling expenses other than losses exceed gross gambling income.”
findings.why: The cited text makes professional status matter in a loss year, but the gate requires gambling winnings greater than $0, so the professional question is suppressed.

findings.situation: The filer is in the trade or business of gambling but has no positive gambling winnings for the year.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: “If you’re in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040)”; gate condition: any gambling winnings > $0.
findings.why: The cited condition for professional gambling is trade-or-business status, not a positive winnings threshold; the gate substitutes a different event.

findings.situation: A casual filer wins a small lottery prize but does not gamble as a trade or business.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8b: “Enter gambling winnings not attributable to a trade or business”; p525 p. 33: “If you’re in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C.”
findings.why: The gate is true, but the IRS text gives no professional-gambling Schedule C amount for a nonbusiness lottery winner; this is only a wrong-yes screening cost.

findings.situation: A filer with no Schedule C deducts part of the qualified passenger vehicle loan interest on Schedule E (rental) or Schedule F (farm). The gate is false, so column (ii) is zero and the same interest can be claimed again on Schedule 1-A.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 110, Line 22: "On line 22, column (ii), enter the amount of the QPVLI, if any, that was deducted elsewhere on your return (for example, on Schedule C, Schedule E, or Schedule F)."
findings.why: Column (ii) covers interest deducted on Schedules E and F as well as C. The gate and the line only count Schedule C, so interest deducted elsewhere is never subtracted.

findings.situation: A filer with no Schedule C has a partnership or S corporation loss suspended in an earlier year (for example, under sections 469, 465, 704(d) or 1366(d)) that is allowed in 2025. A loss from a Schedule C business that closed before 2025 is the same case.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p. 3: "When losses or deductions previously suspended by other Code provisions are allowed in calculating taxable income, the qualified portion ... is treated as a qualified net loss carryforward"; p. 4, Line 3: "even if the loss was from a trade or business that is no longer in existence"
findings.why: Suspended losses that become allowed can come from K-1s, Schedule E, Schedule F, PTPs (line 7) or a closed business, none of which needs a 2025 Schedule C. The gate silently drops the out-of-scope refusal.

findings.situation: A filer with no Schedule C deducts intangible drilling costs or circulation costs in full for the regular tax through an oil and gas partnership K-1, a Schedule E working interest, or Schedule F mining or other activities.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 7, Line 2t: "IDCs from oil, gas, and geothermal wells are a preference"; Line 2o: "Circulation costs ... deducted in full for the regular tax ... must be capitalized and amortized over 3 years for the AMT"
findings.why: These AMT adjustments apply to the costs wherever they are deducted, including pass-through and Schedule E activities. The gate only opens with a Schedule C.

findings.situation: A filer with no Schedule C owes or is due look-back interest as a partner or S corporation shareholder in a long-term contract. Another case is an author or film owner reporting royalties on Schedule E from property depreciated under the income forecast method.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 Schedule 2 (2025), line 17n: "Look-back interest under section 167(g) or 460(b) from Form 8697 or 8866"
findings.why: Line 17n is not limited to Schedule C activities. Pass-through owners and Schedule E income-forecast property can produce it with no Schedule C.

findings.situation: A farmer reporting on Schedule F, with no Schedule C, elects income averaging. So does a filer whose farming or fishing income comes through a K-1 or Form 4835.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36: "If you had income from farming or fishing, your tax may be less if you choose to figure it using income averaging on Schedule J"; i1040sj p. 1: "your trade or business of farming or fishing"
findings.why: Farming income is reported on Schedule F, not Schedule C, so the gate is false for the typical Schedule J filer. The gated question also asks only about fishing, so even a filer who passes the gate and farms truthfully answers no.

findings.situation: A self-employed farmer filing Schedule F, or a partner with self-employment income from a K-1, has no Schedule C and contributes to a qualified (non-SEP, non-SIMPLE) plan for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 16: "If you were self-employed or a partner, you may be able to take this deduc-"
findings.why: The line 16 deduction is open to any self-employed person or partner, not only Schedule C filers. The gate drops the out-of-scope refusal for them.

findings.situation: A partner whose contribution goes to the partnership's qualified plan reads "a retirement plan of your own business".
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 16: "If you were self-employed or a partner, you may be able to take this deduc-"
findings.why: A partner may reasonably think the partnership's plan is not a plan of "your own business" and answer no, though the line 16 deduction applies to partners.

findings.situation: A filer on a 2025 joint return with a new spouse carries in an NOL that arose in a year they filed jointly with a former spouse. The IRS text requires that filer's own share of the old joint NOL to be separated out, but the gate is false because the 2025 return is MFJ, so the joint-year question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "If you and your spouse were not married to each other in all years involved in figuring NOL carrybacks and carryovers, only the spouse who had the loss can take the NOL deduction. If you file a joint return, the NOL deduction is limited to the income of that spouse."
findings.why: The gated line itself cites this paragraph, which explicitly covers a current joint return. A truthful filer here would answer yes to the gated question and should be stopped, but the computed condition (filing status ≠ 'mfj') excludes every joint return.

findings.situation: A single or head-of-household filer who has never been married and carries in an NOL meets the condition, but no joint-year rule can apply to them.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Joint to separate returns: "If you and your spouse file separate returns for a tax year, but filed a joint return for any or all of the tax years involved in figuring the NOL carryover..."
findings.why: The condition is any non-MFJ status rather than 'married filing separately', so it also fires for filers who never filed jointly. They simply answer no, which costs one question. Widening beyond MFS is reasonable because widowed or divorced filers whose loss came from a joint year also need the separation.

findings.situation: A filer who was self-employed before 2025 (for example a freelancer, independent contractor or gig worker filing Schedule C) elected to expense equipment under section 179, and part of it was disallowed by the business income limit. They may not think of themselves as having 'owned a business'.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 10: "the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation"; Line 11: "taxable income from any trade or business you actively conducted"
findings.why: Section 179 applies to any trade or business, including sole self-employment. The scope question asks about owning 'a business', which such a filer could truthfully read as not describing them and answer no. The gate would then drop a real line 10 carryover.

findings.situation: A filer whose pre-2025 section 179 deduction passed through from an LLC taxed as a partnership might not recognize themselves in 'a share of a partnership'.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 6, Column (c): "To report your share of a section 179 expense deduction from a partnership or an S corporation, enter 'from Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)'"
findings.why: LLC members often do not think of their interest as a partnership share. They could answer no even though a carried-over deduction from the K-1 belongs on line 10.

findings.situation: A filer who owned a rental or business before 2025 but never elected section 179, or whose deductions were all fully allowed, passes the scope question even though line 10 is zero.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 10: "the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed"
findings.why: Owning such property does not by itself create a carryover. The second helper resolves this case, so it costs only one question.

locators: p. 5, Line 10, "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation" and "If you filed Form 4562 for 2024, enter the amount from line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562" (owner: the printed amount)

findings.situation: A filer has a section 179 deduction limited by business income and has taxable interest, but all of it is personal or investment interest unrelated to any business's operating funds.
findings.irs_text: p946 p. 19: "Net income or loss from a trade or business includes the following items. ... • Interest from working capital of your trade or business."
findings.why: The computed condition holds because there is taxable interest, but none of it is working-capital interest, so the gated line is zero. The question just collects a zero answer.

findings.situation: A filer’s main home is a houseboat or recreational vehicle and they deduct mortgage interest on it; the gated question asks only about a boat or RV that is not the main home.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 8: “A qualified dwelling for AMT doesn’t include house boats and recreational vehicles”; “If you deducted home mortgage interest ... for a dwelling that isn’t ... qualified dwelling for AMT, include that deducted interest on line 3.”
findings.why: The IRS text excludes houseboats and RVs from qualified dwellings without requiring that they be non-main homes, but the question’s “not your main home” limitation lets a truthful no drop the line.

findings.situation: A filer deducts mortgage interest on a house, apartment, condominium, or mobile home rented out on a transient basis, and that interest alone could make AMT apply, but the computed helper maximizes only private activity bond and boat/camper interest.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 8: “A qualified dwelling for AMT is a house, apartment, condominium, or mobile home not used on a transient basis”; include deducted interest on line 3 if the dwelling is not a qualified dwelling for AMT.
findings.why: The helper condition does not put transient-home mortgage interest at its largest, so it can be false even though adding that interest would make line 7 exceed line 10; the gated question is then not asked.

findings.situation: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, whose only private activity bond income is exempt-interest dividends from a mutual fund (Form 1099-DIV) has no tax-exempt interest or tax-exempt OID from Forms 1099-INT or 1099-OID, so the first part of the computed condition is false and line 2g is set to zero.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 3, Line 2g: "Exempt-interest dividends paid by a mutual fund or other regulated investment company are treated as interest income"
findings.why: The first helper is described as 'Tax-exempt interest and tax-exempt OID, net of amortized premium', which does not cover exempt-interest dividends, yet the instructions put those dividends on line 2g. The gated question also counts only 1099-INT box 9 and 1099-OID box 11, so these dividends would be missed even when the gate opens.

findings.situation: A filer with tax-exempt interest from ordinary governmental bonds and no private activity bonds still gets the question when the worst-case AMT comparison holds.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 3: "Enter on line 2g interest income from “specified private activity bonds”"
findings.why: The gate assumes all tax-exempt interest is private activity bond interest, so it asks more often than needed. This is by design and does not affect the verdict.

findings.situation: The second helper compares line 7 with line 10, while AMT arises only when line 9 (line 7 minus the AMT foreign tax credit) exceeds line 10.
findings.irs_text: f6251 p. 1, line 11: "AMT. Subtract line 10 from line 9. If zero or less, enter -0-."
findings.why: Testing line 7 instead of line 9 opens the gate in a few cases where the AMT foreign tax credit already prevents AMT. This leans toward yes and is acceptable.

findings.situation: A taxpayer exercised an ISO before 2025, but in 2025 the acquired shares first became transferable or free of a substantial risk of forfeiture and were still held.

findings.situation: A foreign child or a U.S. child with special needs was placed with the filer in 2023 or earlier, all costs were paid in 2023 or earlier, and the adoption became final in 2025; the filer may answer no because the child joined the family before 2024.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: 'You paid qualified adoption expenses in connection with the adoption of an eligible foreign child in: a. 2025 or prior years and the adoption became final in 2025' and '2. You adopted an eligible U.S. child with special needs and the adoption became final in 2025.'
findings.why: The gate asks whether the filer 'adopt[ed] a child' since the start of 2024 but never says the adoption counts when it becomes final, so a filer who dates the adoption from placement could answer no. Both s3.adoption and s3.adoption_earlier would then be zero, and a 2025 credit is dropped.

findings.situation: An employer paid costs for a foreign adoption in 2023, and the adoption became final in 2025, with the child already living with the filer before 2024.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Foreign Adoption: 'IF your employer pays for qualifying expenses ... in any year before the year the adoption becomes final THEN take the exclusion in the year the adoption becomes final.'
findings.why: The employer's payment is before 2024, so the gate holds only if the filer reads 'adopt a child' as the adoption becoming final in 2025. The help text does not say this, so scope.adoption_benefits may never be asked.

findings.situation: The filer paid costs in 2024 for a domestic adoption that became final in 2024 and had no other adoption activity.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Domestic Adoption: 'the year the adoption becomes final — the year the adoption becomes final.'
findings.why: The credit for these costs belongs on the 2024 return, so no gated line gets a 2025 amount, yet the gate holds.

locators: p. 1, Purpose of Form, "2024 and the adoption wasn’t final at the end of 2024"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "any year before the year the adoption becomes final"

p. 1, Purpose of Form, "You may be able to take this credit in 2025 if any of the following statements are true"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "any year before the year the adoption becomes final"
p. 24, Line 1f, "Employer-provided adoption benefits should be shown in box 12 of your Form(s) W-2 with code T"

findings.situation: The filer paid qualified expenses in 2024 for a U.S. child, the adoption was not final at the end of 2024, it did not become final in 2025 (or was abandoned), and nothing was paid in 2025. The outer question is answered yes and the inner question is truthfully answered no, so the computed condition is false.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "You paid qualified adoption expenses ... in: a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024"; p. 3 Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final* | the year after the year of the payment" and "you can take the adoption credit or exclusion even if the adoption never became final."
findings.why: Under the domestic table these 2024 payments are credited in 2025 whether or not the adoption is final. The inner question asks only about a 2025 finalization or 2025 payments, so this filer is gated out and the 2025 credit is dropped.

findings.situation: The cited text sets out when the credit may be taken in 2025, and the gate's inner question uses a narrower time frame than that text.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "You may be able to take this credit in 2025 if any of the following statements are true. 1. ... a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024 ... 4. You have a carryforward of an adoption credit from 2024." Gate: "adopt a child whose adoption became final in 2025, or pay expenses in 2025 in connection with adopting a child"
findings.why: The gate leaves out statement 1a (2024 payments with the adoption still unfinished at year-end 2024) and statement 4 (a carryforward from 2024), both of which the cited condition includes.

findings.situation: In 2025 the filer's employer paid adoption expenses under a qualified program, for example for a foreign child whose adoption became final before 2025, and the filer personally paid nothing in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "3. You received employer-provided adoption benefits in connection with the adoption of an eligible foreign child in: ... b. 2025 and the adoption became final before 2025"; p. 3: "IF your employer pays for qualifying expenses ... any year after the year the adoption becomes final | the year of the payment."
findings.why: The outer question says "pay (or have an employer pay)" but the inner question says only "pay expenses in 2025". A filer whose employer did the paying could reasonably answer no and lose the 2025 exclusion.

locators: p. 1, Purpose of Form, "You may be able to take this credit in 2025 if any of the following statements are true"; , Lines 6a Through 6z, "You may be able to take the adoption credit if you paid expenses to adopt a child or you adopted a child with special needs and the adoption became final in 2025"

p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "the year after the year of the payment" and "the year the adoption becomes final"; p. 3, Foreign child, "you can’t take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final"

findings.situation: A filer paid expenses in 2024 for a foreign child's adoption that was not final at the end of 2024; the condition holds, but the gated line ends up false because the answer is No.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3: "If the eligible child is a foreign child, you can't take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final."
findings.why: The gate opens for any 2024 payment on a non-final adoption, not only for a U.S. child. The gated question then sorts out the foreign case, so this only costs one extra question.

findings.situation: A filer paid adoption-related costs in 2024 that are not qualified adoption expenses, such as costs for adopting a spouse's child or costs reimbursed by an employer; the condition holds even though no credit follows.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "You paid qualified adoption expenses in connection with the adoption of an eligible U.S. child ... in: a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024"
findings.why: The helper asks about any expenses paid in connection with an adoption, not only qualified adoption expenses. This leans toward yes, which the gate design intends.

findings.situation: A filer paid expenses in 2024 or 2025 to adopt a U.S. stepchild without special needs, and the adoption was not final by the end of 2025 (or never became final), so the gate is false and the stepchild line defaults to false, which leaves the expenses treated as qualified.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3: "If the eligible child is a U.S. citizen or resident, you can take the adoption credit or exclusion even if the adoption never became final"; p. 2: "Qualified adoption expenses don’t include expenses: ... For the adoption of your spouse’s child"
findings.why: The spouse's-child exclusion applies whether or not the adoption is final. A U.S.-child credit or exclusion can arise without finality, so the stepchild refusal matters in exactly the case where this gate's finality condition is false.

findings.situation: A filer paid domestic adoption expenses in 2024 for an adoption that was not final in 2025, so the credit is taken in 2025, but the inner helper only asks whether the adoption became final in 2025 or expenses were paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final" → "the year after the year of the payment."
findings.why: Expenses paid in 2024 before finality produce a 2025 credit. A filer whose adoption neither became final in 2025 nor had 2025 payments truthfully answers no, so the computed condition is false while the stepchild exclusion still governs that credit.

findings.situation: A filer adopted a stepchild and the employer paid adoption benefits in 2025 for an adoption that is not final, so the exclusion is taken in the year of payment without regard to finality.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "IF your employer pays for qualifying expenses under an adoption assistance program in... any year" → "the year of the payment."
findings.why: The domestic exclusion does not depend on finality. Expenses for a spouse's child are not qualified adoption expenses, but the gate drops the stepchild question whenever the adoption was not final.

findings.situation: A filer with more than one adoption, some final by the end of 2025 and some not, must answer "Was such an adoption final by the end of 2025?"
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Line 1: "If you can’t give complete information about an eligible child you tried to adopt in 2024 because the adoption was either unsuccessful or wasn’t final by the end of 2025"
findings.why: "Such an adoption" can be read as any one adoption or all of them. The gated question then asks only about children "whose adoption was final", so it never reaches a stepchild whose adoption was not final.

locators: p. 2, Qualified Adoption Expenses, "Qualified adoption expenses don’t include expenses" and "For the adoption of your spouse’s child"; p. 3, Child with special needs, "If you adopt a U.S. child with special needs, you may be able to exclude up to $17,280 and claim a credit"

p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "the year after the year of the payment" and "the year the adoption becomes final"; p. 3, Foreign child, "you can’t take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final"

findings.situation: A person under 65 retired on permanent and total disability but has no taxable disability income for 2025, or had reached mandatory retirement age by January 1, 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 1: "all three of the following statements are true. a. You retired on permanent and total disability. ... b. You receive taxable disability income for 2025. c. On January 1, 2025, you had not reached mandatory retirement age"
findings.why: The condition tests only statement (a), so it is true for some people who are not qualified individuals; the only cost is that the credit question is asked needlessly.

findings.situation: Someone on the return is 65 or older (or retired on disability) but cannot take the credit because of income, alien status, or filing separately while living with a spouse.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 3: "If your AGI or your nontaxable pensions, annuities, or disability income are equal to or more than the income limits, you can't take the credit"; p. 1: "if you lived with your spouse at any time during 2025, you can't take the credit"; p. 1: "Generally, you can't take the credit if you were a nonresident alien at any time during the tax year"
findings.why: The condition holds on age or disability retirement alone, so the credit question is asked even though the credit is unavailable; the gate leans to yes by design.

findings.situation: A taxpayer who died in 2025 before reaching 65 would have turned 65 by the end of 2025, and the age helper may count them as 65 if it works from birth date alone.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 1: "if the taxpayer died on February 12, 2025, the taxpayer isn't considered age 65 at the time of death or at the end of 2025"
findings.why: If the helper ignores the date of death, the condition is true for a person the IRS does not treat as 65; this only adds a question.

findings.situation: A filer's home charger was physically installed in late 2024 but only became operational (energized, inspected) in 2025, and the filer got no clean vehicle in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8911 p. 4, Line 5: "Generally, property is placed in service when it is ready and available for a specific use... For example, an EV charger installed at an individual taxpayer's principal residence will be placed in service when it is operational." i8911 p. 1, Purpose of Form: "alternative fuel vehicle refueling property you placed in service during your tax year"
findings.why: The IRS test is the date the equipment is placed in service (operational), not the date it is installed, so this filer can truthfully answer no to "In 2025, did you... install home equipment". The refueling-credit question (s3.ev_equipment) is then never asked and the 2025 credit is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer who only leased an electric vehicle in 2025 (the help says to count leased vehicles) and installed no equipment answers yes, though no gated line has an amount.
findings.irs_text: i8936 p. 2: "If the vehicle is leased, only the lessor and not the lessee is entitled to the credit."
findings.why: The gate holds but the lessee has no clean vehicle credit, no dealer transfer and no refueling credit. This is by design and costs only a few extra questions.

findings.situation: A partner, S corporation shareholder or similar owner made the Form 1062 election for gain passed through from an entity that sold the farmland, and truthfully answers no because they did not personally sell any farmland.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117, Line 13z: "If you made the election to defer net income tax attributable to the gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property, use Form 1062 to figure the amount of your applicable net tax liability. On line 13z, enter 75% of your applicable net tax liability from Form 1062, line 14."
findings.why: The IRS text turns only on the filer having made the election, not on the filer being the seller, while the gate asks "did you (or... your spouse) sell farmland?". The page itself does not mention entity sales, so this rests on reading "you made the election" as wider than "you sold"; a no here silently zeroes the 1062NL amount.

findings.situation: A filer sold or exchanged land they never farmed themselves (for example land leased to a farmer, or pasture, orchard or farm buildings with land) and is unsure whether that counts as selling "farmland".
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117, Line 13z: "gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property"
findings.why: The gate says "farmland" with no explanation, while the IRS text uses the term "qualified farmland property"; a landlord or seller of mixed farm real estate could reasonably answer no.

findings.situation: A filer sold or traded farmland in 2025 but made no Form 1062 election.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117, Line 13z: "If you made the election to defer net income tax attributable to the gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property"
findings.why: The gate holds but line 13z gets no 1062NL amount; the gated follow-up question resolves this, so it costs one extra question.

locators: p. 117, Line 13z, "Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c) with respect to an excess limitation account", "Also use line 13z to report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands" and "If you made the election to defer net income tax attributable to the gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property"

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) elected to pay a net 965 tax liability in installments because of a small interest in a domestic partnership or S corporation that was itself the U.S. shareholder of the foreign company, so the filer's own share of the foreign company, even counted through the entity, was under 10%.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13d: "If you elected to pay your net 965 tax liability in installments, report the deferred amount on line 13d. Enter the amount of net 965 tax liability remaining to be paid in future years."
findings.why: Line 13d depends only on the election and a remaining balance, not on 10% ownership. This filer can truthfully answer no to all three limbs if they never personally paid foreign income tax, so the deferred amount is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer took over someone else's remaining section 965 installments (for example as an heir or other transferee under a transfer agreement) and never owned 10% of a foreign company, paid foreign income tax or had territory income.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13d: "Enter the amount of net 965 tax liability remaining to be paid in future years."
findings.why: The line has an amount whenever installment liability remains, but the gate asks about ownership and foreign tax history that this filer does not have. The 965 question is then never asked.

findings.situation: A filer holding foreign shares through a partnership, S corporation or trust cannot tell whether "count shares held through" means the entity's whole holding or only their proportionate slice when testing the 10% threshold.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13d: "If you elected to pay your net 965 tax liability in installments, report the deferred amount on line 13d."
findings.why: Read as a proportionate slice, a minority owner of the entity answers no even though they carry a 965 installment balance. Read as the entity's whole holding, they answer yes.

findings.situation: A filer whose only foreign income tax was withheld at source or paid by a partnership, S corporation or trust (reported on Schedule K-3) may not regard themselves as having "paid income tax to another country"; the help addresses only fund tax in Form 1099-DIV box 7.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 115, Line 1: "all of that income and the foreign tax paid on it were reported to you on Form 1099-INT, Form 1099-DIV, or Schedule K-3 (or substitute statement)"; p. 117, Line 13z: "Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c) with respect to an excess limitation account."
findings.why: The IRS text treats tax reported through an entity as foreign tax paid by the filer. A filer who reads "paid" as paid directly could answer no and lose the 960(c) question, unless the 10% ownership limb happens to catch them.

findings.situation: A filer who once paid a small amount of foreign income tax years ago (for example on wages abroad, or on fund dividends claimed on Form 1116), or once had Puerto Rico or Guam income, answers yes although none of the three lines applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13z: "Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c) with respect to an excess limitation account ... Also use line 13z to report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands."
findings.why: "Ever" and "any U.S. territory" reach many filers with no 960(c) credit, no 965 installments and no Virgin Islands allocation. This only costs three extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer with an MCC takes the standard deduction, so no home mortgage interest is entered on Schedule A line 8a, yet the credit is still allowed.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Line 3: "If you itemize your deductions on Schedule A, you must reduce the amount of home mortgage interest you would otherwise deduct on Schedule A by the amount on Form 8396, line 3"
findings.why: The credit depends on interest paid on the certified indebtedness, not on itemizing. Unless the tool fills line 8a for non-itemizers too, the computed condition is false and the credit is silently dropped.

findings.situation: The MCC loan interest was not reported on a Form 1098 (for example, a lender that issues only a similar statement), so it goes on Schedule A line 8b and line 8a is zero.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Line 1: "In most cases, this will be the amount in box 1 on Form 1098, Mortgage Interest Statement, or on a similar statement you received from your mortgage holder."
findings.why: Form 8396 line 1 is any interest paid on the certified indebtedness, with or without a Form 1098. A test on line 8a alone misses interest entered on line 8b.

findings.situation: A filer paid no mortgage interest in 2025 (loan paid off, or home sold) but has unused mortgage interest credit carried forward from 2022 to 2024.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 1, lines 4-6: "Enter any 2022 credit carryforward from line 16 of your 2024 Form 8396"; p. 2, Purpose of Form: "Use Form 8396 to figure the mortgage interest credit for 2025 and any credit carryforward to 2026."
findings.why: Carryforwards feed lines 7 and 9 even when line 1 is zero, so the note "the credit is a share of the interest paid" is not true of the whole credit. If the MCC answer is what opens Form 8396 in the tool, forcing it to false drops the carryforward.

findings.situation: The cited text bases the credit on interest paid on the certified indebtedness, while the gate tests the amount deducted on Schedule A line 8a.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Line 1: "Enter the interest you paid during the year on the loan amount (certified indebtedness amount) shown on your MCC"; gate: "sa line 8a > $0"
findings.why: Interest paid on the MCC loan and interest entered on line 8a are different quantities. Line 8a exists only for itemizers, covers only Form 1098 interest, and is itself reduced by Form 8396 line 3.

findings.situation: Most filers with interest on Schedule A line 8a have no MCC, and are still asked the MCC question.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Who Can Claim the Credit: "You can claim the credit only if you were issued a qualified Mortgage Credit Certificate (MCC) by a state or local governmental unit or agency"
findings.why: The condition holds for every itemizer with mortgage interest although only MCC holders get an amount. This is the acceptable lean to yes.

locators: p. 2, Line 1, "Enter the interest you paid during the year on the loan amount (certified indebtedness amount) shown on your MCC"

p. 2, Who Can Claim the Credit, "You can claim the credit only if you were issued a qualified Mortgage Credit Certificate (MCC) by a state or local governmental unit or agency under a qualified mortgage credit certificate program"

findings.situation: A filer whose 2024 return had an AMT liability caused only by exclusion items (for example, the standard deduction or tax-exempt interest) passes the gate, but the deferral-item question then gets a no and the line stays false.
findings.irs_text: i8801 p. 1: "The minimum tax credit is allowed only for the AMT caused by deferral items."
findings.why: The gate asks only about an AMT liability, which is broader than the cited two-part condition; the gated question then applies the second part. This costs extra questions but drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer has an unused District of Columbia first-time homebuyer credit (or a mortgage interest or general business credit) carried from 2023 or earlier, and was not required to file, and did not file, a 2024 return because their income was below the filing threshold.
findings.irs_text: f8859 p. 1, Line 4: "You can carry forward any unused credit shown on line 4 until you have used all of it"; i3800 p. 3: "unused general business credits may be carried back 1 year and carried forward 20 years"; f8396 p. 2: "carry forward to the next 3 tax years or until used"
findings.why: Not filing for 2024 does not end the carryforward, so it still reaches the 2025 Form 8859, 3800 or 8396. The help text "If you did not file for 2024, answer No" makes this filer answer no, and the amount is silently set to zero.

findings.situation: The filer's 2024 return includes Form 8582-CR (or another form whose number has a suffix) and no other attachment.

findings.situation: A filer has three or more qualifying children (line 16b is $5,100 or more), or line 16a is zero, so the bona fide resident of Puerto Rico status changes no amount on Schedule 8812, yet the condition holds and the question is asked.
findings.irs_text: f1040s8812 (2025) p. 2, after line 20: "Next. On line 16b, is the amount $5,100 or more? No. If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico, go to line 21. ... Yes. If line 20 is equal to or more than line 17, skip Part II-B ... Otherwise, go to line 21."

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) made no charitable gifts in 2025 but has a carryover of earlier-year contributions that is still more than this year's percentage limits.
