findings.situation: A taxpayer paid deductible home mortgage interest to a recipient who did not provide Form 1098, so line 8b is positive while line 8a is zero, and the loan proceeds were partly used for other purposes.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 8, Line 8b: 'If you paid home mortgage interest to a recipient who didn’t provide you a Form 1098, report your deductible mortgage interest on line 8b.'; p. 8, Line 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn’t use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.'
findings.why: The computed gate is only line 8a > $0, so it is false even though line 8b can carry the home mortgage interest and the IRS other-use checkbox condition can apply.

findings.situation: The IRS states the line 8 checkbox condition as having an outstanding home mortgage and not using all proceeds to buy, build, or substantially improve the home, while the tool gates on line 8a being positive.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 8, Line 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn’t use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home'; gate cited text p. 8, Line 8a: 'Enter on line 8a mortgage interest and points reported to you on Form 1098.'
findings.why: The tool substitutes a line 8a amount threshold for the IRS’s stated checkbox condition; line 8b or 8c interest, or a zero deductible line 8a, can satisfy the IRS condition while line 8a is $0.

findings.situation: A taxpayer has Form 1098 mortgage interest on line 8a but used all mortgage proceeds to buy, build, or substantially improve the home.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 8, Line 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn’t use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.'
findings.why: The gate is true because line 8a > $0, but the IRS other-use condition is false and no other-use amount matters.

findings.situation: A filer's unreimbursed medical costs are more than 7.5% of adjusted gross income but not more than 7.5% of total or gross income (wages before adjustments such as IRA, HSA or self-employment deductions). Reading 'income' as gross or total income, the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: "You can deduct only the part of your medical and dental expenses that exceeds 7.5% of the amount of your adjusted gross income on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b."
findings.why: The gate question says only 'more than 7.5% of your income' and never names adjusted gross income (Form 1040, line 11b). A filer could reasonably compare against a larger income figure, answer no, and lose a deductible amount on line 1.

findings.situation: A filer pays medical bills for a dependent, a child claimed by the other parent, or a parent who would be a dependent except for $5,200+ of income, and counts only costs for themselves and their spouse.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 2: "You can include medical and dental bills you paid in 2025 for anyone who was one of the following ... All dependents you claim on your return. • Your child whom you don't claim as a dependent because of the rules for children of divorced or separated parents ... • Any person you could have claimed as a dependent on your return except that person received $5,200 or more of gross income or filed a joint return."
findings.why: 'The medical and dental costs you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) paid yourselves' can be read as costs for yourselves rather than costs you paid for anyone. Under that reading, costs for these other people are left out of the 7.5% comparison and the filer may wrongly answer no.

findings.situation: A filer whose costs were paid with tax-free HSA or Archer MSA distributions counts them toward the 7.5% test, answers yes, and then has little or nothing to enter on line 1.
findings.irs_text: p969 p. 9: "You can't deduct qualified medical expenses as an itemized deduction on Schedule A (Form 1040) that are equal to the tax-free distribution from your HSA."
findings.why: The gate question subtracts only what insurance paid, not HSA or MSA payments, so it can hold when line 1 is zero. This costs only extra questions.

findings.situation: A married filer who is 'considered unmarried' files as head of household and itemizes, while the spouse files a separate return, and the two paid itemized expenses (such as medical bills from a joint checking account) jointly; the computed condition is false because the filing status is not married filing separately.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: "If you and your spouse paid expenses jointly and are filing separate returns for 2025, see Pub. 504 to figure the portion of joint expenses that you can claim as itemized deductions." p504 p. 5: "You can claim the standard deduction even if your spouse files a separate return and itemizes deductions."
findings.why: The Schedule A instruction applies to any spouses who paid expenses jointly and file separate returns, not only to married filing separately status. A married head-of-household filer still has a spouse filing a separate return, so the joint-expense allocation can apply to them, but the gate never asks.

findings.situation: An MFS itemizer lives in a community property state, where Pub. 504 Table 1 does not apply, yet the gated question asks only about a joint account or a joint state return.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: "Caution: If you live in a community property state, these rules don't apply. See Community Property."
findings.why: Community-property spouses split income and paid expenses under different rules. A filer whose deductions were paid from community funds held in an individual account could truthfully answer no, even though the amounts must be allocated.

findings.situation: A married filing separately filer who itemizes and paid everything from their own funds, with separate state returns, is still asked the question.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: "file a separate state income tax return | the state income tax you alone paid during the year."
findings.why: That filer deducts only what they alone paid, so the gated line has no effect. The only cost is one extra question, which is acceptable by design.

findings.situation: A married-filing-separately filer whose shared mortgage interest was reported on another borrower's Form 1098 reports their share only on line 8b, so the line 8a helper is false even though the debt exceeds the MFS limit.

findings.why: Interest paid on a shared mortgage can appear only on line 8b and is still subject to the debt limits. The gate keyed to line 8a misses it.

findings.situation: The filer's real estate tax amount includes tax on property, or part of a home such as a home office or rented portion, used in a trade or business. The listed nondeductible items do not include business use, so the filer answers no and the business part stays in line 5b.

findings.situation: The filer pays real estate tax through mortgage escrow and entered the amount paid into escrow. In 2025 the lender actually paid a different, smaller amount to the taxing authority, and the escrow excess is not one of the listed items.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6: "If your mortgage payments include your real estate taxes, you can include only the amount the mortgage company actually paid to the taxing authority in 2025."
findings.why: Escrowed amounts not remitted in 2025 are not deductible, but the question's list does not mention them, so the filer can truthfully answer no.

findings.situation: A filer whose entered amount includes tax paid in 2024 or 2026 (not paid in 2025) may not see it on the list, which mentions only tax not assessed before 2026.

findings.why: The question names the assessment condition but not the year-of-payment condition. A filer could read the list as not reaching tax paid outside 2025.

findings.situation: A filer, or the spouse, receives a Form 1099-INT or 1099-DIV as a nominee for a bank account or stock owned by someone else, and owns no bonds, cashed no savings bonds and received no loan or sale interest, so the computed condition is false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "You received interest or ordinary dividends as a nominee."; "Nominees. If you received a Form 1099-INT that includes interest you received as a nominee ... Subtract this amount from the subtotal"
findings.why: The cited text gives the nominee subtraction Schedule B special treatment, and the gated question's last bullet ('any other adjustment to the interest or dividends shown on your forms') is meant to catch it. The gate's bonds, savings bonds and loan helper does not cover nominee interest or dividends, so the gated line is silently false.

findings.situation: A filer receives a Form 1099-OID for a long-term bank certificate of deposit and reports less OID than the form shows. They truthfully answer no to owning bonds or notes, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "You are reporting original issue discount (OID) of less than the amount shown on Form 1099-OID."
findings.why: Form 1099-OID covers debt instruments generally, including CDs, not only bonds or notes. The gate's helper wording ties the OID adjustment to bonds or notes owned directly, so this case is missed.

findings.situation: A filer holds Treasury or corporate bonds in a brokerage account and may not consider them 'owned directly'.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Accrued interest. When you buy bonds between interest payment dates and pay accrued interest to the seller..."; "Amortizable bond premium. If you elect to reduce your interest income on a taxable bond..."
findings.why: 'Owned directly' can be read to exclude bonds held through a broker, as opposed to a fund. Bonds held through a broker can still produce accrued interest, OID or premium adjustments.

findings.situation: A filer cashed savings bonds or holds bonds bought at par with no premium, discount or accrued interest, and pays no education expenses.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Line 3. If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses..."
findings.why: The condition holds, but no special treatment applies, so the gated question is asked without being needed.

findings.situation: The filer owns more than 50% of a U.S. corporation, partnership or LLC, or is the grantor-owner of or a >50% beneficiary of a U.S. trust, and that entity holds a bank account abroad; the filer has no foreign account or asset in their own name and no 10% interest in a foreign company.
findings.irs_text: fincen114 p. 5, Financial Interest: 'the owner of record or holder of legal title is ... b. A corporation in which the United States person owns directly or indirectly ... more than 50 percent ... c. A partnership ... d. A trust of which the United States person (i) is the trust grantor and (ii) has an ownership interest ... e. A trust in which the United States person has a greater than 50 percent present beneficial interest'; i1040sb p. 3: 'For definitions of "financial interest" ... see the instructions for FinCEN Form 114.'
findings.why: The account belongs to the domestic entity, so a filer can truthfully answer no to 'did you ... have an account in another country.' The trust helper covers only foreign trusts, and the company helper covers only companies set up outside the U.S. Yet line 7a, the FBAR count and possibly Form 8938 all reach this account.

findings.situation: The filer owns a U.S. single-member LLC (a disregarded entity) or is treated as owner of a domestic grantor trust, and that LLC or trust holds a foreign account, foreign stock or another specified foreign financial asset.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 8: 'If you are the owner of a disregarded entity, you have an interest in any specified foreign financial assets owned by the disregarded entity'; 'If you are considered the owner under the grantor trust rules ... of any part of a trust, you have an interest in any specified foreign financial asset held by that part of the trust.'
findings.why: All five helpers ask what 'you' had, owned or were connected to. A filer whose foreign asset is titled to a domestic LLC or domestic trust can truthfully answer no to every helper, which drops Form 8938 and line 7a.

findings.situation: Parents elect on Form 8814 to report their child's interest and dividends, and the child holds a foreign account or other specified foreign financial asset; neither parent has a foreign connection of their own.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 8, Interests in Assets Generating Certain Unearned Income of Children: 'If you file Form 8814 ... you have an interest in any specified foreign financial asset held by the child.'
findings.why: The helpers ask only about the filer and spouse, so the child's foreign asset never makes the computed condition true. The Form 8938 question is then never asked, even though the parent has a reportable interest.

findings.situation: The filer directly holds stock or securities of a foreign issuer outside any account (for example, share certificates kept at home), a foreign partnership interest, or a swap or derivative with a foreign counterparty.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 7: 'Examples of other specified foreign financial assets include ... Stock issued by a foreign corporation ... A capital or profits interest in a foreign partnership ... An option or other derivative instrument ... entered into with a foreign counterparty.'
findings.why: 'Own anything else of value outside the United States' can be read as asking where the property physically sits, not who issued it. A filer holding foreign-issued stock or a contract in the U.S. could answer no, and the company helper requires a 10% stake or an officer role.

findings.situation: The filer holds an interest in a foreign estate, such as being an heir to an estate administered abroad.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 8, Interests in Foreign Estates and Foreign Trusts: 'An interest in a foreign trust or a foreign estate is not a specified foreign financial asset unless you know or have reason to know ... of the interest.'
findings.why: The trust helper names trusts and family foundations, not estates. Whether an expected inheritance counts as 'anything else of value' you 'own' outside the U.S. is open to either reading.

findings.situation: The filer's only connection is an account at a bank in Puerto Rico or Guam, or an officer role in a foreign company that has no accounts the filer can sign for.
findings.irs_text: fincen114 p. 5: 'the United States includes ... all United States territories and possessions'; i1040sb p. 3: 'A financial account is located in a foreign country if the account is physically located outside of the United States.'
findings.why: The condition holds, but line 7a and the FBAR give a territory account no amount; only Form 8938 can reach it. The officer role leads to Form 5471, which is not a gated line.

findings.situation: A filer or spouse holds less than 10% of a foreign corporation's value but 10% or more of its voting power (for example, through voting preferred shares), and reads the helper's 'owner ... of 10% or more' as an equity or value share only.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'You may also have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you owned 10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation's stock, or (b) combined voting power of all classes of a foreign corporation's stock with voting rights.'
findings.why: The gate's '10% or more of one' does not say value or votes. A filer could reasonably read it as an ownership share by value and answer no, while the IRS text also counts the voting-power test.

findings.situation: A filer's 10% of a foreign corporation is held through a partnership, corporation, trust or estate they have an interest in, or through options or warrants, rather than directly or by family members.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'you owned 10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation's stock'
findings.why: The gate counts only ownership 'alone or with your family.' The gated question and its help count shares held by entities and option shares, so a filer whose stake is indirect could truthfully answer the gate no and never reach the gated question.

findings.situation: A filer whose only connection is a bank account, investment or trust in Puerto Rico, Guam or another U.S. territory, with no role in or 10% of a foreign corporation.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'You may have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you were an officer or director of a foreign corporation.'
findings.why: The second helper makes the condition true for territory accounts and investments that have no bearing on Form 5471. This only adds questions.

findings.situation: A filer who is a manager of, or 10% owner of, a foreign entity that is not a corporation, such as a foreign partnership.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'officer or director of a foreign corporation'
findings.why: The gate asks about any 'company set up outside the United States,' which is broader than the foreign-corporation scope of Form 5471.

findings.situation: The trust is administered by U.S. trustees under a state court, but a foreign protector or other non-trustee foreign person can veto substantial decisions, so it is a foreign trust; the filer was its grantor or received a distribution from it, yet truthfully says it is not 'outside the United States' and has no 'trustee abroad'.
findings.irs_text: cfr-26-301-7701-7 p. 4: "Control ... with no other person having the power to veto any of the substantial decisions. To determine whether United States persons have control, it is necessary to consider all persons who have authority to make a substantial decision of the trust, not only the trust fiduciaries."; p. 2: "The term foreign trust means any trust other than a domestic trust."
findings.why: The helper tests foreignness only by location and trustee residence. A trust that fails the control test because of a foreign non-trustee power holder is foreign, but the condition is false.

findings.situation: In 2025 the filer sold or lent property to a foreign trust at arm's length, or borrowed cash or securities from one, or used its property free, and does not see that as having 'gave to it' or as someone who 'may receive from it'.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 3, Line 8: "For this purpose, a loan of cash or marketable securities is generally considered to be a distribution"; "If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025, you may have to file Form 3520."
findings.why: A transferor includes someone who sells or lends to the trust, and a loan from the trust counts as a distribution. The helper's 'gave to it' and 'may receive from it' suggest gifts and future benefits, so a truthful filer can answer no.

findings.situation: The filer received a final distribution in 2025 from a foreign trust that then ended, or made a transfer in an earlier year to a foreign trust that still existed in 2025 but with which the filer no longer has dealings.
findings.irs_text: f1040sb Part III line 8: "During 2025, did you receive a distribution from, or were you the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust?"
findings.why: The helper is in the present tense ('do you ... have anything to do with', 'may receive'). A filer whose connection ended can truthfully answer no, although line 8 asks about any 2025 distribution and about past grantor or transferor status.

findings.situation: A filer received a 2025 distribution from a foreign trust through an intermediary, such as a nominee, a company or a relative.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 3, Line 8: "If you received a distribution from a foreign trust, you must provide additional information."
findings.why: 'Have anything to do with ... as the person who ... may receive from it' does not say whether indirect receipt counts. The gated question's help says it does, but the gate question gives the filer no such guidance.

findings.situation: The filer has only a U.S. territory account, investment or company, with no foreign trust connection.
findings.irs_text: f1040sb line 8: "did you receive a distribution from, or were you the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust?"
findings.why: The territory helper makes the condition true even though line 8 would be no. This costs only an extra question.

findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "You received interest or ordinary dividends as a nominee."; "You received interest from a seller-financed mortgage..."; "You have accrued interest from a bond."
findings.why: Every gated item turns on interest or ordinary dividends, so capital gain distributions alone never give either gated line an amount. The extra yes only costs questions.

findings.situation: A filer with only ordinary dividends and no interest of any kind meets the gate and is asked the bonds, savings-bond and seller-financing question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "You have accrued interest from a bond."; "You are claiming the exclusion of interest from series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989."
findings.why: The items behind sb.bonds_any all concern interest, so dividends alone never give that line an amount. Gates lean to yes by design.

findings.situation: A sole proprietor with no employees in 2025 contributes on their own behalf, as a self-employed person, to a dependent care assistance program and figures the deductible part on Form 2441 for line 14.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 7, Line 14: "If you made contributions on your behalf as a self-employed person to a dependent care assistance program, complete Form 2441, Parts I and III, to figure your deductible contributions to that program."
findings.why: The instructions put a self-employed person's own dependent care contributions on line 14 without requiring any employee. The gate's help says "You are not an employee of your own business," so this filer truthfully answers no, and line 14 is zeroed. The gated question's help ("Not for yourself") also excludes this amount.

findings.situation: A business with no workers during 2025 still pays in 2025 a final paycheck, accident and health or group-term life costs, or deductible plan contributions for people who were employees in an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 10, Line 26: "Enter the total salaries and wages for the tax year"; p. 8, Line 19: "contributions you made for the benefit of your employees to a pension, profit-sharing, or annuity plan"
findings.why: "Did this business have employees in 2025" can be read as asking whether anyone worked for the business in 2025, which gives a no. It can also be read as "people it paid wages to" in 2025, which gives a yes. A filer with only former employees could reasonably answer no and drop 2025 amounts on lines 14, 19 and 26.

findings.situation: A business bought or produced merchandise in 2025, but all of it was destroyed, stolen, or spoiled before sale, so it sold none and held none at the start or end of the year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 15, Part III: "if you engaged in a trade or business in which the production, purchase, or sale of merchandise was an income-producing factor, you must take inventories into account"; f1040sc p. 2, line 36 "Purchases less cost of items withdrawn for personal use"
findings.why: The IRS condition is triggered by production or purchase alone, and lines 36 to 39 would carry those costs. The gate asks only about goods sold or held at the start or end of the year, so this filer can truthfully answer no, and the costs are dropped.

findings.situation: A business holds only raw materials or unfinished work in process at year end, or it sold nothing.
findings.irs_text: Gate: "hold goods for sale at the start or end of the year"; i1040sc p. 15: "you must take inventories into account at the beginning and end of your tax year"
findings.why: A filer could read "goods for sale" as finished goods only. The help text says materials that become part of what you sell count, but that help is easy to miss, and unfinished goods are not clearly "for sale."

findings.situation: A small business taxpayer that sells goods but treats inventory as nonincidental materials and supplies, deducting them as they are used and keeping no inventory, answers yes.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 15: "If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory"
findings.why: This filer may have nothing to enter on lines 35 and 41, and possibly no amounts on Part III at all, but the gate still asks the questions. That is acceptable by design.

findings.why: The IRS text treats expenses as deductible when 'paid or incurred', but the gate asks only whether the business paid in 2025. An accrual filer with incurred but unpaid 2025 travel or meal costs is dropped. The helper wording 'had expenses' would cover this, but the asked question does not.

findings.situation: An owner traveled overnight on business in their own car (deducted on line 9), stayed free with relatives, bought no meals, and claims the optional $5-a-day incidental expense amount on line 24a.

findings.why: The $5-a-day amount is allowed in place of records of actual spending. A filer who paid nothing for lodging, transport or meals on line 24a could truthfully answer no to 'pay for overnight travel' and lose the deduction.

findings.situation: A filer drove their own vehicle on an overnight business trip and paid for gas but no lodging or airfare.

findings.why: A filer could read 'pay for overnight travel' to mean only tickets and hotels, not car costs or incidentals. The filer might then answer no even though the trip had overnight travel that can carry incidental or standard-meal-allowance amounts.

findings.situation: A filer who first bought a passive business interest during 2025 (for example a limited partnership, an S corporation share, or publicly traded partnership units) and has a 2025 loss from it must answer the gate no, so the passive-activity refusal is never reached.

findings.why: The gate is true for church-controlled work, but the cited text limits church employee income to organizations with that certificate.

findings.situation: A retired minister receives retirement benefits from a church plan or housing after retirement.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 1: 'don’t include on line 2: • Retirement benefits you received from a church plan after retirement, or • The rental value of a home or an allowance for a home furnished to you ... after retirement.'
findings.why: The gate is true because the filer was paid by a church or as clergy, but the cited text gives no SE tax amount for these retirement items.

findings.situation: A filer whose only activity in 2025 was receiving royalties, or renting out real estate only, answers yes to the gate and is asked the personal-property question, which has no effect for them.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 5: "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles"
findings.why: The gated line matters only when personal property such as equipment or vehicles was rented out. Royalties and real-estate-only rentals reach the question without needing it, which costs only one question.

findings.situation: A filer who only offered property for rent in 2025 and never rented it out or received rent answers yes to the gate.
findings.irs_text: p527 p. 3: "Rental income is any payment you receive for the use or occupation of property."
findings.why: With no rental and no payment, there is nothing about personal property rental to report, so the gate holds where the gated line has no amount.

findings.situation: A filer or spouse received strike or lockout benefits reported on a Form W-2 and no other non-W-2 wages, tips, or strike benefits, so the helper is truthfully answered no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: 'The following types of income must be included in the total on line 1h. • Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts).'
findings.why: The IRS text requires strike or lockout benefits to be included on line 1h without a not-on-W-2 limitation; the gate drops them when they were reported on a W-2.

findings.situation: A filer had non-W-2 wages or tips but no strike or lockout benefits, so the gate asks the strike-benefit question although the gated line is zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: 'Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts).'
findings.why: The helper is triggered by any non-W-2 wages or tips, not only strike benefits, but the gated line has no amount when no strike benefits were received.

findings.situation: A filer has cash or card tips not reported in full to an employer but no noncash tips, so the gate is true while the noncash-tips line has no amount.

findings.why: The gate is broader than the noncash-tips line because it also turns on unreported cash or card tips. With no noncash tips, the gated line is zero, so this is only an extra question, not a missed amount.

findings.situation: A filer aged 19 to 23 who was not a full-time student, or a filer aged 18 to 23 whose earned income was more than half of their support, is not filing jointly and was under 24, so the condition holds, yet Form 8615 does not apply.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: "b. Was age 18 at the end of 2025 and didn’t have earned income that was more than half of the child's support, or c. Was a full-time student at least age 19 and under age 24 at the end of 2025 and didn’t have earned income that was more than half of the child's support."
findings.why: Being under 24 is broader than condition 3, so some filers get the unearned-income question needlessly. That leans to yes and drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer under 24 who is not filing jointly and whose parents were both dead at the end of 2025 meets the condition, but Form 8615 does not apply to them.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: "These rules don’t apply if neither of the child’s parents were living at the end of the year."
findings.why: The gate does not test condition 4, so it asks some filers the gated question needlessly. That is harmless over-inclusion.

findings.situation: A filer born January 1, 2002 might answer that they were under 24 at the end of 2025, although the IRS treats them as 24.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: "January 1, 2002 24*** ... *** Don’t use Form 8615 for this child."
findings.why: A literal reading could produce a yes where the form does not apply. That only costs an extra question; no IRS-covered filer is dropped.

findings.situation: A child whose biological parents both died before the end of 2025, but whose stepparent was alive, could read 'was a parent of yours alive' as asking only about biological or adoptive parents and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: 'At least one of the child's parents was alive at the end of 2025.' ... 'For these rules, the term "child" includes a legally adopted child and a stepchild.'
findings.why: The instructions treat stepchildren as children, so a living stepparent can satisfy condition 4. The question does not say that stepparents and adoptive parents count, so a filer could answer no and drop Form 8615.

findings.situation: A filer with more than $2,700 of tax-exempt interest or nontaxable benefits, but not more than $2,700 of taxable unearned income, answers yes to the unearned-income question.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: 'It includes taxable interest, dividends, capital gains ... the taxable part of social security and pension payments'
findings.why: The question asks about any income that was not pay for work, without limiting it to taxable amounts. This over-includes, which is acceptable for a gate that leans to yes.

findings.situation: A child born January 1, 2002 counts as age 24 at the end of 2025 but may answer yes to an under-24 question; a non-student born January 1, 2007 counts as 19 but may answer yes as '18'.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: 'January 1, 2002 ... 24*** ... Don't use Form 8615 for this child.'
findings.why: Calendar age and the IRS's age convention differ by a day, so these filers are asked questions they do not need. This over-includes, which is acceptable for a gate that leans to yes.

findings.situation: A child who meets all the other conditions but is not required to file a return, for example because a parent elects Form 8814, still passes the gate.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: '2. The child is required to file a tax return.' ... 'If the parent makes this election, the child won't have to file a return or Form 8615.'
findings.why: Neither the gate nor the gated question tests the filing requirement; only the help text mentions it. This over-includes, which is acceptable for a gate that leans to yes.

findings.situation: The filer alone drives the vehicle partly for business and partly for investment (for example 40% business, 30% investment), with no other user and no entertainment use.
findings.irs_text: i4562 (2025) p. 14: 'Generally, a qualified business use is any use in your trade or business. However, it does not include any of the following. • Investment use.' p463 p. 25: 'It doesn't include use for the production of income (investment use)'
findings.why: Investment use by the filer alone removes miles from qualified business use and can bring it to 50% or less, yet the filer truthfully answers no to the gate. qbu_low is then forced false and the vehicle goes on line 26 instead of line 27.

findings.situation: The filer is regularly engaged in the business of leasing passenger automobiles, and this vehicle is held for lease but was not leased or used by anyone else during the year.
findings.irs_text: i4562 (2025) p. 15: 'The business use requirement and the limits for passenger automobiles generally do not apply to passenger automobiles leased or held by anyone regularly engaged in the business of leasing passenger automobiles.'
findings.why: The exception covers vehicles merely 'held' by a leasing business, so nobody but the filer need use the vehicle. The filer truthfully answers no, and the leasing line is forced false.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse uses the vehicle, for example as compensation for services in the filer's business or under a lease from the filer.
findings.irs_text: i4562 (2025) p. 14: 'The use of the property as compensation for services performed by a 5% owner or related person.' / 'Leasing the property to a 5% owner or related person if the value related to such usage is not reported as income to the individual.'
findings.why: 'Anyone but you' does not say whether a joint-return spouse counts as 'you'. A filer could read the spouse as included in 'you' and answer no, dropping related-person uses that reduce qualified business use.

findings.situation: A filer with a leased vehicle who answers No to the gate (actual expenses were used in an earlier lease year) is still asked the gated question, even though its own wording forces a No for leased vehicles, so the line can only be false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 6, Line 9: "You can take the standard mileage rate for 2025 only if you: • Owned the vehicle and used the standard mileage rate for the first year you placed the vehicle in service, or • Leased the vehicle and are using the standard mileage rate for the entire lease period."
findings.why: For a leased vehicle the owned-and-first-year branch never applies, so asking it costs a question but drops no amount. When the gate is answered Yes, the rate was used in the first year anyway, so making the line false does not lose the owned-and-first-year path.

locators: p. 6, Line 9, "You must use actual expenses if you used five or more vehicles simultaneously" and "You can take the standard mileage rate for 2025 only if you"

findings.situation: A filer answers yes but has no sale that qualifies for the Schedule D totals: a collectible, a sale with no Form 1099-B/1099-DA showing basis reported, an adjustment or code, the Ordinary box or QOF box checked, or a QOF deferral or termination. The routing question is then asked even though every such sale must still go on Form 8949.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 10, Lines 1a and 8a: "the aggregate totals from any transactions (except sales of collectibles) for which: • You received a Form 1099-B or Form 1099-DA ... that shows basis was reported to the IRS and doesn't show any adjustments ... • The Ordinary box ... isn't checked; • The QOF box ... isn't checked; ... • You don't need to make any adjustments"
findings.why: The gate is a free choice and does not test whether a qualifying sale exists, so a yes can lead to questions with no aggregate amount. This costs only extra questions. Reporting every sale on Form 8949 is always allowed ("You can report"), so a no never drops an amount.

locators: p. 10, lines 1a and 8a

findings.situation: A filer has an ordinary loss from the sale or worthlessness of small business (section 1244) or SBIC (section 1242) stock and sold no real estate or business property, so they truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "Use Form 4797 to report the following. ... 4. Ordinary loss on the sale, exchange, or worthlessness of small business investment company (section 1242) stock. 5. Ordinary loss on the sale, exchange, or worthlessness of small business (section 1244) stock."
findings.why: Stock is neither real estate nor business property as the help defines them, and worthlessness is not a sale. A no zeroes the Form 4797 line even though Form 4797 is required.

findings.situation: A trader in securities who made a mark-to-market election has ordinary gains or losses on securities and sold no real estate or equipment, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "6. Ordinary gain or loss on securities or commodities held in connection with your trading business, if you previously made a mark-to-market election."
findings.why: Securities are not what a filer understands as "business property" under the help's examples (equipment, a vehicle or a building). The Form 4797 requirement is dropped.

findings.situation: A filer's business property or long-held investment property was condemned (an involuntary conversion), and the filer answers no because they did not "sell or trade" it.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "2. The involuntary conversion (other than from casualty or theft) of property used in a trade or business and capital assets held more than 1 year for business or profit."
findings.why: The gate asks only about selling or trading, not about condemnations or other involuntary conversions. Investment property other than real estate is also outside "real estate or business property."

findings.situation: A filer sells a noncapital asset that is not inventory and not equipment, such as a self-created copyright, patent or literary work, and answers no because it is not real estate or business property.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "3. The disposition of noncapital assets other than inventory or property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of your trade or business."
findings.why: The help limits business property to things "used in a business or rented out," which a filer would not read to include their own creative works. Form 4797 is missed.

findings.situation: A filer whose rental or business property was taken by eminent domain, or who received insurance or award proceeds for it, may or may not treat that as having "sold" the property.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "The involuntary conversion (other than from casualty or theft) of property used in a trade or business"
findings.why: "Sell or trade" does not clearly include forced dispositions, and the help does not mention them.

findings.why: The gate tests only interest paid and filing status. It does not test dependency or the income limit, so these filers reach questions whose lines end up giving no deduction. That costs only extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer who is not married filing separately paid interest only on loans that are not qualified student loans, such as a loan from a relative.

findings.situation: A filer whose earlier-year lump-sum payment was a railroad retirement benefit treated as social security, reported on Form RRB-1099 rather than Form SSA-1099, may answer no because the question tells them to look for the description on Form SSA-1099.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b: "If you received railroad retirement benefits treated as social security, you should receive a Form RRB-1099."; p. 32 worksheet line 1: "Enter the total amount from box 5 of all your Forms SSA-1099 and RRB-1099."
findings.why: The first sentence of the question covers any benefit, but the second points only to the SSA-1099 box 3 description. An RRB-1099 recipient with an earlier-year payment could read the question as not applying to them, which would drop the lump-sum election.

findings.situation: The benefits include a payment for an earlier year, but none of the 2025 benefits are taxable (for example, the worksheet stops at line 7 or line 9).
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Line 6c: "If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount with the lump-sum election."
findings.why: The lump-sum election only reduces a taxable amount, so it does not matter when nothing is taxable, yet the gate still asks the question.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse—not the filer—received qualified tips from this employer in a listed occupation, so the filer can truthfully answer no to the singular 'you got tips' wording while the IRS still allows the spouse's amount.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 101: “Fill out Schedule 1-A, Part II, only if: • You (and/or your spouse if filing a joint return) received qualified tips in 2025.”; p. 104: “If you and/or your spouse received qualified tips as employees with respect to employment with more than one employer...”
findings.why: The gate asks whether any of “these tips” were for a listed job and the help refers to “the work you got tips for,” without covering the spouse. A spouse's listed-occupation tips from the same employer are still qualified tips on a joint return, so the condition can be false while the gated line has an amount.

findings.situation: A married filer with qualified tips in a listed occupation files separately instead of jointly.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 101: “If you are married, you must file a joint return with your spouse to claim this deduction.”
findings.why: The occupation-list gate would be true, but the IRS gives no deduction amount for married filing separately; this is a deliberately broad gate rather than a missed amount.

findings.situation: The filer gives appreciated property held 1 year or less, such as stock held 5 months, or art or a manuscript the filer created, to a public charity, so no listed item applies and the filer truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: Examples of ordinary income property are inventory, works of art created by the donor, manuscripts prepared by the donor, and capital assets ... held 1 year or less. ... The amount you can deduct ... is its FMV minus the amount that would be ordinary income or short-term capital gain (p526 2025, p. 19)
findings.why: The list only catches appreciation on belongings owned over a year that the charity won't use, and on inventory. If the tool does not apply this reduction to basis, short-term and self-created property would be deducted at full FMV.

findings.situation: The filer gives business property whose gain would partly be ordinary income because of depreciation recapture, or a filer applies the 50% limit instead of the 30% limit to capital gain property, and neither case appears in the list.
findings.irs_text: to the extent of any gain from the property that must be recaptured as ordinary income under section 1245, section 1250 ... the property is treated as ordinary income property (i8283 Dec 2025, p. 3); you must reduce the FMV ... if: ... 2. You choose the 50%-limit instead of the 30% limit for capital gain property (p526 2025, p. 19)
findings.why: Both cases require reducing FMV by the gain, but no item in the question describes them. A filer would answer NO, and the tool would leave FMV unreduced.

findings.situation: The filer gives property subject to a mortgage or other debt, or a bond, and none of the listed items applies.
findings.irs_text: If you contribute property subject to a debt (such as a mortgage), you must reduce the FMV of the property by: 1. Any allowable deduction for interest you paid (or will pay) that is attributable to any period after the contribution (p526 2025, p. 12)
findings.why: The question never asks about debt on the property, so the required reduction is never prompted and the tool would deduct FMV without it.

findings.situation: The filer gives property worth less than its basis, or gives to a nonoperating private foundation that qualifies for the 50% limit. Either way the filer must answer YES even though no reduction applies.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'it went to a private foundation that is not an operating foundation, and it is not publicly traded stock'; IRS: 'The reduced deduction applies to contributions to all private nonoperating foundations other than those qualifying for the 50% limit' and the reduction is 'by any amount that would have been long-term capital gain' (p526 2025, p. 19)
findings.why: The reduction applies only to appreciated property given to nonoperating foundations that do not qualify for the 50% limit. The question also covers depreciated property and 50%-limit foundations, which the plain computation handles correctly.

findings.situation: The filer gives restricted-use property, or an undivided part of the whole interest, with a deduction of $5,000 or less. The filer must answer YES, though the instructions put such gifts in Section A.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'the charity is restricted in how it may use it' / 'less than your whole interest in the property'; IRS: 'You must also file Form 8283, Section B, if conditions were placed on the use of the property or you gave less than an entire interest in a property and the contribution was for more than $5,000' (i8283 Dec 2025, p. 3)
findings.why: The appraisal and Section B requirement applies only above $5,000, and over-$5,000 groups are already checked from the amount entered. These items have no dollar threshold, so they also refuse small Section A gifts.

findings.situation: A filer whose charity restricts use only in a general way, for example by earmarking the gift for a particular program, may not know whether the gift counts as 'restricted in how it may use it'.
findings.irs_text: or (3) Earmarks donated property for a particular use (26 CFR 1.170A-13, p. 3)
findings.why: The question does not say whether a restriction the donor sets, a restriction in the donee's own policy, or simple earmarking counts. Filers could reasonably read it either way.

question:
Is any of these true of this group?

  - it reached you through a Schedule K-1
  - it is a vehicle
  - it is a share of a partnership, an S corporation or another pass-through business
  - it is intellectual property, such as a patent or a copyright
  - it is inventory of a business
  - it is a conservation easement, or less than your whole interest in the property
  - the charity is restricted in how it may use it
  - it went to a private foundation that is not an operating foundation, and it is not publicly traded stock
  - it is stock given to a private foundation that is not an operating foundation, and you and your family have given away more than 10% of the value of that company's stock
  - it is a stuffed or mounted animal that you prepared, or paid to have prepared
  - it is art or other belongings you owned over a year, now worth more than you paid, that the charity will not use for its charitable purpose
  - you gave only the use of it, such as a stay in your vacation home
  - it is a clothing or household item worth more than $500 that is not in good used condition

findings.situation: A filer's EIC was disallowed in an earlier year, but the filer later filed Form 8862, the EIC was allowed for that year, and it has not been reduced or disallowed again, so the filer must answer YES although no Form 8862 is needed for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "But don’t file Form 8862 if either of the following applies. • You filed Form 8862 for another year, the EIC was allowed for that year, and your EIC hasn’t been reduced or disallowed again for any reason other than a math or clerical error."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the credit "for any year after 1996" was "reduced or disallowed" and has no carve-out for a later successful recertification. The tool's computation would be correct for this filer because the IRS text requires no Form 8862.

findings.situation: A filer is taking the EIC without a qualifying child, and the only reason an earlier EIC was reduced or disallowed was that a child on Schedule EIC was found not to be a qualifying child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You are taking the EIC without a qualifying child and the only reason your EIC was reduced or disallowed in the other year was because it was determined that a child listed on Schedule EIC wasn’t your qualifying child."
findings.why: The question's phrase "reduced or disallowed for any reason other than a math or clerical error" requires YES, but the IRS text says not to file Form 8862 here. The tool would refuse a credit it can compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's CTC, ACTC or ODC was denied or reduced in an earlier year, but the filer filed Form 8862 for 2024 and the credit was allowed for that year, or another exception applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 39: "Don’t file Form 8862 if you filed Form 8862 for 2024, and the child tax credit, additional child tax credit, or credit for other dependents was allowed for that year." i1040s8812 p. 2: "you must attach Form 8862 to your tax return to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC unless an exception applies."
findings.why: The question has no exception for an earlier recertification, so this filer must answer YES. The IRS text does not require Form 8862 for this filer, so the tool's computation would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer has a past reduction, disallowance or ban affecting only one credit family, such as the EIC, and claims only the other family, such as the CTC, yet the single answer refuses both lines.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You must file Form 8862 if your EIC for a year after 1996 was reduced or disallowed" and "10 years after the most recent tax year for which there was a final determination that your EIC claim was due to fraud." i1040s8812 p. 2: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced ... you must attach Form 8862 ... to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC" and "you will not be allowed to claim any of these credits for 10 years."
findings.why: The question joins both families with "or" and refers to "one of these credits," so a history with either family produces YES and refuses both lines. The quoted IRS text ties each Form 8862 requirement and ban to its own credit family, so the unaffected line would compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's earlier CTC or ODC was limited only by the income phase-out or by tax liability, and the IRS never denied or adjusted the claim.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 2: "The maximum credit amount of your CTC and ODC may be reduced if either (1) or (2) applies." Compare: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error, you must attach Form 8862."
findings.why: The question's "reduced ... for any reason" does not say the reduction must be an IRS action on a claim, and the instructions also use "reduced" for the ordinary limits. A filer could reasonably answer YES because of a phase-out or tax limit, or NO because the IRS did not change the claim.

findings.situation: A married-filing-jointly filer whose worksheet line 10 is below the applicable $14,000/$15,000/$16,000 threshold must use the Pub. 590-A worksheet even when taking the full IRA deduction.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, IRA Deduction Worksheet: "If married filing jointly and line 10 is less than $14,000 ($15,000 if one spouse is age 50 or older ...; $16,000 if both ...), stop here and use the worksheet in Pub. 590-A to figure your IRA deduction."
findings.why: That filer truthfully answers No because they are not choosing a smaller deduction, but the tool's line 20 then just sums lines 12a and 12b from the regular worksheet and does not perform the required Pub. 590-A computation. This is not the already-listed smaller-deduction/Form 8606 refusal.

findings.situation: A partner has a small 2025 partnership loss within basis but also has nondeductible expenses, charitable contributions, foreign taxes, a property distribution, or a decrease in share of liabilities that reduces basis enough that the loss or those items exceed basis.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: 'Nondeductible expenses ... Decrease the adjusted basis'; i1065sk1 p. 3: a partner’s share of charitable contributions and foreign taxes 'is subject to this basis limitation'.
findings.why: The question tells the filer to subtract only losses and money taken out, omitting other basis decreases, so a filer can truthfully answer NO even though the IRS basis limitation applies; the tool then treats the K-1 as passing the screen.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse has a partnership loss above the spouse’s basis, while the filer’s own basis is sufficient.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: 'a partner may only claim their share of a partnership loss (including a capital loss) to the extent it doesn’t exceed their adjusted basis in the partnership at the end of the partnership’s tax year.'
findings.why: The question asks only about 'your' basis, not the spouse’s basis, so a filer could truthfully answer NO for the spouse’s K-1; the tool would not apply the spouse’s separate basis limitation.

findings.situation: A partner’s 2025 loss is less than basis before the loss but more than the post-loss ending basis because the question’s parenthetical subtracts that loss from basis.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: 'a partner may only claim their share of a partnership loss ... to the extent it doesn’t exceed their adjusted basis in the partnership at the end of the partnership’s tax year.'
findings.why: The parenthetical says to subtract 'losses' in computing basis, so a $100 basis with an $80 loss can look like $80 > $20 and produce YES; the IRS limitation allows the $80 loss because it does not exceed the $100 basis before the loss.

findings.situation: A partner has a deemed distribution under section 752(b) reported in box 19 (Code D) that exceeds basis, so gain is recognized, but the filer did not actually take money out.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: "Code A, however, doesn’t include deemed distributions of money under section 752(b); see Code D, later."
findings.why: The question asks about money the filer “took out,” so a filer with only a liability-decrease deemed distribution can truthfully answer NO, while the IRS rule treats the excess over basis as gain the tool does not compute.

findings.situation: A partner receives a box 19 distribution for services (Codes F or G) that exceeds basis and answers YES because money taken out is more than basis, but the Code A excess-over-basis gain rule does not apply to service distributions.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: "Code A also doesn’t include distributions the partnership made to you for performing services."
findings.why: The question points to all of box 19, not just Code A cash and marketable securities other than for services, so it can force a refusal even though the tool would correctly pass the screen if the filer answered NO.

findings.situation: A partner has multiple distributions during 2025 and cannot tell whether to compare total box 19 to basis before one distribution or to test each distribution separately.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: "immediately before the distribution"
findings.why: The IRS rule applies distribution by distribution, but the question’s singular “basis in it just before you took it out” can reasonably be read as an aggregate box 19 comparison.

findings.situation: A partner used a rental home personally for 15 days while it was rented at fair rental value for 200 days (10% = 20 days).

findings.situation: On a 2025 joint return, the spouse who holds this K-1 filed a separate 2024 return (or a 2024 return before the marriage) and claimed the fuel tax credit from this partnership on it. The filer reads 'your 2024 return' as the filer's own 2024 return and answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 9: "If you claimed a credit for federal tax on gasoline or other fuels on your 2024 Form 1040, 1040-SR, or 1040-NR based on information received from the partnership, enter as income in column (h) or column (k)"
findings.why: The joint 2025 return must include the spouse's 2024 credit as income. The question names only 'your 2024 return' and never mentions a spouse's separate 2024 return, so the tool computes zero.

findings.situation: A filer claimed a fuel tax credit from this partnership on a 2023 or earlier return, but not on a 2024 return, and ticks YES because the heading asks about 'an earlier one'.
findings.irs_text: Question heading: "Does your 2024 return, or an earlier one, show any of these for this partnership?" vs. i1040se p. 9: "enter as income ... the amount of the credit claimed for 2024"
findings.why: Only a credit claimed for 2024 becomes 2025 Schedule E income. For a credit from an earlier year, the tool's zero is correct, but the heading's 'or an earlier one' prompts a YES and a refusal.

findings.situation: The heading covers 2024 'or an earlier one', while the text under the box asks only about the 2024 return, so a filer whose only claim was in an earlier year can reasonably answer either way.
findings.irs_text: Heading: "Does your 2024 return, or an earlier one, show any of these"; What this asks: "Did your 2024 return claim a credit for federal tax on gasoline or other fuels"
findings.why: The two wordings on the same box disagree about which years count, so the answer depends on which one the filer follows.

findings.situation: A filer claimed the fuel credit from this partnership only on an amended 2024 return (Form 1040-X), not on the original return.

findings.situation: An amount used in the activity is protected against loss by an arrangement similar to a guarantee or stop-loss agreement but is not literally one of those two.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8, At-Risk Limitations: 'protected against loss by a guarantee, a stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement'
findings.why: The question asks only about a guarantee or stop-loss agreement, so a filer covered by another similar arrangement could truthfully answer NO even though the IRS text requires Form 6198.

findings.situation: A nonrecourse loan is secured by the filer's own property other than property used in the activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8, At-Risk Limitations: 'Nonrecourse loans ... that aren’t secured by your own property (other than the property used in the activity)' are amounts for which you generally aren’t at risk.
findings.why: The question asks about anything borrowed without personal liability except qualified real estate loans, so a filer would answer YES, but the IRS text treats a loan secured by the filer's other own property as at risk, so no Form 6198 is needed.

findings.situation: The filer acquired the partnership interest before 1987 and has a loss from an activity of holding real property placed in service before 1987.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8, At-Risk Limitations: 'if you acquired your partnership interest before 1987, the at-risk rules don’t apply to losses from an activity of holding real property placed in service before 1987'
findings.why: A nonrecourse loan would make the filer answer YES, but the IRS text exempts this loss from the at-risk rules, so the tool would compute it correctly without refusing for Form 6198.

findings.situation: A nonrecourse loan is secured by real property, and the filer cannot tell whether it is a 'qualified real estate loan' as the question uses that phrase.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8, At-Risk Limitations: 'See the instructions for item K1, later, for the exception for qualified nonrecourse financing secured by real property.'
findings.why: The question says 'qualified real estate loans' rather than the IRS term 'qualified nonrecourse financing secured by real property,' so a filer may read the exception too broadly or too narrowly.

findings.situation: A held-back rental real estate loss came from a prior year in which the filer was a limited partner, even though the filer helped make decisions and owned at least 10% of the activity, and the filer actively participates in the current year.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: “Limited partners can’t actively participate unless future regulations provide an exception”; i8582 p. 10: “If you didn’t actively participate in both years, enter the prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part V.”
findings.why: The question asks only about helping make decisions or owning less than a tenth, so this filer can answer NO; the IRS nevertheless treats the prior-year limited-partner loss as not actively participated in, requiring Part V, which the tool does not compute.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer individually owned less than 10% of the prior-year rental activity, but the spouse also owned an interest so that their combined interest was at least 10%.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: “You aren’t considered to actively participate ... if, at any time during the tax year, your interest (including your spouse’s interest) ... was less than 10% (by value).”
findings.why: The question’s “you owned less than a tenth” does not tell the filer to include the spouse’s interest, so the filer may answer YES even though the IRS 10% test is met and the tool computes the active-participation situation correctly.

findings.situation: The filer owned less than 10% for part of the prior year but not at year-end, or is unsure whether the test is by value.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: “if, at any time during the tax year, your interest ... was less than 10% (by value).”
findings.why: The question says only “owned less than a tenth of it” without stating “at any time during the year” or “by value,” so a filer could reasonably answer either YES or NO.

findings.situation: A Schedule K-1 has no dollar amount in box 12 but an attached statement reports the partner’s allowable share of the cost of qualified enterprise zone or qualified real property placed in service.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 18, Box 12: "The partnership will report on an attached statement your allowable share of the cost of any qualified enterprise zone or qualified real property it placed in service during the tax year."
findings.why: The question only asks whether box 12 itself shows an amount, so a truthful filer can answer NO even though the attached box 12 statement contains information needed to complete Form 4562 Part I; the tool would then treat the item as absent.

findings.situation: Box 12 contains a printed zero dollar amount, and the filer must decide whether a zero counts as “show an amount.”
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 18, Box 12: "Use this amount, along with the total cost of section 179 property placed in service during the year from other sources, to complete Part I of Form 4562."
findings.why: “Show an amount” can reasonably be read as requiring a nonzero entry, but a printed $0 is still an amount shown in the box; the wording does not resolve whether zero triggers the screen.

findings.situation: A partner receives a non-liquidating cash or marketable-securities distribution that exceeds the partner's adjusted basis in the partnership interest but does not sell, trade, or give up any of the interest.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: 'To the extent the cash and the FMV of the securities ... received exceed the adjusted basis of your partnership interest immediately before the distribution, the excess is treated as gain from the sale or exchange of your partnership interest.'
findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer sold, traded, or gave up any share, so the filer can truthfully answer NO to a distribution that leaves the interest intact. The IRS text nevertheless treats the excess distribution as sale/exchange gain reportable on Form 8949, which the tool would ignore.

findings.situation: The filer meets the 750-hour and more-than-half tests but did not materially participate in this partnership's rental real estate activity (for example, a limited partner with under 500 hours in it), so box 2 stays passive and the tool computes it correctly, yet the question makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 14, Box 2: "the income (loss) in box 2 isn't from a passive activity if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier) and you materially participated in the activity"; p. 9: "Limited partners. If you're a limited partner, you must meet item 1, 5, or 6 above"
findings.why: The question asks only about real estate professional status. It never asks about material participation in this partnership's activity, which the IRS also requires before box 2 becomes nonpassive.

findings.situation: The filer worked over 750 hours, and most of their working time, as an employee owning 5% or less of a real estate firm (such as a salaried property manager or an agent employed by a brokerage), so they are not a real estate professional and box 2 stays passive, but they answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "Services you performed as an employee aren't treated as performed in a real property trade or business unless you owned more than 5% of the stock (or more than 5% of the capital or profits interest) in the employer."
findings.why: "Work more than 750 hours in 2025 in real estate businesses" counts employee hours that the IRS excludes from both tests.

findings.situation: The filer's real estate hours were spent in real property businesses in which they did not materially participate, so they are not a real estate professional, but the hours make them answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "a. More than half of the personal services you performed in trades or businesses were performed in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated. b. You performed more than 750 hours of services in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated."
findings.why: The question counts any hours in real estate businesses. The IRS counts only hours in real property businesses in which the filer materially participated.

findings.situation: A filer whose 750+ hours were in construction, reconstruction, development, conversion or brokerage may not regard that work as "real estate businesses" and could answer NO even though they qualify and box 2 is nonpassive.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "A real property trade or business is any real property development, redevelopment, construction, reconstruction, acquisition, conversion, rental, operation, management, leasing, or brokerage trade or business."
findings.why: "Real estate businesses" is narrower in everyday use than the IRS's "real property trade or business." A contractor or developer could reasonably read it to exclude their work, and if they answer NO, a nonpassive amount is computed as passive.

findings.situation: A filer has a current-year partnership loss that exceeds the amount they are at risk for, so Form 6198 is required for the current year.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: 'if you have (a) a loss or other deduction ... and (b) amounts in the activity for which you aren’t at risk, you’ll have to complete Form 6198 ... to figure your allowable loss for the activity.'
findings.why: The question asks only whether a loss was held back on an earlier return, so a current-year at-risk limitation can truthfully be answered NO even though the tool does not compute Form 6198.

findings.situation: A filer has a prior-year at-risk disallowed deduction, such as a section 179 expense deduction, rather than a disallowed loss.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: 'These losses and deductions include ... the section 179 expense deduction'; p. 13: 'If you have losses, deductions, or credits from a prior year that weren’t deductible or usable because of ... the at-risk limitations, take them into account...'
findings.why: The question asks only about 'a loss,' so a filer with only a prior-year at-risk deduction can truthfully answer NO, while the cited IRS text requires the carryforward to be taken into account.

findings.situation: A filer had a loss from this partnership held back by the at-risk rules on an earlier return, but that loss was fully allowed in a later year before 2025 and no carryforward remains.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 10: 'Losses Not Allowed in Prior Years Due to the Basis or At-Risk Rules • Enter your total prior-year unallowed losses that are now deductible...'
findings.why: The question asks historically whether a loss was ever held back on an earlier return, so it draws YES even though only a prior-year unallowed loss that is still relevant to the current computation matters.

findings.situation: On a joint return, only the spouse had a prior-year at-risk loss from this partnership; the question says 'your' loss and does not mention the spouse.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 13: 'If you have losses, deductions, or credits from a prior year that weren’t deductible or usable because of ... the at-risk limitations, take them into account...'
findings.why: A filer could reasonably read 'your' as covering only the filer or as covering the joint return including the spouse, so it is unclear whether the spouse's prior-year at-risk loss must be reported.

findings.situation: The filer worked 100 or fewer hours in this K-1 activity but, together with other businesses where the filer worked more than 100 hours, has over 500 hours.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'A significant participation activity is any trade or business activity in which you participated for more than 100 hours during the year...'
findings.why: Test 4 requires this K-1 activity itself to be a significant participation activity (more than 100 hours). The question counts this K-1 activity even when it is 100 hours or less, so a truthful YES can occur when test 4 does not apply and the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: The filer has over 500 hours counting other businesses with more than 100 hours, but in one or more of those other businesses the filer materially participated under another material participation test.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'A significant participation activity is any trade or business activity in which you participated for more than 100 hours during the year and in which you didn’t materially participate under any of the material participation tests (other than this test).'
findings.why: The question counts every business where the filer worked over 100 hours, while test 4 counts only significant participation activities. Businesses where the filer materially participated under another test should be excluded.

findings.situation: The filer's spouse worked in another business and their combined hours exceed 100, but the filer alone did not work over 100 hours there.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: 'Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership ... is counted toward material participation.'
findings.why: It is unclear whether 'where you worked over 100 hours' applies the 100-hour threshold to the filer alone or to the combined work of the filer and spouse.

findings.situation: A filer materially participated for three prior years in a non-listed trade or business in which capital is not a material income-producing factor, so the parenthetical list lets the filer answer NO even though the IRS personal-service test applies.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "A personal service activity involves ... or any other trade or business in which capital isn’t a material income-producing factor."
findings.why: The screen lists only health, law, engineering, architecture, accounting, actuarial science, performing arts, and consulting; it omits the catch-all, so the tool would ignore a test 6 situation that the filer can truthfully screen out.

findings.situation: A filer’s spouse materially participated in the service business in three earlier years before the filer owned the partnership interest, but the question still calls for YES because it adds the spouse’s participation without the ownership-at-the-time limitation.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership (where you own your partnership interest at the time the work is done) is counted toward material participation."
findings.why: The question tells the filer to count the spouse’s work/participation whether or not filing jointly but does not limit it to work done while the filer owned the partnership interest; the IRS text does not count pre-ownership spouse work, so a NO answer would compute the lines correctly.

findings.why: The IRS test 7 has no more-than-100-hours requirement; the question adds that threshold, letting a filer who meets test 7 with 100 hours or less answer NO and avoid the required refusal.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer's spouse paid partnership expenses required by the partnership agreement and not reimbursed.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 10: "You can deduct unreimbursed ordinary and necessary partnership expenses you paid on behalf of the partnership on Schedule E if you were required to pay these expenses under the partnership agreement."
findings.why: The question asks only whether 'you paid,' so a filer whose spouse paid can truthfully answer NO, leaving the spouse's deductible UPE out even though a joint return must include it.

findings.situation: The filer paid partnership expenses required by the partnership agreement that are not ordinary and necessary trade or business expenses under section 162.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 10: "You can only deduct unreimbursed expenses on Schedule E that are trade or business expenses under section 162."

findings.situation: Losses were suspended for basis in a year before Form 7203 existed, or in a year the filer tracked basis without filing Form 7203. A filer who follows the help text finds no earlier Form 7203 Part III column (e) and answers NO, although a carryforward still exists.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1: "Form 7203 and its separate instructions are developed to replace the 3-part Worksheet for Figuring a Shareholder's Stock and Debt Basis"; "Any losses and deductions not allowed this year because of the basis limit can be carried forward indefinitely"; i7203 p. 4 Column (b): "Enter any loss or deduction items disallowed due to basis limitations in prior years that were carried forward."
findings.why: The label "(Form 7203)" and the help "Your earlier Form 7203 shows it" tie the question to a form that may never have recorded the carryforward. Column (b) still needs the old worksheet amounts or unfiled amounts.

findings.situation: A basis-suspended loss carries forward even though it was not limited on any return the filer filed. Examples are a year with no return filed, or a loss carried in from another holder of the stock under section 1366(d) exceptions. The filer truthfully answers NO to "held back on an earlier return".
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1: "limited to the basis of your stock and loans from you to the corporation. For details and exceptions, see section 1366(d)."; i7203 p. 4: "Loss and deductions in excess of basis are suspended and carried forward indefinitely"
findings.why: The IRS test is whether an amount was disallowed in a prior year and carried forward, not whether it was held back on a return the filer filed. The wording "on an earlier return" excludes some carryforwards that column (b) requires.

findings.situation: A loss was suspended for basis in an earlier year but was fully allowed in a later year, so nothing carries into this year. The filer still truthfully answers YES.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was a loss or deduction from this corporation held back on an earlier return because your basis in it was too low?"; i7203 p. 4 Column (b): "Enter any loss or deduction items disallowed due to basis limitations in prior years that were carried forward."
findings.why: Column (b) needs only amounts still carried forward into this year. A loss held back once and since used leaves column (b) at zero, which the tool computes correctly, yet the question forces a refusal.

findings.situation: On a joint return where this K-1 belongs to the spouse, the filer may read "your basis" as the filer's own basis and answer NO, even though the spouse has a basis carryforward from this corporation.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 2: "If you are married filing jointly and you received a Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) for you and your spouse, complete a separate Form 7203 for each spouse."
findings.why: Basis and carryforwards are tracked per shareholder spouse. The question says "your" without saying whether it means the spouse who owns this K-1.

findings.situation: A filer whose earlier year suspended only foreign taxes, or other Part III items that are not obviously a "loss", may not see them as a "loss or deduction held back".
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 15 Code F: "Report this amount in column (a) of Form 7203, Part III, line 46"; i7203 p. 4: "Loss and deductions in excess of basis are suspended and carried forward indefinitely and the character of the loss and deduction items is retained."
findings.why: Part III carries forward every basis-reducing loss and deduction item, including foreign taxes. A filer could reasonably read "loss or deduction" more narrowly.

findings.irs_text: i1120ssk (2025) p. 6: "For those informational items that can't be reported as a single dollar amount, the corporation will enter an asterisk in the left column and enter 'STMT' in the dollar amount entry space"; p. 8, Code I: "The corporation will attach a statement that provides ... your share of the amount realized ... You must figure your gain or loss from the disposition"
