findings.situation: A shareholder has personally loaned money to the S corporation and the loan basis has been reduced by prior losses or nondeductible expenses, but the corporation made no repayment this year, so box 16 shows neither code E nor code F; the filer answers NO, yet Form 7203 Part II still must be completed.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 3: “You must complete this section if you have personally loaned money to the corporation.”; i1120ssk p. 3: “Basis of loans. The basis of your loans to the corporation is generally the balance the corporation owes you, adjusted for any reductions and restorations of loan basis.”
findings.why: The question only asks whether box 16 shows code E (a repayment) or code F; it does not ask about an outstanding loan or reduced debt basis. A truthful NO lets the tool treat code E/F as zero and assert Form 7203 support, even though Part II debt basis is still required and the refusal says the tool does not prepare Part II.

findings.why: The IRS text requires a statement but does not require box 8c itself to say STMT or carry a pointer. Box 8c also has no code column for the asterisk convention on p. 6. So a filer whose box shows an amount can truthfully answer NO, and the tool then reports all of it as business-asset gain on line 5.

findings.situation: All of the shareholder's box 8c gain is of a single non-business type, such as REIT or partnership-interest gain, and the corporation reports it on a statement.
findings.irs_text: If the corporation reports only unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of its business assets, it will enter a dollar amount in box 8c. If it reports the other two types of unrecaptured gain, it will provide an attached statement (i1120ssk p. 7)
findings.why: The help text says a statement is attached 'when the gain is of more than one type.' A filer with only one type that is not business-asset gain could conclude the statement does not apply to them and answer NO. Under the IRS text, any non-business type triggers the statement and a line other than line 5.

findings.situation: The Schedule K-1’s box 9 total is zero or blank, but an attached statement reports section 1231 gain or loss from one or more activities, so the filer truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk (2025) p. 8: “If the corporation had net section 1231 gain (loss) from more than one activity, it will attach a statement that will identify the section 1231 gain (loss) from each activity.”
findings.why: The question asks only whether box 9 itself shows an amount; it does not ask about the attached activity statement. The tool therefore ignores the statement and treats box 9 as zero, even though the IRS text requires each activity’s section 1231 amount to be reported.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse’s separate Schedule K-1 for the same S corporation shows box 9 while the filer’s own K-1 does not, so the filer answers NO for “this Schedule K-1.”
findings.irs_text: i7203 (Rev. 12-2022) p. 2: “If you are married filing jointly and you received a Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) for you and your spouse, complete a separate Form 7203 for each spouse.”
findings.why: The wording is limited to “this Schedule K-1” and does not cover the spouse’s K-1. The tool then computes one Form 7203 for the corporation and ignores the spouse’s box 9 section 1231 amount, which the IRS text requires to be handled separately.

findings.why: The question asks only what “you” did, so a filer whose spouse alone disposed of stock can truthfully answer NO; the tool then computes one Form 7203 and misses the spouse’s required Form 7203/Form 8949.

findings.situation: The shareholder disposed of stock during the S corporation’s fiscal tax year ending in 2025, but the sale occurred in 2024 rather than calendar 2025.

findings.why: The question fixes the period as “In 2025,” so a filer can truthfully answer NO for a 2024 disposition that is nevertheless “during the year” of a fiscal-year S corporation; the tool would compute only one Form 7203.

findings.situation: A shareholder borrows money and lends it to the S corporation (a shareholder loan, not a capital contribution) and pays interest on that borrowing in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 9: "If you used loan proceeds to buy an interest in, or make a contribution to the capital of, an S corporation (debt-financed acquisition)"
findings.why: The IRS text covers only buying an interest or contributing capital. A filer could reasonably read "put money into it as an owner" as including money lent to the corporation and tick YES, so the tool would refuse a case these lines do not cover.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse who owns the S corporation shares took out the acquisition loan, and the filer answering the screen did not personally borrow or pay the interest.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 9: "If you used loan proceeds to buy an interest in, or make a contribution to the capital of, an S corporation ... report your share of deductible S corporation interest expense"
findings.why: The question asks only whether "you" paid the interest, with no mention of a spouse. A filer could read it as asking about themselves only and answer NO, so the tool would treat the spouse's debt-financed acquisition interest as zero.

findings.situation: A shareholder of a multi-activity S corporation materially participates by test 2, 4, or 7 in one activity but not in the corporation as a whole, so the entity-level question can be truthfully answered no.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation".
findings.why: Material participation is tested activity by activity, but the question asks 'For this S corporation' and about 'its work,' so an activity-level test can be missed.

findings.situation: A spouse did almost all the work, or enough hours, before the filer owned the stock, or did only investor-type work, so the filer answers yes even though that work is not counted.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: work by "you or your spouse" is counted "where you own your stock at the time the work is done"; work done in an investor capacity is not counted.
findings.why: The question does not include the ownership-timing and investor-work limits, so it can trigger a refusal when the tool would correctly find no material participation.

findings.situation: A filer has over 500 hours in significant participation activities including an activity outside the S corporation; 'all such businesses' could mean only S corporations or all significant participation activities.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "you participated in all significant participation activities (including activities outside the corporation) during the year for more than 500 hours".
findings.why: The question's 'all such businesses' does not reproduce the IRS phrase or say whether outside-corporation activities count, so it can be read either way.

findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "covered by nonrecourse indebtedness (except for certain qualified nonrecourse financing, as defined in section 465(b)(6))"
findings.why: The help treats any loan the filer is not personally liable for as a YES, but the IRS at-risk text expressly excepts qualified nonrecourse financing. No Form 6198 is needed for that financing, so the tool computes it correctly.

findings.situation: A filer borrows from their own relative, who is not a shareholder or other interested person, to buy stock or make a loan to the S corporation.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "from a person related to a person (except you) having such an interest"
findings.why: The question counts a relative of anyone with a stake, including the filer, but the IRS related-person rule excludes the taxpayer. The loan is at risk unless the relative is related to another interested person, so the tool computes it correctly without Form 6198.

findings.situation: A filer who meets the 750-hour and more-than-half tests but did not materially participate in this S corporation's rental real estate activity must answer YES, yet the box 2 amount stays passive and the tool computes it correctly.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 6, Box 2: "the income (loss) in box 2 isn't from a passive activity if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier) and you materially participated in the activity"; p. 7, item 3: "If you were a real estate professional and you materially participated in the activity, report box 2 income (loss) in column (i) or (k)"
findings.why: Box 2 becomes nonpassive only if the filer is a real estate professional and also materially participated in the activity. The question asks only about professional status, so filers whose box 2 is still passive are refused.

findings.situation: A filer who worked over 750 hours, most of their working time, as a W-2 employee of a real estate company in which they owned 5% or less must answer YES, although they are not a real estate professional.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "Services you performed as an employee aren't treated as performed in a real property trade or business unless you owned more than 5% of the stock (or more than 5% of the capital or profits interest) in the employer."
findings.why: The question counts all work in real estate businesses. The IRS test excludes most employee hours, so this filer is not a professional and box 2 stays passive, which the tool computes.

findings.situation: A filer whose real estate hours came from real property businesses in which they did not materially participate must answer YES, although those hours do not count toward either test.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "a. More than half of the personal services you performed in trades or businesses were performed in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated. b. You performed more than 750 hours of services in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated."
findings.why: The question's wording has no material-participation qualifier on the hours, so it counts hours the IRS definition excludes.

findings.situation: A filer who works full time in construction, development, or brokerage may read "real estate businesses" as meaning only renting property and answer NO, although they are a real estate professional.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "A real property trade or business is any real property development, redevelopment, construction, reconstruction, acquisition, conversion, rental, operation, management, leasing, or brokerage trade or business."
findings.why: The label "real estate businesses" does not state the IRS's broad list. A builder or developer could truthfully answer NO even though box 2 may be nonpassive, which the tool does not compute.

findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: Generally, if you have (a) a loss or other deduction from any activity carried on as a trade or business or for the production of income by the corporation, and (b) amounts in the activity for which you aren’t at risk, you will have to complete Form 6198, At-Risk Limitations, to figure your allowable loss for the activity.
findings.why: The question asks only about a loss held back on an earlier return, so the filer can truthfully answer NO even though a current-year at-risk limitation requires Form 6198, which the tool does not prepare.

findings.situation: A prior-year at-risk limitation held back a deduction from this S corporation, such as the section 179 expense deduction, rather than a loss.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: These losses and deductions include a loss on the disposition of assets and the section 179 expense deduction.
findings.why: The question asks only whether a loss was held back; a filer whose at-risk carryover is a disallowed deduction can answer NO even though Form 6198 is required.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer’s spouse had a loss from this S corporation held back by the at-risk rules on an earlier return, while the filer did not.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 2: If you are married filing jointly and you received a Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) for you and your spouse, complete a separate Form 7203 for each spouse.
findings.why: The question is phrased as the filer’s own loss and does not say you or your spouse, so the filer could answer NO for themselves even though the spouse’s at-risk carryover requires Form 6198 on the joint return.

findings.situation: A filer had a loss from this S corporation held back by the at-risk rules on an earlier return, but that suspended loss was fully allowed in a later year and no at-risk carryover remains for the current year.

findings.why: The question asks about any earlier return, not whether a suspended at-risk loss is still carried into the current year; a filer answers YES even though no current Form 6198 is needed.

findings.situation: A settlement for emotional distress caused by a nonphysical personal injury, such as unlawful discrimination, includes damages for medical care.
findings.irs_text: Pub. 525 p. 32: 'If the emotional distress is due to a personal injury that isn’t due to a physical injury or sickness ... you must include the damages in your income, except for any damages you receive for medical care due to that emotional distress.'
findings.why: The question asks only whether the case was about a physical injury or physical sickness, so a filer could answer NO; the tool would then treat the medical-care portion as taxable even though Pub. 525 excludes it.

findings.situation: Damages for a nonphysical personal injury are paid under a written binding agreement in effect on or before September 13, 1995.
findings.irs_text: Pub. 525 p. 32: 'If you receive damages under a written binding agreement ... in effect (or issued on or before) September 13, 1995, don’t include in income any of those damages received on account of personal injuries or sickness.'
findings.why: The screen is limited to physical injury or sickness, so a filer with a nonphysical personal injury under the pre-existing agreement could answer NO, and the tool would tax damages that Pub. 525 says to exclude.

findings.situation: The entire settlement is punitive damages paid in a case about a physical injury.
findings.irs_text: Pub. 525 p. 32: 'Punitive damages in most cases. It doesn’t matter if they relate to a physical injury or physical sickness.'
findings.why: The question makes the filer answer YES because the case is about a physical injury, but if the item is only punitive damages, the tool could correctly include the full amount as ordinary income and no compensatory/punitive split is needed.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the physical-injury settlement was paid to the filer’s spouse, not the filer.
findings.irs_text: Pub. 525 p. 32: 'Don’t include in your income compensatory damages for personal physical injury or physical sickness.'
findings.why: The question says 'Was any of it paid' without saying 'you or your spouse'; a filer could read it as limited to the filer’s own damages, even though the joint return’s line 8z treatment must cover the spouse’s damages.

findings.situation: A caregiver paid on Form 1099-NEC for home care to several unrelated clients, often through an agency or a state program, who would not describe this as 'running a business of my own' but whose regular, profit-seeking work is a separate trade or business of providing home care.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1d: "If you are a sole proprietor in a business of providing home care services, see the Schedule C instructions ... If you do not have a separate trade or business of providing these services, enter on Form 1040, line 1d, your Medicaid waiver payments reported on Form 1099-MISC or Form 1099-NEC."
findings.why: The IRS test is whether the person has a separate trade or business, which can exist without the person setting up or thinking of a business of their own. A contract caregiver could truthfully answer NO to 'Do you run a business of your own', and the tool would then put Schedule C income on line 1d. Another contract caregiver could answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer caring for a family member or one client who gets a 1099-NEC may answer YES because the parenthetical says the pay 'belongs on a business schedule, Schedule C', and 1099-NEC pay is commonly reported on Schedule C.

findings.why: The question reads 'Its pay belongs on a business schedule, Schedule C.' A filer could read that note as describing their 1099-NEC pay rather than as a consequence of a YES answer. That filer would answer YES and be refused, even though the tool computes line 1d correctly for someone with no separate home-care business.

findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 9: "You won't incur a tax on a contribution to your ABLE account that is in excess of the contribution limit if the qualified ABLE program returns the contribution, including all net income attributable to the contribution, to the person who made the contribution ... on or before the due date (including extensions)"
findings.why: The question has no exception for excesses corrected by timely withdrawal. A filer who owes nothing is refused even though the tool's zero is right.

findings.situation: A filer missed an RMD whose deadline fell in an earlier year, and that tax belongs to that year's return, but the filer still truthfully answers YES to 'a required minimum distribution ... that you did not receive in full by its deadline'.
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 9: "The tax is due for the tax year that includes the last day by which the minimum required distribution must be taken."
findings.why: The question does not limit the shortfall to an RMD whose deadline fell in 2025. Shortfalls belonging to other tax years trigger a refusal although 2025 Part IX would be zero.

findings.situation: A filer had an HSA excess remaining at the end of 2024 that was fully absorbed in 2025 by under-contributing or by taxable distributions, and could read 'had not removed or used up before 2025' either way.

findings.situation: A filer's Form 1099-DIV box 5 includes REIT dividends on shares held 45 days or fewer, or dividends whose payment is obligated to someone else.

findings.situation: In 2025 the filer is repaid a 2024 nonitemized deduction, such as a previously deducted bad debt, that reduced the 2024 tax; the filer can truthfully answer NO because it was not paid or deducted before 2024, and the tool reports zero.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: 'You may also have recoveries of nonitemized deductions (such as payments on previously deducted bad debts)'; p525 p. 25: 'the total of all other recoveries as other income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8z'.
findings.why: The IRS taxes qualifying nonitemized-deduction recoveries and reports them on line 8z, but the tool computes line 8z only for a 2024 repayment when the filer itemized 2024; the screen does not catch a 2024 nonitemized recovery.

findings.situation: A 2024 itemized deduction recovery where the underlying expense was paid before 2024 but the deduction was claimed on the 2024 return; the tool computes the 2024 recovery, yet the question's 'paid . . . before 2024' wording makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27, Worksheet 2: 'Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted.'
findings.why: The recovery year is determined by the year the expense was deducted, not merely by when it was paid, so the 'paid' branch of the question over-includes a 2024 deduction and causes an unnecessary refusal.

findings.situation: The phrase 'for something paid or deducted before 2024' leaves unclear whether the controlling date is the original payment date or the year the deduction/credit was claimed, so a filer with a pre-2024 payment and a 2024 deduction may not know how to answer.

findings.situation: A filer who itemized in 2023 (or another year other than 2024) gets a refund in 2025 of property tax, mortgage interest or medical costs deducted that year, and truthfully answers NO because the refund is for an itemized deduction that lowered tax.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27, Worksheet 2: "If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year, such as a state income tax refund from 2024 and a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year"; p525 p. 25: "the total of all other recoveries as other income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8z"

findings.situation: A filer who itemized for 2024 recovers an amount deducted above the line that year, such as a bad debt or a business expense, and reads "taken without itemizing" as meaning "in a year you did not itemize," so answers NO.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 28, Nonitemized Deduction Recoveries: "If you recover an amount that you deducted in an earlier year when you were figuring your AGI, you must generally include the full amount of the recovery in your income"
findings.why: "A deduction taken without itemizing" can mean either a deduction that does not require itemizing or a deduction taken in a year the filer did not itemize. Under the second reading, an itemizer answers NO, and the tool's Worksheet 2 line C then leaves out the AGI-deduction recovery.

findings.situation: A filer who received a rebate or downward price adjustment on an item for which a credit was claimed in 2024 must answer YES, although that recovery does not belong on line 8z, so the tool's line 8z computation would be correct.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 28, Amounts Recovered for Credits: "you must increase your 2024 tax by the amount of the recovery, up to the amount by which the credit reduced your tax in the earlier year"
findings.why: The question's wording "or for something you took a credit for" forces a YES and a refusal of line 8z. The IRS text treats a credit recovery as an increase in tax, not as other income on Schedule 1, line 8z.

findings.situation: A sole proprietor whose only income is business income gets a refund of the state's ordinary individual income tax, which has no Form 1099-G box 8 check, and may answer YES because the tax was charged only on their business income.
findings.irs_text: f1099g p. 5, Box 8: "the amount in box 2 is attributable to an income tax that applies exclusively to income from a trade or business and is not a tax of general application"
findings.why: "A tax charged only on income from a business" can be read as describing this filer's own tax base, not a tax that by law applies only to business income. A general-application income tax refund is one the tool computes, so a YES here would wrongly end the interview.

findings.situation: A farmer who got no Form 1099-G, or one without box 8 checked, receives a refund of a state or local income tax imposed only on farming or trade income and may answer NO because they do not think of the farm as a "business."
findings.irs_text: f1099g p. 5, Box 8: "applies exclusively to income from a trade or business ... If taxable, report the amount in box 2 on Schedule C or F (Form 1040), as appropriate"
findings.why: The question asks only about "income from a business." The Schedule F case appears only in the help text, so a filer reading just the question could leave out a farm-only tax. The tool would then send that refund through the Schedule 1, line 1 computation.

findings.situation: The filer bought a leasehold on separate property used for this rental, such as an adjacent parking lot, storage space or access strip leased for the tenants, rather than on the rental property itself or the land under it.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 5, Rental of property: "If you buy a leasehold for rental purposes, you can deduct an equal part of the cost each year over the term of the lease."
findings.why: The IRS rule covers any leasehold bought for rental purposes, but the question only asks about a lease "on it, or on the land under it." A filer whose bought lease is on other property serving the rental truthfully answers NO, and the tool leaves the amortized cost out of line 19.

findings.situation: A filer who pays ordinary periodic ground rent under a land lease beneath the rental building may read the question as asking whether they paid for a lease on the land.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 5: "You can deduct the rent you pay for property that you use for rental purposes. If you buy a leasehold for rental purposes, you can deduct an equal part of the cost each year..."
findings.why: The question's "pay ... to buy a lease on ... the land under it" and the help's "bought a ground lease" do not clearly separate a lump-sum leasehold purchase from ongoing ground rent. Ground rent is deductible currently on line 19, which the tool computes, so a YES there would wrongly refuse.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer's spouse alone bought the leasehold on the rental property.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 5: "If you buy a leasehold for rental purposes, you can deduct an equal part of the cost each year over the term of the lease."
findings.why: The question asks only whether "you" paid and never mentions a spouse. A filer could read it as asking about themselves alone and answer NO, which would drop the spouse's amortizable leasehold cost.

findings.situation: The filer inherited or was gifted the property, or got it in an exchange. Its unadjusted basis (for example, FMV at death or a carryover basis) is more than zero, but the filer paid nothing. So the filer reads 'its cost' as zero, finds rent cannot be under 2% of zero, and answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 3: "less than 2% of the smaller of the unadjusted basis or the FMV of the property. Unadjusted basis is the cost of the property without regard to depreciation deductions or any other basis adjustment described in section 1016."
findings.why: The test uses unadjusted basis, which equals purchase cost only for purchased property. The question and help say only 'cost (before depreciation)', so a filer who did not buy the property can truthfully answer NO even though the exception applies.

findings.situation: The filer or spouse owns an interest in an activity carried on in anticipation of starting a trade or business, or in a section 174/174A research activity, and the property was mainly used in it. The filer does not think of this as 'a business'.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 3: "A trade or business activity is an activity ... that: 1. Involves the conduct of a trade or business ..., 2. Is conducted in anticipation of starting a trade or business, or 3. Involves the conduct of research or experimental activities"
findings.why: The question asks only about 'a business you or your spouse owned a part of'. A filer whose activity is still pre-startup or is research could reasonably answer NO.

findings.situation: The filer has made capital improvements to the property and does not know whether to add them to 'its cost'.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 3: "Unadjusted basis is the cost of the property without regard to depreciation deductions or any other basis adjustment described in section 1016."
findings.why: The help excludes only depreciation. A filer could reasonably add improvements, which are section 1016 adjustments, to 'cost' or leave them out. Adding them raises the 2% threshold and can produce a YES where the IRS test gives NO.

findings.situation: The question repeats a year phrase, and a filer cannot tell which condition each year phrase attaches to.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 3: "a. You own an interest in the trade or business activity during the tax year, b. The rental property was mainly used in the trade or business activity during the tax year or during at least 2 of the 5 preceding tax years"
findings.why: The question reads 'a business you or your spouse owned a part of in 2025, in 2025 or in 2 of the 5 years before'. One reading lets ownership in a prior year count. Another reading requires use in 2025 only. The IRS text needs ownership in 2025 and use in 2025 or in 2 of the 5 prior years.

findings.situation: A filer holds land mainly for its rising value but leases it out for gross rent of at least 2% of the smaller of its unadjusted basis or FMV, so it is still an ordinary rental activity the tool computes correctly, yet the filer answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 3, Exceptions item 3: "The rental of property is incidental to an activity of holding property for investment if the main purpose of holding the property is to realize a gain from its appreciation and the gross rental income is less than 2% of the smaller of the unadjusted basis or the fair market value (FMV) of the property."
findings.why: The question asks only "Do you hold it mainly to sell at a gain rather than to rent (as an investment ...)" and omits the 2% gross-rent test. An appreciation-motivated holder whose rent meets or exceeds 2% still has a rental activity, but must answer YES. The help text's "small farm or hunting lease" hints at small rent without stating the test.

findings.situation: A filer rents self-storage units or offices, each leased for one tenant's exclusive use, with access limited to set business hours, and answers YES, although this is an ordinary rental the tool computes correctly.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 4, Exceptions item 4: "You customarily make the rental property available during defined business hours for nonexclusive use by various customers."
findings.why: The question says "make it available during set business hours for use by many customers" and drops the word "nonexclusive". Exclusive-use rentals with business-hour access therefore fall within the wording but not the exception.

findings.situation: Spouses on a joint return co-own a rental, and only one of them holds it mainly for appreciation or is a real estate dealer.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6: "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from rentals of real estate you held for sale to customers in the ordinary course of your business as a real estate dealer."
findings.why: The question asks "Do you hold it" and never says whether "you" includes the spouse. A filer could reasonably answer NO when only the spouse is the dealer or investor.

findings.situation: The filer paid mortgage interest on the rental to a bank but received no Form 1098 for that loan, for example because the interest was under $600 or the lender never sent one.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7: "If you paid $600 or more in interest on a mortgage during 2025, the recipient should send you a Form 1098 ... Note: If the recipient was not a financial institution or you did not receive a Form 1098 from the recipient, report your deductible mortgage interest on line 13."
findings.why: With no Form 1098, a filer may read "more than your Forms 1098 show in total" as more than zero and answer YES, or as not applying to them and answer NO. On a NO, the tool puts interest that needs the no-1098 treatment on line 12 as ordinary 1098-backed interest.

findings.situation: On a joint return, one spouse's payments or Form 1098 on the rental loan are in that spouse's name only, so it is unclear whether "you" and "your Forms 1098" mean the filer alone or both spouses together.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7: "If you paid more mortgage interest than is shown on your Form 1098 or similar statement ... Attach a statement to your return explaining the difference." and "(other than your spouse if you file a joint return)"
findings.why: If the filer compares only their own payments to only their own 1098 (or the reverse), the comparison can come out NO even though the couple's combined interest is more than their combined Forms 1098. The help text does not say to include the spouse's payments and statements.

findings.situation: A filer funded the rental's purchase or repairs with an unsecured personal loan from a co-owner or the co-owner's relative, so the borrowed money is not a 'debt on it' and is not 'money you put in.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'Amounts borrowed for use in the activity from a person who has an interest in the activity (other than as a creditor) or who is related under section 465(b)(3)(C) to a person (other than you) having such an interest.'
findings.why: The question only reaches money the filer put in or 'any debt on it,' which reads as debt secured by the property. A filer could truthfully answer NO about an unsecured loan from an interested person, even though the IRS text treats those borrowed amounts as not at risk.

findings.situation: A filer's nonrecourse mortgage comes from a bank or regular lender that is related to the filer on non-commercial terms, or that receives a fee because of the filer's investment (or is related to someone who does).
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'A qualified person cannot be: • Related to you (unless the nonrecourse financing obtained is commercially reasonable ...), • The seller of the property (or a person related to the seller), or • A person who receives a fee due to your investment in real property (or a person related to that person).'
findings.why: The question exempts any 'mortgage on it from a bank, government or other regular lender,' and the help names only seller and co-owner ties. A filer with such a lender would answer NO, but the loan is not qualified nonrecourse financing and is not at risk.

findings.situation: A filer contributed property other than money (for example, equipment or land) to the rental, and that contribution is protected by a guarantee or stop-loss arrangement.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'Cash, property, or borrowed amounts used in the activity ... that are protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement.'
findings.why: The question asks only about 'money you put in' or 'debt on it,' so a protected contribution of non-cash property can truthfully be answered NO.

findings.situation: A filer's rental real property was placed in service before 1987 and carries nonrecourse seller financing or a loan from a co-owner.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'the at-risk rules do not apply to losses from an activity of holding real property placed in service before 1987.'
findings.why: The question ('owed by no one personally ... or lent by someone with a stake in it') makes this filer answer YES and be refused. The at-risk rules do not apply to this property, so the tool's line 22 computation would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer's nonrecourse loan on the rental is also secured by the filer's own property outside the activity, such as a home, or is a government-guaranteed loan from a lender that is not a regular lender.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: not at risk covers 'Nonrecourse loans ... that are not secured by your own property (other than property used in the activity)'; qualified nonrecourse financing includes debt 'Loaned or guaranteed by any federal, state, or local government.'
findings.why: The question 'owed by no one personally (other than a mortgage on it from a bank, government or other regular lender)' makes these filers answer YES. Under the IRS text these amounts can be at risk or qualified nonrecourse financing.

findings.situation: A filer whose only lender is an ordinary bank holding a recourse mortgage could read the mortgage holder as 'someone with a stake in it.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'from a person who has an interest in the activity (other than as a creditor)'
findings.why: The question's 'stake' does not exclude an interest held only as a creditor. A filer could reasonably answer YES for an ordinary lender, while the IRS text expressly excludes creditor-only interests.

findings.situation: A filer who carries property or liability insurance on the rental may count that insurance as a 'similar arrangement' protecting against loss.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement (excluding casualty insurance and insurance against tort liability)'
findings.why: The question omits the IRS exclusion for casualty and tort liability insurance, so a filer could reasonably answer YES just for being normally insured.

findings.situation: A filer used a dwelling unit as a home and rented it for fewer than 15 days, so it must not be reported on Schedule E, but the filer can truthfully say it was rented to make a profit and answer NO.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 28: "If you use a dwelling unit as a home and you rent it less than 15 days during the year, its primary function isn't considered to be rental and it shouldn't be reported on Schedule E (Form 1040)."
findings.why: The question only asks about profit motive. This minimal-rental case is a separate exclusion that the wording does not reach, so the tool would compute line 21 for a rental that belongs off Schedule E.

findings.situation: A filer has royalty income for the property, which the IRS line 21 includes, but the question asks only about profit motive, so the filer answers NO.
findings.irs_text: f1040se (2025) p. 1, line 21: "Subtract line 20 from line 3 (rents) and/or 4 (royalties)."
findings.why: The tool subtracts line 20 from rents only, so royalties are silently left out of line 21, and nothing in the not-for-profit wording leads a royalty holder to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer runs a for-profit rental but let a relative or friend stay some days at below-market rent; following the example, the filer answers YES even though the property stays on Schedule E.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Line 2: a day of personal use includes any day the unit is used by "Anyone who pays less than a fair rental price for the unit"; the rental is still reported on Schedule E with expenses allocated.
findings.why: The question's example, "for example to a friend at a low rent", equates any low-rent arrangement with not-for-profit. The IRS treats below-fair-rent days as personal-use days on Schedule E, not as a not-for-profit activity.

findings.situation: A filer whose rental lost money this year may read the label as asking whether the rental made a profit and tick YES.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 17: "don't use that schedule to report a not-for-profit activity"; f1040se line 21: "If result is a (loss), see instructions..."
findings.why: The label "It was not rented to make a profit" can be read as describing the outcome (no profit) rather than the intent (no profit motive). Line 21 handles loss rentals, so a YES from a loss-making but profit-motivated filer would be wrong.

Anyone in your family ... ; Anyone who pays less than a fair rental price for the unit" and "Regardless of whether you used the unit as a home, expenses related to days of personal use do not qualify as rental expenses. You must allocate your expenses..."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer lives in or uses the property, so family use or a below-market tenancy draws a truthful NO. The tool then subtracts all of line 20 from rents and never removes the personal-use share of expenses.

findings.situation: On a joint return, only the spouse used the rental property personally, for example for vacation days.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Line 2: "A day of personal use is any day ... that the unit was used by: You for personal purposes; ... Anyone in your family"
findings.why: "You" and "yourself" can be read as only the filer answering the screen, so a filer whose spouse alone used the property could answer NO. The personal-use allocation then goes uncomputed.

findings.situation: The rental is a whole dwelling unit, such as a vacation house or condo, that the filer also used personally for some days in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Line 2: "If you rented out a dwelling unit that you also used for personal purposes during the year, you may not be able to deduct all the expenses for the rental part."
findings.why: The label reads "Part of a building you lived in or used yourself," which suggests only partial-building rentals count. The explanation adds "unit," so the owner of a whole vacation home with personal days could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: The filer stayed at the rental only on days spent working substantially full time on repairs and maintenance, or used it only for business purposes.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Line 2: "Do not count as personal use: Any day you spent working substantially full time repairing and maintaining the unit"; question: "Is it a room, unit or part of a building you ... use yourself"
findings.why: "Use yourself" covers this non-personal use, so the filer answers YES and is refused. The IRS treats those days as rental days, and the tool's full-expense computation would be correct.

findings.situation: The filer lived in the property as a main home earlier in 2025 and then converted it to a rental offered for at least 12 consecutive months, with no personal use after conversion.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Line 2: "Do not count as personal use: ... Any days you used the unit as your main home before or after renting it or offering it for rent, if you rented or tried to rent it for at least 12 consecutive months"; question: "or lived in during 2025"
findings.why: "Lived in during 2025" forces a YES. The IRS does not treat those days as personal use, so the rental-period income and expenses fit the tool's straightforward subtraction.

The excess expenses that can't be used to offset income from other sources are carried forward to the next year and treated as rental expenses for the same property... This limitation will apply to expenses carried forward to another year even if you don't use the property as your home for that subsequent year."; i8582 p. 10: "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 4: "if at any time during the tax year your interest (including your spouse's interest) in the activity was less than 10% (by value) of all interests in the activity"
findings.why: Owning nothing before buying or after selling is literally owning "less than a tenth." The question doesn't say whether to count only the period the filer held an interest, so such filers may answer YES or NO.

findings.situation: A filer whose spouse holds a separate interest could read "you (with your spouse)" as covering only shares the two of them hold jointly, rather than adding the spouse's own share to the filer's.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 4: "your interest (including your spouse's interest) in the activity"
findings.why: The IRS adds both spouses' interests together whatever the filing status. A filer who owns 5% while the spouse separately owns 10% could wrongly answer YES. A married filer filing separately might also not realize the spouse's share counts.

findings.situation: The question measures the filer's share of "this rental property," but the IRS test measures the share of "the activity," which can include more than one property.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 4: "less than 10% (by value) of all interests in the activity"
findings.why: When several properties are grouped as one activity, the filer's share of a single property can differ from their share of the whole activity, so the answer depends on which one the filer measures.

findings.situation: A filer receives a nonqualified distribution from a Roth IRA, or a code T distribution, and has made no conversion, recharacterization or rollover this year, so none of the listed items applies and they answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "2. You received a distribution from a Roth IRA. But if either (a) or (b) below applies, enter -0- on line 4b ... a. Distribution code T is shown in box 7 ... and you made a contribution (including a conversion) to a Roth IRA for 2020 or an earlier year. b. Distribution code Q ..."
findings.why: Any Roth IRA distribution other than code Q, or code T with a pre-2021 contribution, needs Form 8606 to find the taxable part, and the question never mentions it. The tool would treat everything not rolled over as taxable, or treat the distribution as a qualified Roth distribution and tax none of it.

findings.situation: A filer receives a distribution from one traditional IRA in a year when they converted a different traditional IRA to a Roth IRA, and answers NO because this distribution was not itself a conversion.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "If any of the following apply, enter the total distribution on line 4a and see Form 8606 ... 3. You converted part or all of a traditional IRA or traditional SIMPLE IRA to a Roth IRA in 2025."
findings.why: Exception 2 is triggered by a conversion anywhere in the filer's year, and it then governs every IRA distribution. The question asks whether "this distribution" involves a conversion, so a filer can truthfully answer NO for a separate distribution that still needs Form 8606.

findings.situation: A filer takes a non-annuity distribution, before the annuity starting date, from a 401(k) or other qualified plan that holds after-tax contributions (box 5 or 9b), or rolls over such a distribution, and answers NO because only post-start-date nonperiodic payments are listed.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 17: "If you receive a nonperiodic distribution before the annuity starting date from a qualified retirement plan, you can generally allocate only part of it to the cost of the contract ... Cost of contract x Amount received / Account balance = Tax-free amount"; i1040gi p. 30, Rollovers: "From this amount, subtract any contributions (usually shown in box 5) that were taxable to you when made."
findings.why: The tool figures cost recovery only by the Simplified Method for an annuity, so it would tax the whole distribution or the whole part not rolled over. The question names only nonperiodic payments made on or after the annuity starting date.

findings.situation: A filer with nondeductible contributions to a traditional IRA receives a pension or 401(k) distribution, or a code Q Roth IRA distribution, and is unsure whether that distribution 'involves' the nondeductible contributions.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "1. You received a distribution from an IRA (other than a Roth IRA) and you made nondeductible contributions to any of your traditional IRAs"
findings.why: The IRS condition applies only to distributions from non-Roth IRAs. The bullet "nondeductible contributions to any traditional IRA" can be read as a filer-level fact, which would wrongly refuse pension and qualified Roth distributions that the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer has a Schedule E royalty loss with amounts not at risk and no condition making the royalty a business/service/creative/NIL/working-interest royalty; the filer can answer NO, but the tool computes the full line 21 loss without Form 6198.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 21: 'If you have amounts for which you are not at risk, use Form 6198 to determine the amount of your deductible loss.'
findings.why: The question asks only about the royalty's source, not whether any amount is at risk, so a truthful NO leaves the at-risk limitation uncomputed.

findings.situation: A filer receives NIL royalty income that is not self-employment income; the question's broad 'name, image and likeness pay' wording makes the filer answer YES, but the IRS says to report that NIL royalty on Schedule E.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 4: 'However, if your NIL income is royalty income that is not self-employment income, report the NIL royalty income and expenses on Schedule E.'
findings.why: The question and help refer to NIL pay/sponsorship pay without excluding non-self-employment NIL royalties, so it can force a refusal for a royalty the tool would compute correctly on line 21.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer's spouse has royalty income from the spouse's own self-employed writing or creative business, and the filer answers NO because the question says 'your own'; the tool then computes the spouse's Schedule C royalty on Schedule E.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 4: 'If you are in business as a self-employed writer, inventor, artist, etc., report your royalty income and expenses on Schedule C, not on Schedule E.'
findings.why: The wording uses 'your own' and does not mention the spouse, so it does not make the joint filer answer YES for the spouse's Schedule C royalty.

findings.irs_text: i1040se 2025 p. 3: "Cash, property, or borrowed amounts used in the activity (or contributed to the activity, or used to acquire your interest in the activity) that are protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement"
findings.why: The question asks only about 'money you put in', so a filer whose protected contribution was property can truthfully answer NO. The tool then computes a loss that Form 6198 would limit.

findings.situation: The filer borrowed from a corporation, partnership or trust that is related under section 465(b)(3)(C) to someone with an interest in the activity, for example an entity controlled by the royalty payer.
findings.irs_text: i1040se 2025 p. 3: "Amounts borrowed for use in the activity from a person who has an interest in the activity (other than as a creditor) or who is related under section 465(b)(3)(C) to a person (other than you) having such an interest."
findings.why: Section 465(b)(3)(C) relationships include controlled entities and other non-family relationships. An entity is not a 'relative', so the filer can truthfully answer NO.

findings.situation: The filer borrowed without personal liability, but the loan is secured by the filer's own property that is not used in the activity, so the amount is at risk.
findings.irs_text: i1040se 2025 p. 3: "Nonrecourse loans used to finance the activity ... that are not secured by your own property (other than property used in the activity)."
findings.why: The question says 'borrowed without personal liability', and the help says such a loan is not at risk 'whoever lent it'. Neither has the IRS carve-out for loans secured by the filer's other property, so this filer answers YES and the tool refuses a loss it could compute.

findings.situation: The filer borrowed with full personal liability from the filer's own relative, and that relative has no interest in the activity.
findings.irs_text: i1040se 2025 p. 3: "related under section 465(b)(3)(C) to a person (other than you) having such an interest"
findings.why: The filer is a 'someone with a stake', so the question's 'a relative of such a person' and the help's 'or a relative' pull in the filer's own relatives. The IRS text excludes relationship to the filer, so this loan is at risk and the tool computes it correctly.

findings.situation: The filer has property or casualty insurance, or tort liability insurance, on the royalty property.
findings.irs_text: i1040se 2025 p. 3: "other similar arrangement (excluding casualty insurance and insurance against tort liability)"
findings.why: The question's 'protected from loss by ... or similar arrangement' does not mention the insurance exclusion. A filer could reasonably treat insurance as a similar arrangement and answer YES.

findings.situation: The lender's only stake in the activity is as a creditor, such as a bank that holds the loan.
findings.irs_text: i1040se 2025 p. 3: "a person who has an interest in the activity (other than as a creditor)"
findings.why: The question's 'someone with a stake in it' does not exclude a creditor's interest, so a filer could read any lender as having a stake and answer YES.

findings.situation: The filer has car, truck, or travel costs for the royalty that are not ordinary and necessary, so they are not deductible and do not affect line 21.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 6: 'You can deduct ordinary and necessary auto and travel expenses...'
findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer 'has' car, truck, or travel costs, not whether they are deductible ordinary and necessary expenses. A filer with nondeductible costs would answer YES and be stopped even though the tool would compute line 21 correctly by excluding them.

findings.situation: The filer has only meal expenses incurred while traveling away from home for the royalty and is unsure whether 'travel costs' includes meals.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 6: 'including 50% of meal expenses incurred while traveling away from home.'
findings.why: The screen says 'car, truck or travel costs' and does not mention meals, while the IRS line expressly includes 50% of away-from-home meal expenses in the travel deduction. A filer could reasonably read the question either way.

findings.why: This owner uses standard MACRS straight line with the mid-month convention, so would truthfully answer NO to 'another way' and to 'a longer period (ADS)'. The tool would then apply the wrong 39-year rates.

findings.situation: Real property acquired in a like-kind exchange or involuntary conversion must have its carryover basis depreciated over the remaining recovery period of the old property, and any excess basis depreciated separately.
findings.irs_text: you must depreciate the carryover basis of property you acquire in a like-kind exchange or involuntary conversion ... over the remaining recovery period of the property exchanged ... Figure depreciation separately for the carryover basis and the excess basis (i4562 2025, p. 9, Section B)
findings.why: Nothing in the screen mentions acquiring the property in an exchange or conversion, and its basis did not change after depreciation began. The filer answers NO, and the tool applies a single table rate from the new acquisition month.

findings.why: The screen asks whether 'you sold, gave away or stopped renting it', which reads as the whole property, so a partial disposition gets a NO. The tool then applies the table to the unreduced basis.

findings.situation: A pre-2019 alimony agreement was later modified after 2018 to state expressly that alimony is neither deductible nor includible, so the 2025 payments should not be reported as alimony.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 89: 'unless that agreement was changed after December 31, 2018, to expressly provide that alimony received isn’t included in your income'; p504 p. 12: 'The same is true of alimony paid under a divorce or separation instrument executed before 2019 and modified after 2018, if the modification expressly states that the alimony isn’t deductible to the payer or includible in the income of the recipient.'
findings.why: The screen does not ask about a post-2018 modification that expressly removes alimony treatment; a filer with such an agreement can truthfully answer NO, and the tool would then compute the amount as alimony.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse has alimony subject to recapture, multiple agreements/payees, or child support, while the filer’s own alimony has none.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 89: 'Enter amounts received as alimony or separate maintenance pursuant to a divorce or separation agreement entered into on or before December 31, 2018... If you are including alimony payments from more than one divorce or separation agreement in your income, enter the total of all alimony received on line 2a.'
findings.why: The question asks about 'that alimony' without saying it covers the spouse’s alimony; a truthful NO for the filer’s own alimony would let the joint line be computed without the required refusal for the spouse.

findings.situation: The alimony payments are for a home owned by the recipient spouse, such as mortgage or real estate tax payments made to a third party under the agreement, which can still qualify as alimony.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 13: 'Cash payments, checks, or money orders to a third party on behalf of your spouse under the terms of your divorce or separation instrument can be alimony ... These include payments for ... housing costs (rent, utilities, etc.)'; Example 2 says mortgage and real estate taxes on a home owned by your spouse can be alimony.
findings.why: The question says YES to any payments that 'are for a home,' so it stops even though the tool could compute these recipient-owned-home payments as ordinary alimony.

findings.situation: Alimony decreased within the first three years, but the decrease is excluded from recapture because, for example, the recipient remarried or the payments varied as a fixed part of the payer’s income.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 16: 'When you figure a decrease in alimony, don’t include ... Payments required over a period of at least 3 calendar years that vary because they are a fixed part of your income ... Payments that decrease because of the death of either spouse or the remarriage of the spouse receiving the payments before the end of the third year.'
findings.why: The wording 'fell sharply within the first three years' would make a filer answer YES, but no recapture computation is required in those excluded cases, so the tool would compute the line correctly if allowed.

findings.situation: The phrase 'more than one person paid' could mean the filer paid alimony to more than one recipient, or that more than one payer paid alimony to the filer.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 12: 'If you paid alimony to more than one person, enter the SSN or ITIN of one of the recipients. Show the SSN or ITIN and amount paid to each other recipient on an attached statement.'
findings.why: The IRS refusal context is about paying to more than one person, but the question omits 'to,' so a filer can reasonably read it either way.

question: Does any of these apply to that alimony: more than one agreement, or more than one person paid; payments that fell sharply within the first three years; or payments that are partly child support, are for a home, or go on after the recipient dies?

findings.situation: A filer has a canceled personal loan or credit card debt whose Form 1099-C shows forgiven interest in box 3. That interest would not have been deductible if paid, so the whole box 2 amount is taxable and the tool computes it correctly.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 20: "If the interest would not be deductible (such as interest on a personal loan), include in your income the amount from box 2 of Form 1099-C."
findings.why: The question says "it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount ... that would have been deductible." A filer can read this as "any box 3 interest, or other deductible amounts," so any box 3 entry triggers YES. Many credit card 1099-Cs carry a box 3 amount, so these filers are refused even though the tool's box 2 figure is right.

findings.situation: A filer who takes the standard deduction, or whose medical costs would not clear the AGI floor, has a forgiven unpaid medical bill or forgiven mortgage interest.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 6: "If you use the cash method of accounting, you don't realize income from the cancellation of debt if the payment of the debt would have been a deductible expense."
findings.why: Filers can read "would have been deductible if you had paid it" two ways. Some will take it to mean a deductible type of expense; others will take it to mean it would actually have lowered their tax given their own deduction choice. So similar filers will answer differently.

findings.situation: A creditor accepts the filer's services instead of money in full satisfaction of a nonbusiness debt. The filer reports the forgiven amount as canceled debt with no Form 1099-C.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 3: "You both agreed that you would provide your friend with services (instead of money) in full satisfaction of the debt. You don't have canceled debt. Instead, you have income from services."
findings.why: None of the listed conditions covers a debt paid off with services, so the filer truthfully answers NO. The tool then puts the amount on line 8c as canceled debt, when the IRS treats it as income from services.

question:
Does any of these apply to a canceled debt?

- it was canceled in a bankruptcy case or while you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) were insolvent, or is otherwise excluded from income (Form 982, for example qualified principal residence indebtedness)
- it was a student loan, was canceled as a gift or inheritance, was a reduction of the price of property you bought from the seller, or was owed to a corporation in which you hold stock
- it was a business, rental or farm debt
- it was canceled in connection with a foreclosure, repossession or abandonment of property (Form 1099-C box 7, or a Form 1099-A)
- it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount (for example an unpaid medical bill) that would have been deductible if you had paid it
- you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) were not personally liable for it (box 5)
- you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) were liable for it together with someone who is not on this return

findings.situation: A filer has a line 8z item the tool never asks about, such as a taxable Coverdell ESA or QTP distribution or the taxable part of disaster relief payments, and reads the exception for line 8z as covering all line 8z income.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8z: "Use line 8z to report any taxable income not reported elsewhere ... Examples ... • Taxable part of disaster relief payments ... • Taxable distributions from a Coverdell education savings account (ESA) or a qualified tuition program (QTP)."
findings.why: The question exempts "the other income asked item by item for line 8z" but never says which 8z items those are. A filer could treat any 8z income as exempt and answer NO, and the tool would then count an unasked 8z item as zero. Another filer could read it to mean only the items the tool actually asks about and answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer who rents out personal property but not for profit (income the tool computes on line 8j) answers YES because the question gives "income from the rental of personal property" as an example of unsupported income.
findings.irs_text: f1040s1 p. 1, line 8l: "Income from the rental of personal property if you engaged in the rental for profit but were not in the business of renting such property"; i1040gi p. 91, Line 8j: "Activity not engaged in for profit income."
findings.why: The question's example "income from the rental of personal property (8l)" drops the for-profit condition. A not-for-profit rental belongs on line 8j, which the tool supports, yet the example tells that filer to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer whose stock option income is already in wages on Form 1040 line 1a or 1h answers YES because the question lists "stock options (8k)" without qualification.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h."
findings.why: Line 8k covers only stock option income not reported elsewhere. The bare example "stock options" could lead a filer with no line 8k amount to answer YES and be refused unnecessarily.

findings.situation: A filer whose entire carryover arose in 2018 or later, in a year that began after December 31, 2017, and is larger than 80% of 2025 taxable income figured without the NOL, QBI or section 250 deductions, correctly answers No, so the tool deducts the full carryover with no 80% cap.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1: "your NOL deduction ... cannot exceed the sum of: (1) the NOLs carried to the year from tax years beginning before January 1, 2018; plus, (2) the lesser of: (a) the NOLs carried to the year from tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, or (b) 80% of the excess (if any) of taxable income computed without regard to deductions for NOLs, or Qualified Business Income (QBI), or section 250 deductions..."
findings.why: The question only asks about losses from before 2018. The limit that binds post-2017 losses is never screened, and the computed line subtracts the whole carryover rather than the limited deduction.

findings.situation: On a 2025 joint return, the NOL came from one spouse's year before the marriage or from a year the spouses were not married to each other, and it arose after 2017; the filer answers No, and the tool deducts it against the couple's combined income.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3: "If you and your spouse were not married to each other in all years involved in figuring NOL carrybacks and carryovers, only the spouse who had the loss can take the NOL deduction. If you file a joint return, the NOL deduction is limited to the income of that spouse."
findings.why: The wording asks only about the year the loss arose. It does not ask about a change in marital status, so the limit to that spouse's own income is not applied.

findings.situation: A filer whose carryover is entirely from a year that began before 2018 and is no larger than 2025 income must answer Yes and is refused, although subtracting the full carryover is the correct deduction.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Did any of the net operating loss carried into 2025 arise in a tax year that began before January 1, 2018?"; i172 p. 1: "cannot exceed the sum of: (1) the NOLs carried to the year from tax years beginning before January 1, 2018; plus..."
findings.why: Pre-2018 NOLs are not subject to the 80% limit. When they are the whole carryover and do not exceed income, the tool's simple subtraction already gives the right line 8a.

findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 101: "You must also file Form 4137 if your Form(s) W-2, box 8, shows allocated tips that you must report as income."; f1040s2 p. 1, line 5: "Social security and Medicare tax on unreported tip income. Attach Form 4137"
findings.why: The only tip example in the question is 'tax on unreported tips (Form 4137)', which does not cover allocated tips the filer sees printed on the W-2. The tool would then set Schedule 2 lines 5 and 21, Schedule 8812 line 22, and the Form 4137 qualified tips on Schedule 1-A line 4b and worksheet column 1(c) to zero.

findings.situation: A filer with an HSA excess contribution from a prior year that was not withdrawn, and so still owes the 6% tax in 2025, cannot tell whether that is 'the 2025 HSA excess' the tool figures or an 'other amount'.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 p. 1, line 8: "Additional tax on IRAs or other tax-favored accounts. Attach Form 5329 if required."
findings.why: 'The 2025 HSA excess' can mean only contributions made for 2025, or the whole excess subject to tax for the 2025 year, which includes carryover. The filer could answer YES or NO, and if the tool figures only current-year contributions, a NO answer leaves line 8 and line 21 understated.

findings.situation: The filer paid qualified expenses in 2024 toward adopting a U.S. child, the adoption was not final at the end of 2024 and did not become final in 2025 (still pending, or the attempt failed), and the filer paid nothing in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 (2025) p. 1, Purpose of Form: "You paid qualified adoption expenses in connection with the adoption of an eligible U.S. child ... in: a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final* ... the year after the year of the payment" and "an adoption credit may be allowable for an attempted or unsuccessful adoption, as well as for an adoption that isn't final."
findings.why: The credit for 2024 payments is taken on the 2025 return, but the question asks only about an adoption final in 2025 or expenses paid in 2025. This filer truthfully answers NO and lines 30 and Schedule 3 line 6c/7 are computed as zero.

findings.situation: The filer has an unused adoption credit carried forward from 2024 (for example, from an adoption finalized in 2023 or 2024), with no adoption becoming final in 2025 and no adoption expenses paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 (2025) p. 1, Purpose of Form: "4. You have a carryforward of an adoption credit from 2024. Any amount of the carryforward credit from 2024 remains a nonrefundable credit."
findings.why: The carryforward is claimed on Form 8839 and flows to Schedule 3 line 6c and so line 7, but nothing in the question mentions a carryforward or earlier-year adoptions. The filer answers NO and line 7 is computed as zero.

findings.situation: The filer first paid adoption expenses in 2025 for a U.S. child whose adoption was not final by the end of 2025 (or for a foreign child whose adoption is not yet final), with no 2024 expenses and no carryforward.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or pay expenses in 2025 in connection with adopting a child or trying to adopt one?" with help "Yes also if the costs paid in 2025 were for an adoption that is not finished." i8839 (2025) p. 1: "b. 2025 and the adoption became final in or before 2025"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final* ... the year after the year of the payment"; p. 3, Foreign child: "you can't take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final."
findings.why: No adoption credit is allowed on the 2025 return for these payments (the domestic credit is taken in 2026, the foreign one in the year the adoption becomes final). Zero on line 30 and line 6c would be correct, yet the wording and help text force YES and a refusal.

findings.situation: An adoption became final in 2025, but the child is not a special-needs child and the filer paid no qualified adoption expenses in any year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "adopt a child whose adoption became final in 2025". i8839 (2025) p. 1: "2. You adopted an eligible U.S. child with special needs and the adoption became final in 2025. (In this case, you may be able to take the credit even if you didn't pay any qualified adoption expenses.)"
findings.why: Without qualified expenses, only a special-needs adoption gives a credit, so zero is correct here. The question still makes this filer answer YES on finality alone.

findings.situation: The filer's adoption costs in 2025 were paid by an employer under an adoption assistance program rather than out of pocket.
findings.irs_text: i8839 (2025) p. 1: "Qualified Adoption Expenses don't include expenses reimbursed by an employer under a written qualified adoption assistance program ... you must complete Form 8839, Part III, before you can figure the credit, if any, in Part II."
findings.why: "Pay expenses" can be read as covering only the filer's own payments or also employer-paid or reimbursed costs. A filer with only employer-paid costs could answer either way.

findings.why: The question asks only about a bond or fund credit, so this filer answers NO, but line 7 requires adding all line 6 credits; the tool then enters $0 and omits the mortgage interest credit.

findings.situation: A filer holds a tax credit bond on a credit allowance date but receives no Form 1097-BTC or issuer statement for the credit.
findings.irs_text: i8912 (Rev. Dec. 2024), p. 2, Line 2: 'This amount is the total bond credits from bonds held by you or your nominee(s) and not reported to you on Form(s) 1097-BTC.'
findings.why: The help says the credit is 'Reported on Form 1097-BTC or by the bond’s issuer,' so a filer without such a report can answer NO; the tool then enters $0 on line 7 even though Form 8912 Part IV allows the unreported bond credit.

findings.situation: A filer receives a federal tax credit from a mutual fund that is not a bond credit, such as a foreign tax credit reported by the fund.
findings.irs_text: i8912 (Rev. Dec. 2024), p. 1, Purpose: 'Use Form 8912 to claim the credit for the following tax credit bonds'; p. 2, Line 1: 'This amount is the total bond credits reported to you on Form(s) 1097-BTC.'
findings.why: The box label and 'What this asks' say 'a fund' and 'federal tax credit' without limiting the fund to a bond credit, so this filer could answer YES; Form 8912 covers only tax credit bonds, so the tool would otherwise compute the non-bond fund credit correctly without Form 8912.

findings.situation: A filer has an unused credit from a qualified tax credit bond or Build America bond carried forward from an earlier year and received no Form 1097-BTC for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 2, Line 3: "Enter the amount of the credit carryforward (from prior years) that is attributable to a qualified tax credit bond or a BAB." i8912 p. 3: "you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year"

findings.situation: An audited or AAR partnership furnished its Forms 8986 during 2025 to a pass-through partner, which furnished the filer's Form 8986 in early 2026.
findings.irs_text: i8978 p. 2, Definitions: "Reporting year is the partner's tax year(s) that includes the date the audited or AAR partnership furnished the Forms 8986 to its partners." Example 1 on the same page treats a statement furnished by a pass-through partner on January 15, 2025 as a 2024 reporting year because the audited partnership furnished on March 1, 2024.
findings.why: The filer was not personally furnished a Form 8986 "during 2025" and answers NO. The reporting year is nonetheless 2025, so Form 8978 (line 6l) is required with the 2025 return.

findings.situation: A pass-through partner furnished the filer a Form 8986 in early 2025, but the audited partnership had furnished its Forms 8986 in 2024, so the filer's reporting year is 2024.
findings.irs_text: Question: "were you furnished a Form 8986 ... during 2025". i8978 p. 2, Example 1: "On January 15, 2025, the pass-through partner, in turn, furnishes Forms 8986 ... The reporting year for all three individuals is the tax year that includes March 1, 2024 ... the reporting year is the 2024 tax year."
findings.why: The filer truthfully answers YES and is refused, although Form 8978 belongs on the 2024 return. The 2025 line 6l is correctly zero.

findings.situation: A filer receives a Form 8986 and cannot tell whether "furnished during 2025" means the date they personally received it or the date the audited or AAR partnership furnished its statements (Form 8986, Part II, item G).
findings.irs_text: i8978 p. 2: "The date the audited partnership or BBA partnership that filed an AAR furnished Forms 8986 to its partners is found on Form 8986, Part II, item G."
findings.why: The question and its help text do not point to item G. A filer in a tiered structure could reasonably use either date and reach opposite answers.

findings.situation: A filer has a non-Schedule R other nonrefundable credit on Schedule 3, such as an adoption credit on line 6c or a mortgage interest credit on line 6g, and no credit for the elderly or disabled.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025), line 7: 'Total other nonrefundable credits. Add lines 6a through 6z'; i1040gi (2025) p. 116: 'Line 6c... adoption credit' and 'Line 6g... mortgage interest credit.'
findings.why: The question asks only about Schedule R, so a truthful NO is correct for a filer with only line 6c or 6g; the tool then computes line 7 as zero, omitting credits the IRS line 7 covers.

findings.situation: A filer under 65 retired on permanent and total disability but with no taxable disability income, or who had reached mandatory retirement age, wants to claim because the help says someone retired on disability and low income may claim.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr (2025) p. 1, Qualified Individual: for a person under 65, 'You receive taxable disability income for 2025' and 'On January 1, 2025, you had not reached mandatory retirement age.'
findings.why: The help's 'retired on disability' omits the taxable-disability-income and mandatory-retirement-age conditions, so it invites YES even though no Schedule R credit is allowable and the tool would compute zero correctly.

findings.situation: A nonresident alien age 65 with low income wants to claim the credit based on the help's age and income description.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr (2025) p. 1, U.S. Citizen or Resident Alien: 'You must be a U.S. citizen or resident alien ... Generally, you can't take the credit if you were a nonresident alien at any time during the tax year.'
findings.why: The help mentions only age, disability, and low income, so it can lead a nonresident alien to answer YES even though the IRS disallows the credit and the tool would correctly compute zero.

findings.situation: A married taxpayer filing separately cannot tell whether the help's phrase 'a person not filing with a spouse' includes married filing separately.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr (2025) p. 1, Married Persons: 'If your filing status is married filing separately and you lived apart from your spouse at all times during 2025, you can claim the credit. However, if you lived with your spouse at any time during 2025, you can't take the credit...'
findings.why: The help omits the separate-return rule and uses wording that could mean either single/HOH filers or any filer not on a joint return, so a filer could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A filer buys a new or previously owned clean vehicle from a registered dealer in 2025 but does not transfer the credit to the dealer, so the filer claims the clean vehicle credit on Schedule 3 line 6f or 6m by filing Form 8936.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025), lines 6f and 6m: 'Clean vehicle credit. Attach Form 8936' and 'Credit for previously owned clean vehicles. Attach Form 8936'; line 7 adds lines 6a through 6z.
findings.why: The question asks only whether the dealer gave or transferred the credit; a no-transfer clean vehicle credit still belongs on line 6f or 6m and makes line 7 nonzero, but the tool sets line 7 to zero when the filer truthfully answers NO.

findings.situation: A filer installs qualified alternative fuel vehicle refueling property, such as an EV charger at their main home, in 2025 and claims the alternative fuel vehicle refueling property credit on Schedule 3 line 6j.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025), line 6j: 'Alternative fuel vehicle refueling property credit. Attach Form 8911'; i8911 p. 1, Purpose of Form: 'Use Form 8911 ... to figure your credit for alternative fuel vehicle refueling property you placed in service during your tax year.'
findings.why: The dealer-credit question does not ask about home refueling equipment even though the gate condition expressly includes installation of home charging or fueling equipment; a truthful NO leaves line 6j out and line 7 at zero.

findings.situation: A filer acquires a clean vehicle after September 30, 2025, and the dealer shows or gives a purported clean vehicle credit off the price.
findings.irs_text: i8936 (2025) p. 1, What's New: 'Taxpayers cannot claim clean vehicle credits for new, previously owned, or commercial clean vehicles that they acquired after September 30, 2025.'
findings.why: The literal dealer-credit question makes this filer answer YES, but the IRS text allows no clean vehicle credit for a vehicle acquired after that date, so the tool's zero line 7 and passed credits screen would be correct without the Form 8936 refusal.

findings.situation: A filer leases an EV in 2025 and the dealer or lessor applies a clean vehicle credit as a capitalized cost reduction; the filer does not know whether the question's word 'bought' includes a lease.
findings.irs_text: i8936 (2025) p. 1, Purpose of Form: 'You must file Form 8936 ... if you purchased a new or used clean vehicle from a registered dealer and reduced the amount you paid at the time of sale by transferring the credit to the dealer.'
findings.why: The refusal text says 'purchased,' while the gate help says to count a vehicle bought or leased; a lease is not clearly a purchase, so the filer could reasonably answer either way.
