findings.situation: A taxpayer placed qualified alternative fuel vehicle refueling property in service at a business location, not at their main home; the question asks only about home charging or fueling equipment.
findings.irs_text: i8911 p. 1: 'credit for alternative fuel vehicle refueling property you placed in service during your tax year'; 'The part of the credit attributable to business/investment use is treated as a general business credit.'
findings.why: Form 8911 covers business/investment-use property, and Schedule 3 line 7 includes the general business credit on line 6a, but the question's home limitation lets the filer answer No and omit it.

findings.situation: A taxpayer installed qualifying home EV charging equipment before 2025, but the equipment first became operational and was placed in service in 2025; the question asks only about equipment installed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8911 p. 1: 'credit for alternative fuel vehicle refueling property you placed in service during your tax year'; i8911 p. 4: 'an EV charger installed at an individual taxpayer's principal residence will be placed in service when it is operational.'
findings.why: The IRS tests placed-in-service in the tax year, not the installation year, so a truthful filer can answer No and have line 7 zeroed even though a 2025 Form 8911 credit is needed.

findings.situation: A taxpayer installed home charging equipment in 2025, but it was not operational and not placed in service until 2026; they could answer Yes to the question even though no 2025 Form 8911 credit is allowed.
findings.irs_text: i8911 p. 1: 'placed in service during your tax year'; i8911 p. 4: 'an EV charger installed at an individual taxpayer's principal residence will be placed in service when it is operational.'
findings.why: The question keys on installation in 2025 rather than placed-in-service, so it can force a refusal for equipment that does not qualify until a later year.

findings.situation: A filer with home charging equipment cannot tell from the help whether the certain low-income or rural areas phrase is the actual eligibility test or just a general description of the eligible census tract rule.
findings.irs_text: i8911 p. 2: 'The property must be located in an eligible census tract.'
findings.why: The help uses low-income or rural areas instead of the IRS term eligible census tract, leaving a reasonable filer unsure whether their location must be checked against a specific census-tract list.

findings.why: The question asks only about a 2024 AMT liability, so this filer truthfully answers NO and line 6b (inside line 7) is computed as $0 although a credit may be allowed. This is a gap unless a separate screen, not shown among the listed refusals, asks about the Form 8801 carryforward.

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 AMT liability came entirely from exclusion items (for example the standard deduction, certain itemized deductions, certain tax-exempt interest or depletion) and there is no carryforward, so no minimum tax credit exists and $0 on line 6b is correct.

findings.situation: A filer first has a tax credit bond credit for 2025 (bought a pre-2018 qualified tax credit bond or BAB during 2025, or first received a Form 1097-BTC or a pass-through share of bond credit for 2025) and had no Form 8912 in the 2024 return.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 1: "A taxpayer holding a CREB or qualified tax credit bond ... on one or more credit allowance dates can claim the credit by filing Form 8912 for each tax year in which it holds the bond on a credit allowance date." f1040s3 p. 1: "6k Credit to holders of tax credit bonds. Attach Form 8912"
findings.why: The question asks only whether the 2024 return included Form 8912, so this filer truthfully answers NO and line 7 is computed as $0 although a 2025 line 6k credit exists. Among the refusals listed here, none asks about a current-year bond credit.

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 return included Form 8912, but the whole credit was used in 2024 (or it was a CREB or pre-October 4, 2008 QZAB credit, which cannot be carried forward) and the bond was sold, redeemed or matured before any 2025 credit allowance date, so nothing belongs on 2025 line 6k.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 3: "If you can't use all of the credit from Part I (for example, line 12 is smaller than line 4), you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year"; i8912 p. 2: "Credits attributable to a CREB, or a QZAB issued before October 4, 2008, can't be carried forward."
findings.why: The question ("Does your ... 2024 federal return include Form 8912") forces a YES and a refusal on the mere presence of the form, while a carryforward exists only if part of the credit went unused. For this filer the tool's $0 on line 7 would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer who filed Form 8912 for 2024 and used the full credit reads the help text and cannot tell whether the question is about the form being present or about having an unused credit.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 3: "you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year and add it to any credit allowable to the holder of the same bond in the next tax year"
findings.why: The question asks about the form, but the help says "a credit not used in 2024 carries into 2025", which suggests only an unused credit matters. Such a filer could reasonably answer either YES or NO.

findings.situation: A filer claims a 2025 alternative fuel vehicle refueling property credit on Form 8911 but has no prior-year listed carryover form.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025), line 6j: 'Alternative fuel vehicle refueling property credit. Attach Form 8911'; i8911 (Rev. December 2025), p. 1: 'Use Form 8911 ... to figure your credit for alternative fuel vehicle refueling property you placed in service during your tax year.'
findings.why: The question asks only whether the 2024 return contains one of the listed carryover forms, so this filer truthfully answers NO; the tool then enters $0 on line 7 and omits the current-year line 6j credit. The refusal text covers only credits carried from an earlier year.

findings.situation: A filer filed 2024 Form 8396 but fully used the mortgage interest credit and has no unused carryforward for 2025, yet the question asks 'Is any of those forms Form 3800, 8396, 8801, 8582-CR, 8839, 8859 or 8912?'
findings.irs_text: f8396 (2025), p. 2: 'If the amount on line 9 is less than the amount on line 7, you may have an unused credit to carry forward to the next 3 tax years or until used, whichever comes first.'
findings.why: The wording tests the presence of the form, not whether it produced an unused carryforward; the filer answers YES and the tool refuses even though the correct 2025 amount from that form is zero.

findings.situation: A filer who received Form 2439 from a mutual fund or REIT showing tax paid on undistributed long-term capital gains has a line 13a amount but none of the four listed situations applies, so they answer NO.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025) p. 1: "13 Other payments or refundable credits: a Form 2439 . . . 13a" and "14 Total other payments or refundable credits. Add lines 13a through 13z"
findings.why: The question lists only line 13d and line 13z items, so this filer truthfully answers NO and the tool enters $0 on line 14, dropping the refundable credit for tax paid on their behalf.

findings.situation: A filer who repaid more than $3,000 of income included in an earlier year under a claim of right, and chooses the section 1341 credit, has a line 13b amount but answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117: "Line 13b If you are claiming a credit for repayment of amounts you included in your income in an earlier year because it appeared you had a right to the income, enter the amount on line 13b."
findings.why: The question does not mention the claim-of-right repayment credit, so line 14 is computed as $0 although the IRS text requires line 13b to be included in the line 14 total.

findings.situation: A filer with a net elective payment election amount from Form 3800, Part III, line 6, column (j) has a line 13c amount but answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117: "Line 13c Enter any net elective payment election amount from Form 3800, Part III, line 6, column (j)."
findings.why: None of the four listed situations describes an elective payment election, so the filer answers NO and the tool treats line 14 as $0, omitting the line 13c amount (unless a separate Form 3800 screen, not shown here, already refuses this filer).

findings.situation: A filer has a refundable credit or payment on Schedule 3 line 13a, 13c, 13d or 13z, such as a Form 2439 undistributed capital gains credit, a net elective payment from Form 3800, a deferred 965 amount, or a section 960(c) or Form 1062 amount, and has repaid nothing. That filer truthfully answers NO, and the tool enters $0 on line 14.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025) line 14: "Total other payments or refundable credits. Add lines 13a through 13z"; line 13a "Form 2439"; i1040gi p. 117, Line 13z: "Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c)... Also use line 13z to report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands... enter 75% of your applicable net tax liability from Form 1062, line 14."
findings.why: The tool computes the whole of line 14 as zero, but this question only asks about repaid income, which is line 13b. Nothing in its wording leads a filer with amounts on 13a, 13c, 13d or 13z to answer YES.

findings.situation: On a joint return, each spouse repaid $3,000 or less, but together they repaid more than $3,000, for example $2,000 each. A filer could read the question per person and answer NO.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 36, Caution: "When determining whether the amount you repaid was less than $3,000, consider the total amount being repaid on the return. Each instance of repayment isn't considered separately."
findings.why: The wording "you (or, on a joint return, your spouse)... more than $3,000 in total" and the help text "Add up everything you (or... your spouse) paid back" can be read as testing each spouse separately. The IRS test uses the combined total on the return.

findings.situation: A filer repaid more than $3,000 of income from an earlier year that was not held under a claim of right, for example misappropriated funds. No line 13b credit is available, so the tool's $0 would be correct, yet the wording makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 36: "you can deduct the repayment... if you included the income under a claim of right. This means that at the time you included the income, it appeared that you had an unrestricted right to it"; i1040gi p. 117, Line 13b: "amounts you included in your income in an earlier year because it appeared you had a right to the income"
findings.why: The question asks only whether more than $3,000 "that you had reported as income in an earlier year" was paid back. It leaves out the claim-of-right condition that makes the line 13b credit available.

findings.situation: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, has an unused contribution carryover from an earlier year (for example from 2021 through 2024), but their 2025 gifts are small and not limited, so they truthfully answer NO and line 13 is computed as zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 11, Line 13: "You may have contributions that you couldn't deduct in an earlier year because they exceeded the limits on the amount you could deduct. In most cases, you have 5 years to use contributions that were limited in an earlier year."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the 2025 gifts are large enough to be limited. It never asks about carryovers from prior years, which line 13 needs and the tool sets to zero.

findings.situation: A filer gives appreciated property, such as stock or land, or the use of property, worth well under 20% of AGI, answers NO, and line 12 reports the full value before limits without the reduction Pub. 526 may require.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10, Limit on the amount you can deduct: "See Pub. 526 to figure the amount of your deduction if any of the following applies. ... 3. You gave gifts of property that increased in value or gave gifts of the use of property."
findings.why: Under the instructions, this condition needs Pub. 526 no matter how large the gifts are. The question's statement that a limit "can happen only when they total more than 20% of your income" tells this filer to answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer whose cash gifts exceed 30% of AGI (Form 1040 line 11b) but are below 30% of total or gross income could answer either way.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10: "1. Your cash contributions or contributions of ordinary income property are more than 30% of the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b. 2. Your gifts of capital gain property are more than 20% of the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b."
findings.why: The question and its help say "your income", not adjusted gross income (Form 1040 line 11b). A filer could measure against total or gross income, which is larger, and wrongly conclude the limit does not apply.

findings.situation: A filer whose gifts are over 20% of AGI cannot tell whether the law actually limits them without working through Pub. 526, so they may guess either way.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10, Line 11: "Enter on line 11 the total value of gifts you made in cash or by check (including out-of-pocket expenses) unless a limit on deducting gifts applies to you."
findings.why: The question asks the filer to decide whether "the law limits what you can deduct", which is the very calculation the tool does not do. The 20/30/50/60% help gives no rule for which percentage applies to which gift, so filers above 20% cannot answer reliably.

findings.situation: A filer aged 25 to 64 who is permanently and totally disabled and lives with a parent who files a return, but who provides more than half of their own support, is a qualifying child of the parent for the EIC but cannot be claimed as the parent's dependent, so the filer truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 42, Step 4, question 5: "Could you be a qualifying child of another person for 2025? ... Yes. STOP You can't take the credit."; p. 41: a qualifying child is one who was "Any age and permanently and totally disabled" and "lived with you in the United States for more than half of 2025" (no support test)
findings.why: The question asks only whether someone can claim the filer as a dependent, which is Step 4 question 6, and its refusal cites only question 6. Step 4 question 5 is a separate bar, because the EIC qualifying-child test has no support test and a person can meet it without being a dependent, so a filer who is only a qualifying child of another person answers NO and the tool allows the credit unless it asks about question 5 separately.

findings.situation: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico or American Samoa excludes unearned income from sources there, such as interest, dividends or rents, and reads 'income earned in Puerto Rico or in American Samoa' as meaning only pay for work, so answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "if you're filing ... Form 4563, Exclusion of Income for Bona Fide Residents of American Samoa; or are excluding income from Puerto Rico, add ... the amount of income you excluded"; f1040s8812 line 2a: "Enter income from Puerto Rico that you excluded"
findings.why: The IRS trigger is any excluded Puerto Rico-source income or any Form 4563 exclusion, whether or not it is earned income. The word 'earned' invites a NO from someone whose excluded income is investment income, so the tool would treat the add-back as zero.

findings.situation: A service member leaves nontaxable combat-zone pay earned abroad out of income, or a filer excludes foreign income under a tax treaty, without filing Form 2555 or 4563 and without excluding Puerto Rico income.
findings.irs_text: Question: "leave out of this return any income earned abroad"; i1040gi p. 40: "Are you filing Form 2555 (relating to foreign earned income)?"; i1040sca p. 7: "if you completed Form 2555, Form 4563, or excluded income from Puerto Rico"
findings.why: The IRS lines are triggered only by Form 2555, Form 4563 or excluded Puerto Rico income. The broad phrase 'leave out ... any income earned abroad' makes these filers answer YES, and they are then refused even though the lines are correct for them. Combat pay, for example, has its own handling on Form 2441 and the EIC.

findings.situation: A Form 2555 filer reports foreign wages on Form 1040 line 1 and then subtracts the exclusion as a negative amount on Schedule 1, so the income does appear on the return.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 4: "The amount shown on Form 1040, 1040-SR, or 1040-NR, line 1z, minus any amount: a. Excluded as foreign earned income (including any housing exclusion) on Form 2555, line 43"
findings.why: The foreign income is entered on the return and then excluded, so it is not literally 'left out of this return'. A literal reader could answer NO, although the parenthetical '(Form 2555)' points toward YES.

findings.situation: A filer married filing separately has a casualty loss from a federally declared disaster on a home owned with the spouse as tenants by the entirety, and paid nothing from a joint account and files no joint state return.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: casualty loss ... have a casualty loss resulting from a federally declared disaster on a home you own as tenants by the entirety ... half of the loss, subject to the deduction limits. Neither spouse may report the total casualty loss.
findings.why: A casualty loss is not an amount paid from an account, so the filer truthfully answers NO. The tool then takes the full entered loss, but only half is deductible.

findings.situation: A filer in a community property state paid itemized expenses from community funds held in an account titled only in their own name or in their spouse's name.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: Caution: If you live in a community property state, these rules don't apply. See Community Property.
findings.why: Community funds belong to both spouses, so the expenses were paid jointly under i1040sca p. 1 and must be divided under Pub. 504's community property rules. The question asks only about account titling and joint state returns, so the filer answers NO.

findings.situation: A filer files a joint state return on which both spouses are jointly and individually liable for the full state tax, and enters on Schedule A only the state income tax they alone paid.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: file a joint state income tax return and you and your spouse are jointly and individually liable for the full amount of the state income tax ... the state income tax you alone paid during the year.
findings.why: Pub. 504 lets this filer deduct exactly what they alone paid, which the tool computes from the entry. The question still forces YES through 'or do the two of you file a joint 2025 state income tax return?'

findings.situation: A filer paid medical expenses from a joint checking account, can show they alone paid them, and enters only those amounts.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: half of the total medical expenses, subject to certain limits, unless you can show that you alone paid the expenses.
findings.why: When the filer can show sole payment, the deductible amount is what they alone paid, which the tool computes. The question's wording 'paid from an account you hold with your husband or wife' still requires YES.

findings.situation: A filer paid deductible expenses from a joint account in which the spouses do not have equal interests, or with a joint credit card.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: paid with funds deposited in a joint checking account in which you and your spouse have an equal interest
findings.why: Pub. 504 states the half rule only for equal-interest joint accounts. A filer could reasonably read 'an account you hold with your husband or wife' either to include or to exclude unequal-interest accounts and joint credit card accounts.

findings.situation: A filer has charitable contributions from an earlier year that they could not deduct because of the limits and are carrying over into 2025. None of the listed items applies to them, so they answer NO, and the tool enters zero on line 13.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 11, Line 13, Carryover From Prior Year: "You may have contributions that you couldn't deduct in an earlier year because they exceeded the limits on the amount you could deduct. In most cases, you have 5 years to use contributions that were limited in an earlier year... enter the amount of your carryover that you are allowed to deduct this year."
findings.why: The screen lists casualty and disaster losses, line 16 items, foreign and GST taxes, mortgage items, and the sales-tax election. It never mentions a charitable contribution carryover, yet line 13 is computed as zero whenever the answer is NO, so the carryover is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer whose Form 1098 mortgage interest may be reduced by the debt limit or the use limit cannot tell from the question whether their loan is affected.

findings.why: The question says "debt over the limit" but gives no dollar limit and does not say whether a refinanced loan or a home equity loan counts. A filer could answer either way without knowing whether the tool's figure would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer sells a long-term holding of collectible tangible property that is not on the question's list, such as sports memorabilia, trading cards or comic books, and answers NO.
findings.irs_text: Collectibles include works of art, rugs, antiques, metals (such as gold, silver, and platinum bullion), gems, stamps, coins, alcoholic beverages, and certain other tangible property. (i1040sd 2025, p. 11, Line 18)
findings.why: The question gives a closed list with no catch-all for 'certain other tangible property.' A filer whose item is not named can truthfully answer NO, and the tool then leaves out the code C reporting and the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet.

findings.situation: A filer sells depreciated real property held more than 1 year that was used in their own business or farm, not rented out and not a home office, and answers NO.
findings.irs_text: You sold or otherwise disposed of section 1250 property (generally, real property that you depreciated) held more than 1 year. (i1040sd 2025, p. 11, Line 19)
findings.why: The question limits real estate to property 'you once rented out or took a home office deduction for.' Other depreciated real property, such as a building used in a sole proprietorship or a farm building, needs the Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain Worksheet but falls outside that wording.

findings.situation: A filer who excludes 100% of the gain on qualified small business stock may read 'exclude part of the gain' as not covering a full exclusion and answer NO.
findings.irs_text: You sold or exchanged QSB stock and can exclude part of the gain ... enter the amount of the exclusion as a negative number (in parentheses) in column (g). (i8949 2025, p. 9, code Q); Don't make an entry for any section 1202 exclusion that is 100% of the gain. (i1040sd 2025, p. 11)
findings.why: 'Part of the gain' can be read to exclude a full exclusion. A 100% exclusion still needs code Q and a column (g) adjustment, and the tool would instead treat the whole gain as taxable.

findings.irs_text: Question: 'Do you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) have to file the report of foreign accounts (the “FBAR”, FinCEN Form 114) for 2025?' IRS: 'If you are required to file FinCEN Form 114, list the name(s) of the foreign country or countries in the space provided on line 7b.' (i1040sb p. 3) and 'Report on line 1 all of your taxable interest.' (i1040sb p. 1)
findings.why: An FBAR requirement changes only the Part III answers on line 7a Question 2 and the country list on line 7b. It does not change how interest is added for line 2, the line 3 exclusion, or the line 6 dividend total, so refusing these three lines on a Yes covers cases the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer, or the spouse, cashed Series EE or I savings bonds issued after 1989 and paid qualified higher education expenses, but has no FBAR obligation and truthfully answers No, so the tool sets line 3 to the zero year parameter and misses the Form 8815 exclusion.

If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses for yourself, your spouse, or your dependents, you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815' (i1040sb p. 2)
findings.why: Line 3 is always computed as zero, and the only screen attached to it asks about the FBAR. Nothing in the question's wording leads a filer with the savings bond exclusion to answer Yes.

findings.why: The line 6 helper is the box 1a total with no nominee subtraction, and the FBAR question gives a nominee recipient no reason to answer Yes.

findings.situation: A filer who holds 10% or more of, or is a manager of, a foreign partnership or other foreign entity that is not a corporation answers YES because the question says "company", even though the Form 5471 trigger is limited to foreign corporations.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2, Part II TIP: "You may have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you were an officer or director of a foreign corporation ... owned 10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation’s stock, or (b) combined voting power of all classes of a foreign corporation’s stock"
findings.why: The question asks about "a company organized outside the 50 states and the District of Columbia", and a lay filer reads "company" to include partnerships and LLCs. The IRS trigger covers only foreign corporations, so these filers are refused although nothing in the cited text takes their lines 2, 3 and 6 out of the tool's computation.

findings.situation: A filer who holds a non-officer title such as general manager, branch manager or LLC manager at a foreign corporation cannot tell whether "manager" applies to them.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2, Part II TIP: "You may have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you were an officer or director of a foreign corporation"
findings.why: The question lists "officer, director or manager", but the IRS text names only officers and directors. One filer may read "manager" as any managerial job and answer YES, while another reads it as a formal officer-like role and answers NO.

findings.situation: A filer who owns less than 10% directly but reaches 10% only after adding the shares of parents, grandchildren or other related parties listed in the help answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2, Part II TIP: "You may also have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you owned 10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation’s stock, or (b) combined voting power"
findings.why: The cited IRS text says only "you owned" and does not mention adding family or entity holdings, so the help's instruction to "add the shares of your spouse, children, grandchildren and parents" pushes YES beyond the cited text. Whether this is justified depends on constructive-ownership rules in the Form 5471 instructions, which are not in the cited text.

findings.situation: A filer had a foreign financial account (or signature authority over one) below the Form 8938 thresholds, so Form 8938 is not required, but Schedule B Part III still requires reporting the foreign account.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 3: “Check the ‘Yes’ box if at any time during 2025 you had a financial interest in or signature authority over a financial account located in a foreign country. ... Check the ‘Yes’ box even if you aren't required to file FinCEN Form 114.”
findings.why: The question asks only whether Form 8938 must be filed; a truthful NO is possible for a small foreign account, yet the IRS text still requires a Part III foreign-account answer that the tool does not compute.

findings.situation: A filer with a small foreign account (so no Form 8938) received a Form 1099-INT that included nominee interest, or has an accrued-interest, OID, or amortizable-bond-premium adjustment that reduces Schedule B line 2.

findings.situation: A filer with a small foreign account (so no Form 8938) received a Form 1099-DIV that included ordinary dividends as a nominee and distributed them to the actual owner.

findings.why: The filer truthfully answers NO to Form 8938, but the tool computes line 6 as the 1099-DIV box 1a total and ignores the required nominee subtraction.

findings.situation: A filer owns directly held foreign real estate worth more than the stated threshold but has no foreign financial account or other specified foreign financial asset, so no Form 8938 is required.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: “A financial account includes ... a securities, brokerage, savings, demand, checking, deposit, time deposit, or other account maintained with a financial institution...”
findings.why: The question's phrase “foreign accounts and assets” can sweep in direct real estate, but the IRS definition is of a financial account; the wording can produce YES and an unnecessary refusal even though the tool could compute the interest and dividend lines.

findings.situation: A filer bought a tax-exempt municipal bond at a premium and nets the amortized premium only against the tax-exempt interest on Form 1040 line 2a, which does not change Schedule B lines 2, 3 or 6.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "if you acquired a tax-exempt bond at a premium, only report the net amount of tax-exempt interest on line 2a of your Form 1040 or 1040-SR"; question: "bond premium adjustment"
findings.why: The question says "bond premium adjustment" without limiting it to taxable bonds, so this filer would truthfully answer YES. The ABP Adjustment on Schedule B applies only to "interest income on a taxable bond," so the tool computes these lines correctly for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer's payer already reported a net amount of interest or OID that reflects amortizable bond premium or acquisition premium, so no Schedule B reduction is allowed and the 1099 amount is correct as reported.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "if the payer reported to you a net amount of interest income on the bond reflecting the offset of the gross amount of interest income by the amortizable bond premium, no reduction of the amount of interest income reported to you by the payer is permitted on Schedule B"
findings.why: A filer who holds premium bonds may answer YES to "bond premium adjustment" even though no adjustment is made on Schedule B. The tool's unadjusted sum of the reported amounts is correct here.

findings.situation: A filer has OID that differs from Form 1099-OID, or has OID with no Form 1099-OID at all, and the wording "in an amount other than on Form 1099-OID" does not match the IRS trigger of reporting less than box 1 or box 8.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "If you are reporting OID in an amount less than the amount shown in box 1 or box 8 of Form 1099-OID ... identify the amount to be subtracted as 'OID Adjustment.'"
findings.why: "Other than" can be read as "different from" (which includes reporting more) or as "not on a 1099-OID." A filer cannot tell whether OID that has no 1099-OID, or OID above the form amount, counts.

findings.situation: A filer sold a market discount bond and part of the gain is treated as interest under the market discount rules, but the filer never elected to accrue market discount.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Also include any accrued market discount that is includible in income and any gain on a contingent payment debt instrument that is includible in income as interest income."
findings.why: "Accrued market discount" may read to a filer as applying only after a current-inclusion election. Some filers in this situation could answer NO and leave includible interest out of line 2.

findings.situation: A filer has some unusual interest or dividend item and must decide whether it is "other special treatment."
findings.irs_text: question: "or other special treatment?"; i1040sb p. 1: "Report on line 1 all of your taxable interest."
findings.why: The catch-all has no defined scope, so filers could reasonably answer either way for items such as interest not reported on any Form 1099 or tax-exempt items that do not affect these lines.

findings.situation: A statutory employee has Form W-2 box 1 income that must be reported on Schedule C line 1 but claims no business credit, so the filer can truthfully answer NO to the business-credit screen.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 5, Line 1: 'Enter your statutory employee income from box 1 of Form W-2 on line 1 of Schedule C and check the box on that line.'
findings.why: The screen asks only about business credits, so a statutory employee with no credit answers NO; the tool's line 1 input covers 1099 and other gross receipts but does not capture the W-2 statutory-employee amount.

findings.situation: A partner or S-corporation shareholder claims a general business credit passed through from the entity, not from 'this business,' and could answer NO to the screen for a separate Schedule C business.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 116: 'The general business credit consists of a number of credits that usually apply only to individuals who are partners, shareholders in an S corporation, self-employed, or who have rental property.'
findings.why: The question asks whether 'this business' claims the credit; a pass-through credit is claimed by the individual on the return, so a truthful NO is possible while Form 3800 is still required and outside the tool.

findings.situation: A business generates a 2025 general business credit that is limited and carried forward rather than used this year, leaving unclear whether it 'claims' the credit.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 116: 'The general business credit consists of a number of credits... See Form 3800 or Pub. 334.'
findings.why: The help says to count a credit carried from an earlier year, but 'claims' can reasonably be read as only a credit used on the current return; a current-year unused carryforward could get either answer even though Form 3800 is needed.

findings.irs_text: i4136 p. 2, Line A: "Exemption: If you are claiming a credit for the tax on undyed kerosene you purchased (other than from a blocked pump) and used in your home during the tax period for heating, lighting, or cooking. Answer "Yes" on line A"; i1040gi p. 117, Line 12: "Enter any credit for federal excise taxes paid on fuels ... Attach Form 4136."
findings.why: The question asks only about this business, and its help says personal use does not count. A filer with a home kerosene claim truthfully answers NO, or never sees the screen because they have no business, so a Form 4136 credit goes uncomputed.

findings.situation: A business that used fuel off-highway and already got the excise tax back during the year through Form 8849 or Form 720 has nothing left to claim on Form 4136, yet may still read itself as one that 'wants fuel tax back'.
findings.irs_text: i4136 p. 3: "Claims by registered credit card issuers and registered ultimate vendors ... must be made on Form 8849; or Form 720, Schedule C"; i1040gi p. 117, Line 12: "Attach Form 4136."
findings.why: The question asks whether the business 'want[s] the federal fuel tax back', not whether it is claiming the credit on this income tax return through Form 4136. A filer whose refund is already settled through another form could answer YES and be refused needlessly, or answer NO; the wording supports either reading.

findings.situation: A business changes only how it physically counts inventory during 2025, such as moving from an annual physical count to cycle counting, without changing its tax inventory method or valuation method.
findings.irs_text: "If you are changing your method of accounting beginning with 2025, refigure last year’s closing inventory using your new method of accounting and enter the result on line 35." (i1040sc (2025) p. 15, Line 35)
findings.why: Line 35 requires a refiguring only for an inventory method change beginning with 2025; a mid-year physical counting change does not affect beginning inventory, which the tool computes as the prior year's closing inventory. The question's wording, "did the way it counts or values inventory change during 2025," makes the filer answer YES and stop even though the line could be computed correctly.

findings.situation: A filer keeps rental books on the accrual basis for bookkeeping but reports the rental activity on the cash method for tax.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025), p. 4, When To Deduct: "You generally deduct your rental expenses in the year you pay them. If you use the accrual method, see Pub. 538 for more information."
findings.why: The question asks whether the filer keeps "rental books on the accrual method," so an accrual-book/cash-tax filer truthfully answers YES and the tool refuses; but the IRS text keys the exception to using the accrual method for tax, and the tool computes the cash-method return correctly.

findings.situation: A filer has grouped two rentals, or a rental with a business, but every grouped rental shows net income on line 21, so line 22 is blank and line 26 is just line 24 whatever the grouping.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'Do you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) treat a rental and another activity, such as another rental or a business, as one activity?' vs. f1040se p.1 line 22: 'Deductible rental real estate loss after limitation, if any, on Form 8582'; i8582 p.1: 'A PAL occurs when total losses ... from all your passive activities exceed the total income'
findings.why: Grouping changes line 26 only through the Form 8582 loss limit on line 22. A filer with no rental losses must still answer YES and is refused, even though Add line 24 and line 25 gives the correct line 26.

findings.situation: A filer has combined several rental properties into one rental real estate enterprise under the QBI safe harbor (Rev. Proc. 2019-38) or the section 199A aggregation rules, but has made no passive activity grouping.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p.1: 'Rev. Proc. 2019-38 provides a safe harbor under which a rental real estate enterprise will be treated as a trade or business for purposes of the QBI deduction.'
findings.why: The question does not say it means grouping under the passive activity rules (Form 8582 / section 469). A filer who treats rentals as one enterprise for QBI could reasonably answer YES and be refused for an arrangement that does not affect line 26.

findings.situation: A real estate professional (or, on a joint return, a spouse who is one) has elected to treat all interests in rental real estate as one activity.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p.3: 'each interest in rental real estate is a separate activity unless you elect to treat all your interests in rental real estate as one activity. To make this election, attach a statement to your original tax return'
findings.why: This election is a statutory aggregation, not the i8582 grouping the refusal cites. Filers could read 'treat a rental and another activity ... as one activity' as including it or excluding it.

findings.situation: The filer's rentals are treated as one activity because the IRS regrouped them, or because a grouping chosen in an earlier year must be continued, and the filer does not think of this as something they currently 'treat' as one activity.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p.6: 'you must continue using that grouping in later tax years ... The IRS may regroup your activities if your grouping fails to reflect one or more appropriate economic units'
findings.why: 'Do you ... treat' suggests a choice the filer actively makes this year. A filer bound by an earlier grouping or by an IRS regrouping could truthfully read it as NO, even though Form 8582 must apply the grouping.

findings.situation: A filer works more than 750 hours, and more than half of their work time, in real estate businesses, but does not materially participate in those businesses (for example, a minority partner or passive investor in several real estate firms).
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "More than half of the personal services you performed in trades or businesses during the year were performed in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated" and "You performed more than 750 hours of services during the year in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated."
findings.why: The question asks only about hours 'in real estate businesses' and drops the 'in which you materially participated' condition, so filers who are not real estate professionals answer YES. Their rentals stay passive, and the tool's computation of line 26 is correct for them.

findings.situation: A filer meets both real estate professional tests through a brokerage or construction business but does not materially participate in any of their own rental properties (for example, the rentals are run by a property manager).
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "If you qualify as a real estate professional, rental real estate activities in which you materially participated are not passive activities." f1040se line 43: "from all rental real estate activities in which you materially participated"
findings.why: Professional status changes nothing for rentals in which the filer did not materially participate. Those rentals stay passive, line 43 is zero, and the tool computes line 26 correctly, yet the question forces a YES.

findings.situation: A filer is unsure whether 'your own work time' includes hours worked as an employee in an unrelated job, which affects whether real estate work is more than half.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "More than half of the personal services you performed in trades or businesses during the year"
findings.why: The help explains how employee work counts toward real estate hours but does not say that all employee hours elsewhere count in the total. A filer could leave out a salaried job from the total and wrongly answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer whose Form W-2 box 1 includes wages earned while an inmate in a penal institution reads 'wages' as a kind the question is not about and answers NO, so the tool leaves the amount on line 1a and puts nothing on line 8.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 23, Line 1a: "If you earned wages while you were an inmate in a penal institution, report these amounts on Schedule 1, line 8u. Do not report these wages on line 1a."
findings.why: The question excludes 'wages' and names only 'wages or tips not on a Form W-2', so W-2 wages that must move to Schedule 1 line 8u (and into Form 1040 line 8) are not caught.

findings.situation: A filer with wages plus a receipt that is not reportable income (a state general-welfare payment, a utility rate reduction, a reimbursed union convention expense) answers YES because it is 'other income' outside the six listed kinds, although line 8 is correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 23: "Generally, you must report all income except income that is exempt from tax by law." p525 (2025) p. 36: "The amount of the rate reduction or nonrefundable credit isn't included in your income."
findings.why: The catch-all 'any other outside the wages, interest, dividends...' is not limited to income that must be reported on the return, so exempt receipts trigger a refusal the lines do not need.

findings.situation: A filer with only wages who would claim a credit or special computation (for example the claim-of-right repayment credit, a foreign tax credit, or a mortgage interest credit carryforward) cannot tell whether that is a 'return treatment outside the kinds listed'.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 36: "if the amount you repaid is more than $3,000, you may be able to take a credit against your tax for the year in which you repaid it"; f1040 (2025) line 20 "Amount from Schedule 3, line 8" and line 31 "Amount from Schedule 3, line 15"
findings.why: 'Return treatment' is undefined, and the listed kinds and examples are all income items, so a filer could read the question as being about income only and answer NO while lines 20 and 31 are computed as zero.

findings.situation: A filer who received a qualified disaster recovery distribution in 2025 on a Form 1099-R, or who made a 2025 repayment of a distribution received in a year other than 2023 or 2024, cannot tell whether the Form 8915-F item applies to them.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 35: "Use Form 8915-F to report qualified disaster recovery distributions and repayments." and "you can include $6,000 in your income in 2023, 2024, and 2025. However, you can elect to include the entire distribution in your income in the year it was received."
findings.why: The wording names only distributions 'received in 2023 or 2024' and 'a 2025 repayment of one', while 'Form 1099-R distributions' is listed as a kind the question is not about, so a 2025 distribution or its repayment can be read as either NO or YES.

- wages
- interest
- dividends
- supported securities sales

findings.situation: A filer (typically an S corporation shareholder) had a section 965(i) triggering event in 2025 with no transfer agreement, so the triggered deferred net 965 tax liability belongs on line 16, but nothing in the question's list names it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36, Line 16: "Triggering event under section 965(i). If you had a triggering event under section 965(i) during the year and did not enter into a transfer agreement, check box 3 and enter the amount of the triggered deferred net 965 tax liability and enter “965INC” on the line next to that box."
findings.why: The list omits 965(i)/965INC, and a triggering event such as selling the S corporation stock can leave the filer owning no CFC or PFIC stock, so a truthful NO is plausible. The only catch is the vague stem "any additional Form 1040 line 16 tax", which a filer cannot be expected to map to this item.

findings.situation: A filer who claims the foreign earned income exclusion, housing exclusion or housing deduction on Form 2555 must figure line 16 with the Foreign Earned Income Tax Worksheet, which the computed line (Schedule D Tax Worksheet or the non-SDTW method) does not use.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36, Line 16: "If you claimed the foreign earned income exclusion, housing exclusion, or housing deduction on Form 2555, you must figure your tax using the Foreign Earned Income Tax Worksheet."
findings.why: Form 2555 is not named in the question, and it is a different way of figuring the tax rather than an "additional" line 16 tax, so the filer can answer NO. This is a gap only if no other screen (not shown here) already refuses Form 2555 filers.

findings.situation: A filer born on January 1 (2008, 2007 or 2002) counts their age at the end of 2025 by ordinary reckoning and answers YES to the Form 8615 age test, although the IRS treats them as a year older and Form 8615 may not be required (for example, born January 1, 2002 and a full-time student, or born January 1, 2008 with earned income over half of support).
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36: "A child born on January 1, 2008, is considered to be age 18 at the end of 2025; a child born on January 1, 2007, is considered to be age 19 at the end of 2025; and a child born on January 1, 2002, is considered to be age 24 at the end of 2025."
findings.why: The question says "you were under 18 at the end of 2025, or 18 with earned income of not more than half your support, or a full-time student 19 to 23" without the January 1 birthday rule. These filers answer YES and are refused even though the ordinary tax computation the tool performs would be correct for them.

question:
Any additional Form 1040 line 16 tax or filing, including any of the following?

A child's unearned income:
- filing Form 8814 (even with no tax)
- Form 8615, required if all of these apply:
  - you had more than $2,700 of unearned income
  - you are required to file
  - you do not file jointly
  - you have a parent who was alive at the end of 2025
  - you were under 18 at the end of 2025, or 18 with earned income of not more than half your support, or a full-time student 19 to 23 with earned income of not more than half your support

Foreign corporations:
- a section 962 election
- Form 8621
- stock you own, directly or indirectly, in a controlled foreign corporation (CFC) or a passive foreign investment company (PFIC), even with nothing to include in income for 2025 (its distributions, dispositions and related adjustments can make the modified AGI of Form 8960 line 13 differ from AGI)

Other:
- Form 4972
- a Form 8978 amount
- recapture of an education credit
- income averaging of farming or fishing income on Schedule J (if you choose it)

findings.situation: A filer whose only Schedule 1 item is a Schedule C business in which they do not materially participate (a passive activity) answers NO, because Schedule C is one of the items 'this tool asks about separately'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 40, Step 2, question 4: "Do any of the following apply for 2025? ... You have income or loss from a passive activity. Yes. Use Worksheet 1 in Pub. 596 to see if you can take the credit."
findings.why: The question names passive activities only through Schedule E and K-1 items and carves Schedule C out, so eic.step2_other computes 'No' and skips Pub. 596 Worksheet 1 for a passive Schedule C activity.

findings.situation: A self-employed Schedule C filer (such as the tour guide in the IRS example) who received qualified tips in the business answers NO, because Schedule C is asked separately, and the tool enters $0 on Schedule 1-A line 5.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 104: "Line 5. Include the qualified tips you and/or your spouse received in the course of a trade or business, but only to the extent the trade or business in which you received the qualified tips has net income." and "You enter $7,000 on Schedule 1-A, line 5."
findings.why: Nothing in the wording makes a tipped Schedule C filer answer YES; the question even says Schedule C and Schedule 1-A are handled elsewhere, yet this screen is what guards the line 5 zero.

findings.situation: A filer with qualified overtime compensation included in Form 1099-NEC box 1 or Form 1099-MISC box 3, reported on Schedule C or as other income the tool asks about, answers NO and the tool enters $0 on Schedule 1-A line 14b.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 108: "Enter on Line 14b only the qualified overtime compensation amount that is included in Form 1099-NEC, box 1, or Form 1099-MISC, box 3."
findings.why: The question never mentions overtime paid on a Form 1099, and the Schedule C carve-out means a truthful NO, so the deduction is silently zeroed instead of refused.

findings.situation: An options or commodities dealer filing Schedule C has section 1256 contract gains or losses (reported through Form 6781 and Schedule D, not Schedule 1) that must be added to earned income, and answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 8, Earned Income Worksheet line 2b: "Options and commodities dealers must add any gain or subtract any loss (in the normal course of dealing in or trading section 1256 contracts) from section 1256 contracts or related property"
findings.why: This adjustment does not arise from any Schedule 1 item other than Schedule C, so the screen is answered NO and, as far as the listing shows, s8812.eiw_3 is figured without it.

findings.situation: A filer with church employee income under $108.28, or a minister with an approved Form 4361 who has only W-2 wages and files no Schedule SE, must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 42, Step 5, question 1: "Are you filing Schedule SE because you were a member of the clergy or you had church employee income of $108.28 or more? ... No. Complete the following worksheet. 1. Enter the amount from Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1z"
findings.why: The question's bullets "church employee income (wages from a church ... that elected exemption ...)" and "income as a minister" have no Schedule SE or $108.28 condition, although the IRS text sends these filers to the ordinary line 1z worksheet the tool computes.

findings.situation: A filer who rents out personal property (for example equipment) as a business reported on Schedule C cannot tell whether the bullet 'rental of personal property' applies to them.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 40, Step 2, question 4: "You are reporting income from the rental of personal property not used in a trade or business."
findings.why: The question drops the IRS qualifier 'not used in a trade or business', so a Schedule C rental business could read it as YES (bullet) or NO (Schedule C is asked separately).

findings.situation: A filer with a Schedule 1 line 8 item (for example gambling winnings, prizes or hobby income) cannot tell from 'the line 8 items asked one by one' whether their item is one the tool asks about separately.
findings.irs_text: f1040 p. 1, line 8: "Additional income from Schedule 1, line 10"
findings.why: The exclusion list does not name the supported line 8 items, so the filer could reasonably answer either YES or NO for the same income.

findings.situation: The help text tells the filer to answer Yes for anything 'other than the items in the parentheses', but the question contains no single parenthetical list of the separately asked items.
findings.irs_text: f1040 p. 1, line 10: "Adjustments to income from Schedule 1, line 26"
findings.why: The only parentheses in the question sit inside YES bullets (Form 4797, Schedule E or K-1, Schedule F, line 8s, solo 401(k)), so a filer following the help literally could treat those refused items as the excluded ones and answer NO.

question:
Any income or adjustment requiring Schedule 1 other than the ones this tool asks about separately, including any of the following?

Income:
- statutory-employee wages or income as a minister, a member of a religious order who has not taken a vow of poverty, or a Christian Science practitioner
- church employee income (wages from a church or qualified church-controlled organization that elected exemption from social security and Medicare taxes)
- a refund or other recovery of an amount you deducted or took a credit for in an earlier year, other than a state or local income tax refund, for example:
  - a refund of general sales tax, real estate tax or personal property tax
  - a refund of mortgage interest in box 4 of Form 1098
  - a reimbursement of medical expenses
  - a payment on a bad debt you deducted
- sales of business property (Form 4797)
- a net operating loss deduction
- rental real estate, royalties, partnerships, S corporations, estates or trusts (Schedule E or a Schedule K-1)
- rental of personal property
- farm income (Schedule F)
- an exclusion of Medicaid waiver payments (Schedule 1 line 8s)

Adjustments:
- other qualified retirement plans for the self-employed (such as a solo 401(k) or other Keogh plan)
- an adjustment on Schedule 1 line 12, 14 or 23

The ones this tool asks about separately:
- business income or loss from Schedule C
- a taxable state or local income tax refund
- alimony under an agreement made before 2019
- unemployment compensation
- the line 8 items asked one by one
- educator expenses
- the HSA deduction
- the deductible part of self-employment tax
- self-employed SEP and SIMPLE contributions
- the self-employed health insurance deduction
- the penalty on early withdrawal of savings
- the IRA deduction
- student loan interest
- jury duty pay you gave your employer

Schedule 1-A deductions are asked separately.

findings.situation: A filer born before January 2, 1961 has income high enough that the enhanced senior deduction phases out to zero, so Schedule 1-A line 38 is $0. The tool's $0 on line 13b would be correct, but the filer answers YES because of their birth date.

findings.situation: A filer whose only Form 4797 amount is a loss or a gain that is not a Part I gain (for example, ordinary gain from Part II) must answer YES, although nothing from that form reaches Schedule D and the zero on line 11 is correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797..."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: Line 11 takes only gain from Form 4797, Part I, while the question counts any gain or loss on the form. The filer is refused on these Schedule D lines even though the tool's zero is correct for them.

findings.situation: A filer with a personal casualty or theft whose Form 4684 result is a loss that does not go to Schedule D, or that is not deductible, is told to count it and answers YES, although lines 4 and 11 are correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count section 1256 contracts and a casualty or theft of property whether you held the property directly or through an entity."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 4: "short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The lines take only amounts that Form 4684 sends to Schedule D, but the question counts a casualty or theft without that limit. The routing of personal casualty losses comes from Form 4684, which is not in the supplied text, so this rests on knowledge of that form.

findings.situation: A filer with a casualty or theft that produced no gain or loss, such as one fully reimbursed at basis, cannot tell whether the event itself counts or only a resulting gain or loss.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count ... a casualty or theft of property"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The second sentence can be read as an instruction to count every such event, or only as clarifying what counts as a gain or loss under the first sentence. The first reading gives YES and the second gives NO, and with no amount for Schedule D the correct answer is NO.

findings.situation: A filer with a fully deferred like-kind exchange on Form 8824 has a realized gain but no recognized gain, and could read "gains" either way.
findings.irs_text: Question: "gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms ... 8824"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The question does not say whether a deferred gain counts or only an amount the form carries to Schedule D. If nothing carries over, line 11 is correctly zero, but a filer could still answer YES because the deferred gain appears on the form.

findings.situation: A filer whose Schedule K-1 shows only net section 1231 gain might answer NO because the K-1 does not label it a capital gain, even if that gain belongs on Form 4797, Part I and reaches line 11.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: The clause "or that belong on" Form 4797 technically requires YES, but the K-1 clause suggests that only items labeled capital count. A filer who does not know this routing could answer NO, and the tool would then wrongly treat line 11 as zero. The routing of K-1 section 1231 gain comes from text not supplied here.

findings.situation: On a joint return, only the spouse received the earlier-year lump-sum payment and wants to make the lump-sum election, but the question asks only whether 'you' want to use it, so the filer can truthfully answer NO and the tool computes line 2 without the spouse's election.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Line 6c: 'Check the box on line 6c if you elect to use the lump-sum election method for your benefits. If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year...'
findings.why: The gate expressly covers a spouse's prior-year payment, but the screening question's 'you' does not say 'you or your spouse'; a NO answer lets the tool compute a joint line 2 that ignores the spouse's election.

findings.situation: A filer has an earlier-year lump-sum payment in 2025 benefits but none of the 2025 benefits are taxable, yet answers YES because the question does not condition the election on benefits being taxable; the tool refuses although the standard worksheet would correctly produce no taxable benefits.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 32, worksheet TIP: 'If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount.'
findings.why: The IRS text makes the election relevant only when some benefits are taxable; the question omits that condition, so it can force a refusal in a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer receives Social Security disability benefits for an injury that was caused by a terrorist attack but was not incurred as a direct result of the attack.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31: “Don’t include in your income any disability payments ... you receive for injuries incurred as a direct result of a terrorist attack directed against the United States (or its allies)...”
findings.why: The question asks only whether the injury is “from” an attack and omits the IRS’s “direct result” requirement, so a filer could answer YES even though the exclusion does not apply and the tool computes line 2 correctly from line 1.

findings.situation: A filer has a current-year 2025 box 12 code H elective deferral to a 501(c)(18)(D) plan, with no year designation.
findings.irs_text: f8880 p. 2, Line 2: 'Contributions to a 501(c)(18)(D) plan'; iw2w3 p. 20: 'Code H—Elective deferrals under section 501(c)(18)(D) tax-exempt organization plan.'
findings.why: The screen asks only about a year after the code, so a code H amount without a year gets a truthful NO; the computed w2.sav_listed line never adds code H even though Form 8880 line 2 includes 501(c)(18)(D) contributions.

findings.situation: A box 12 code G amount is a prior-year USERRA make-up for a nongovernmental or nonelective section 457(b) plan.
findings.irs_text: iw2w3 p. 20: Code G covers 'any governmental or nongovernmental section 457(b)' and requires separate year entry for 'nonelective contributions under a section 457(b) plan'; f8880 p. 2, Line 2 includes only elective deferrals to a 'governmental 457(b)' plan.
findings.why: The question says any box 12 amount with a year, so this filer answers YES and stops, but Form 8880 line 2 and the tool's code G helper count only the governmental 457(b) elective part, so the amount would be correctly excluded.

findings.situation: A filer sees a code D amount of $24.00 displayed as 'D 24' and cannot tell whether the 24 is a year or the dollar amount.
findings.irs_text: iw2w3 p. 20 example: 'D 23 2250.00, D 24 1250.00' shows a year designation is followed by a separate contribution amount.
findings.why: The question's example 'D 24' omits the trailing amount and describes an amount followed by a year, so a two-digit dollar amount can reasonably be read as a year designation.

question: Is any box 12 amount on this W-2 followed by a year, such as "D 24"?
